meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Each question supports two views. The default view explains why the key is correct: 'takeaway' is the clinical rule and each option carries its own rationale. The strategy view uses 'elimination', which names the test-taking strategies in play, walks the options out one at a time, and ends with the verdict. Both views describe the same question, so a student who is short on content can still reason to the answer. All fields are plain text with no markup, so render 'strategy' in italic with CSS rather than expecting tags.

questionTypes.multiple_choice: one correct option; answer is a string
questionTypes.sata: select all that apply; answer is an array and is scored all or nothing

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Client-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the client
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the client beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny client feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates vital signs on a stable client to assistive personnel. She states the task and the client but does not say what readings should be reported back. The assistive personnel records a blood pressure of 86/50 and does not report it. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The assistive personnel is accountable for failing to recognize an abnormal value
options.rationale: Recognizing significance requires interpretation, which is outside that scope.

options.text: Vital signs should never be delegated
options.rationale: Routine data collection on a stable client is within scope.

options.text: The delegation was incomplete, because the nurse did not state what must be reported
options.rationale: Right directions and communication includes the reporting threshold. Without it the delegation is not finished, and the RN retains accountability.

options.text: The delegation was appropriate and the outcome was unforeseeable
options.rationale: A reporting threshold exists precisely because such values are foreseeable.

questions.takeaway: A delegation without a reporting threshold is incomplete, and the RN retains accountability for it.
questions.strategy: The task was delegable and the delegation was not complete. Separate the two before answering. The task itself was appropriate to delegate. Consider what was missing from how it was delegated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Task and client, and no reporting threshold.
Interpretation is outside that scope.
The value was foreseeable and the task is delegable.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the missing piece is what must be reported back.

questions.stem: A nurse with four years of experience on a medical unit is asked by a provider to perform a procedure she has never done. The provider offers to talk her through it, and two colleagues say they have done it before on this unit. The procedure is not addressed in the hospital's policy manual. Which factors determine whether she may legally perform it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act
options.rationale: Scope is the ceiling. If the act does not permit it, nothing else matters.

options.text: Her demonstrated competence to perform it safely
options.rationale: Competence is the floor. Being permitted is not the same as being able.

options.text: Agency policy and procedure
options.rationale: The agency may permit less than the practice act allows, and its policy binds her.

options.text: The provider offering to supervise her
options.rationale: Supervision does not expand legal scope. A provider cannot authorize what her license does not permit.

options.text: The client consenting to her performing it
options.rationale: Consent does not extend scope. A client cannot authorize an act outside your license.

options.text: Whether other nurses on the unit perform it
options.rationale: Common practice is not a legal authority and may itself be outside scope.

questions.takeaway: The nurse practice act sets what is legal, competence sets what is safe for you, and agency policy narrows both further. A Nurse Practice Act is state law overseen by the State Board of Nursing. It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer.
questions.strategy: Options offering permission from a provider, a peer, or the client are attempts to expand scope from outside. None work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. This is a select all that apply, so there is no single best answer. Judge each option separately.
Supervision does not expand legal scope.
Consent does not extend scope.
Common practice is not a legal authority and may itself be outside scope.

elimination.verdict: Keep A, B, C. In a SATA, judge each option as its own true or false statement rather than picking a single best answer.

questions.concept: A Nurse Practice Act is state law overseen by the State Board of Nursing. It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews evidence-based practice with her staff after the unit council proposed revising the fall prevention protocol. Staff have brought a published guideline, their own experience, and the way a neighboring unit does it. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If the unit has always done it this way, that counts as our evidence."
options.rationale: Tradition is precisely what evidence-based practice exists to replace. The three components are research evidence, clinical expertise, and client values.

options.text: "Evidence-based practice combines research, my clinical expertise, and what matters to the client."
options.rationale: Accurate. All three components are required.

options.text: "Client values are part of it, not something we add at the end."
options.rationale: Accurate, and client values is the component most often dropped.

options.text: "A published guideline still has to fit the client in front of me."
options.rationale: Accurate. Standard interventions are individualized to the client.

questions.takeaway: Evidence-based practice is research evidence, clinical expertise, and client values. Tradition is none of the three.
questions.strategy: Any statement that treats how we have always done it as a source of authority is the one to correct.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Research, expertise, client values.
One statement substitutes habit for evidence.
Each of the other three states a component accurately.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: habit is not evidence.

questions.stem: A new graduate is assigned to float to a pediatric unit where she has never worked and has cared for no children since her clinical rotation. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask another nurse to co-sign her documentation
options.rationale: A signature does not supply the competence the assignment requires.

options.text: Accept the assignment and do her best
options.rationale: Leaves the competence gap in place and the clients exposed.

options.text: Refuse to float to the unit
options.rationale: Unfamiliarity alone is not refusal grounds when support can be arranged.

options.text: Inform the charge nurse of her limitations
options.rationale: Competence is her own responsibility, and naming the gap allows a safe assignment to be made.

questions.takeaway: If an assignment is beyond your competence, saying so is part of practicing safely, not an admission of failure.
questions.strategy: The answer is rarely refuse or comply. It is usually communicate and negotiate.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Leaves the competence gap in place and the clients exposed.
Unfamiliarity alone is not refusal grounds when support can be arranged.
A signature does not supply the competence the assignment requires.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: competence is her own responsibility, and naming the gap allows a safe assignment to be made.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked by a provider to perform a procedure she has never done and that is not addressed in her hospital's policy manual. What should she consider first?

options.text: Whether her state nurse practice act permits it
options.rationale: The nurse practice act is state law and it defines the outer limit of what a nurse may legally do. That question comes before competence or policy, because if an act is outside her scope, no amount of training or supervision makes it lawful.

options.text: Whether other nurses on the unit perform it
options.rationale: Common practice on a unit is not a legal authority and may itself be outside scope.

options.text: Whether the provider will supervise her
options.rationale: Supervision does not expand legal scope. The provider cannot authorize what her license does not permit.

options.text: Whether the client consents to her performing it
options.rationale: Consent does not extend scope. A client cannot authorize an act outside your license.

questions.takeaway: Your state nurse practice act sets the legal limit of what you may do. Nobody outside it can raise that limit for you. A Nurse Practice Act is state law overseen by the State Board of Nursing. It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: first. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
Consent does not extend scope.
Common practice on a unit is not a legal authority and may itself be outside scope.
Supervision does not expand legal scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Check the law first: if the act is outside her scope the other questions are irrelevant, and if it is within scope she then addresses competence and asks for training and supervision.

questions.stem: A nurse with three years on a cardiac unit notes her client's telemetry shows a run of eight wide complexes at 140, with a blood pressure of 92/58. She recognizes the rhythm and its significance before the monitor technician calls. Which stage of Benner's model does this reflect?

options.text: Expert
options.rationale: Experts no longer rely on analytic principles at all and act with deep intuitive grasp. Three years and one strong perception fits proficient better.

options.text: Proficient
options.rationale: The proficient nurse perceives the situation as a whole and recognizes when the expected picture does not appear, even without a specific abnormal finding.

options.text: Advanced beginner
options.rationale: Advanced beginners can recognize recurring components but still need help setting priorities and rely on rules.

options.text: Competent
options.rationale: Competent nurses plan deliberately and see actions in terms of long-range goals, but lack the perceptual grasp described here.

questions.takeaway: Benner's levels are sorted by perception, not by years of experience. Benner's stages run novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, expert, describing how clinical judgment develops with experience rather than with knowledge alone.
questions.strategy: Look for what the nurse notices, not how long she has worked. Seeing the whole picture and sensing that it deviates is proficient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Experts no longer rely on analytic principles at all and act with deep intuitive grasp.
Advanced beginners can recognize recurring components but still need help setting priorities and rely on rules.
Competent nurses plan deliberately and see actions in terms of long-range goals, but lack the perceptual grasp described here.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. The proficient nurse perceives the situation as a whole and recognizes when the expected picture does not appear, even without a specific abnormal finding.

questions.concept: Benner's stages run novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, expert, describing how clinical judgment develops with experience rather than with knowledge alone.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed heart failure tells the nurse he does not want the cardiac catheterization his provider has recommended. The nurse arranges a meeting so the client can ask the provider his remaining questions and states the client's concerns clearly during that meeting. Which role is the nurse performing?

options.text: Caregiver
options.rationale: Caregiving is direct care. Nothing physical is being delivered here.

options.text: Advocate
options.rationale: Advocacy protects the client's right to make an informed decision and gives his position a voice in the room.

options.text: Manager
options.rationale: Managing coordinates resources and personnel rather than defending a client's choice.

options.text: Educator
options.rationale: She is not primarily teaching content. She is making sure his voice reaches the decision.

questions.takeaway: Advocacy protects the choice, not the outcome. You defend the client's right to decide even when you would decide differently.
questions.strategy: If the nurse is making sure the client's position is heard by someone with power, that is advocacy.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
She is not primarily teaching content.
Managing coordinates resources and personnel rather than defending a client's choice.
Caregiving is direct care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Advocacy protects the client's right to make an informed decision and gives his position a voice in the room.

questions.stem: A nurse in her second year wants to strengthen her professional practice and reviews her activities with her manager before her annual evaluation. Some describe the care she delivers and others describe how she contributes to the profession. Which 2 activities reflect ANA Standards of Professional Performance?
questions.takeaway: Standards of Practice are the care you deliver. Standards of Professional Performance are how you conduct yourself. ANA Standards of Professional Performance describe how a nurse conducts herself as a professional: quality of practice, education, collaboration, ethics, resource use, and professional practice evaluation. ANA Standards of Practice describe the care a nurse delivers, and they map onto the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, outcomes, planning, implementation, evaluation.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. The four wrong options map directly onto steps of the nursing process, which is the giveaway. Four options correspond to steps of the nursing process.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four options are assessment, planning, or implementation.
Council work and precepting.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Serving on the unit practice council to revise a protocol
options.rationale: Quality of practice, concerning how she contributes to the profession rather than the care she gives.

options.text: Precepting a nursing student on the unit
options.rationale: Education and the professional development of others.

options.text: Assessing a client's pain before and after analgesia
options.rationale: Assessment and evaluation, which are Standards of Practice.

options.text: Writing a plan of care with measurable outcomes
options.rationale: Planning, a Standard of Practice.

options.text: Administering medications accurately and on time
options.rationale: Implementation, a Standard of Practice.

options.text: Collecting a client's history on admission
options.rationale: Assessment, a Standard of Practice.

questions.concept: ANA Standards of Professional Performance describe how a nurse conducts herself as a professional: quality of practice, education, collaboration, ethics, resource use, and professional practice evaluation. ANA Standards of Practice describe the care a nurse delivers, and they map onto the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, outcomes, planning, implementation, evaluation.

questions.topic: Standards of Practice vs Professional Performance
questions.stem: A nurse manager is orienting new graduates and explains that the American Nurses Association describes two different kinds of standards: those covering the care a nurse delivers, and those covering how a nurse conducts herself as a professional. She asks the group to sort several everyday activities between the two. Which activity reflects a Standard of Practice rather than a Standard of Professional Performance?

options.text: Serving on the hospital ethics committee
options.rationale: Ethics is Standard 7, a Professional Performance standard. No individual client is receiving care.

options.text: Reviewing current literature to update a wound care protocol
options.rationale: Evidence-based practice, a Professional Performance standard.

options.text: Precepting a newly licensed nurse
options.rationale: Mentoring falls under education and leadership, both Professional Performance.

options.text: Reassessing a client's pain 30 minutes after an analgesic
options.rationale: This is Standard 6, Evaluation. Standards 1 through 6 are the nursing process and describe care delivered to a client.

questions.takeaway: Standards 1 through 6 are ADPIE. Everything above 6 is about how you conduct yourself in the role. ANA Standards of Practice describe the care a nurse delivers, and they map onto the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, outcomes, planning, implementation, evaluation. The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.
questions.strategy: Ask whether there is a client in the sentence. Committee, policy, mentoring, and self-evaluation are always Professional Performance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Ethics is Standard 7, a Professional Performance standard.
Mentoring falls under education and leadership, both Professional Performance.
Evidence-based practice, a Professional Performance standard.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. This is Standard 6, Evaluation.

The nursing process has five steps in order: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. Each depends on the one before it.

questions.stem: A nurse is considering further study and asks which advanced practice role focuses on managing a caseload of clients with a specific condition, including diagnosis and prescribing, rather than on education or administration. Which role is she describing?

options.text: Nurse practitioner
options.rationale: An advanced practice registered nurse who assesses, diagnoses, and manages client care including prescribing, within her state's regulations.

options.text: Nurse educator
options.rationale: Teaches students or staff rather than managing a clinical caseload.

options.text: Nurse researcher
options.rationale: Generates evidence rather than delivering direct care.

options.text: Nurse administrator
options.rationale: Manages services, staffing, and resources.

questions.takeaway: Advanced practice includes assessment, diagnosis, and management of a caseload, with prescribing governed by state regulation. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Sort the four roles by what the nurse spends her day doing: caring, teaching, managing, or investigating.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Caseload, diagnosis, prescribing.
Teaching and management.
Research generates evidence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the nurse practitioner manages a clinical caseload.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A nurse locates a systematic review supporting early mobility after abdominal surgery. Her client tells her he is frightened of falling and does not want to get up today. Which action best reflects evidence-based practice?

options.text: Follow the systematic review and mobilize the client today
options.rationale: Evidence alone is not EBP. Overriding the client's stated concern drops one of the three required elements.

options.text: Document the refusal and try again tomorrow
options.rationale: This abandons both the evidence and the client's concern rather than addressing either.

options.text: Explore his fear, address it, and plan mobility in a way he will accept
options.rationale: EBP combines best evidence, clinical expertise, and client values. All three have to be present.

options.text: Ask the provider to write an order requiring ambulation
options.rationale: An order does not resolve fear, and using authority to override a client's values is not EBP.

questions.takeaway: Evidence-based practice is evidence plus clinical expertise plus client values. Drop any one and it is no longer EBP. Evidence-based practice combines three things: the best available research evidence, the nurse's clinical expertise, and the client's values and preferences.
questions.strategy: When an option applies research while ignoring what the client said, it is testing whether you remember the third element.

strategies: Negative polarity
Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
This abandons both the evidence and the client's concern rather than addressing either.
Evidence alone is not EBP.
An order does not resolve fear, and using authority to override a client's values is not EBP.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. EBP combines best evidence, clinical expertise, and client values.

questions.concept: Evidence-based practice combines three things: the best available research evidence, the nurse's clinical expertise, and the client's values and preferences.

questions.stem: A nurse administers a dose of insulin that a colleague drew up and left at the bedside during a busy round. The syringe contained 20 units rather than the 10 units ordered, and the client's glucose falls to 42 mg/dL. The colleague states she drew it correctly. Which statement describes the nurse's position?

options.text: The colleague is solely accountable, since she prepared the dose
options.rationale: Preparation and administration are separate acts, and each nurse answers for her own.

options.text: Neither is accountable, since the error was a system failure
options.rationale: Systems contribute and individual accountability remains.

options.text: The provider is accountable for prescribing the medication
options.rationale: The prescription is not what was wrong.

options.text: She is accountable, because the nurse who administers a medication answers for it
options.rationale: Accountability means answering for your own actions. Administering a drug someone else prepared does not transfer responsibility for it.

questions.takeaway: You do not administer a medication another nurse prepared. Accountability follows the act, not the intention. Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.
questions.strategy: Options spreading responsibility to a colleague, a system, or a provider are the pattern here. Accountability is personal. More than one person contributed. Consider who answers for the act described.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She administered it.
Each nurse answers for her own act.
Systems and prescriptions do not remove personal accountability.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the nurse who gives the medication answers for it.

questions.concept: Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing her annual professional review and must list activities that demonstrate how she conducts herself as a professional, rather than the direct client care she provides. Which activities reflect ANA Standards of Professional Performance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serving on the unit practice council to revise a policy

options.text: Performing an admission assessment on a new client

options.text: Precepting a newly licensed nurse
options.rationale: Education and leadership, both Professional Performance.

options.text: Reviewing current literature before updating a protocol
options.rationale: Evidence-based practice, a Professional Performance standard.

options.text: Reassessing pain 30 minutes after an analgesic
options.rationale: Standard 6, Evaluation. This is care delivered to a client.

options.text: Completing an annual self-evaluation of practice
options.rationale: Professional practice evaluation, a Professional Performance standard.

Evidence-based practice combines three things: the best available research evidence, the nurse's clinical expertise, and the client's values and preferences.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her unit's fall rate for the past quarter, finds it above the national benchmark, trials an hourly rounding protocol for 60 days, then re-measures. Which QSEN competency does this best demonstrate?

options.text: Evidence-based practice
options.rationale: EBP is searching outward for what the research says works best. Nothing in the stem describes a literature search.

options.text: Quality improvement
options.rationale: She measured her own unit, changed something, and re-measured. The measure, change, re-measure loop is the signature of QI.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Falls are a safety issue, but safety names the goal rather than the method. The stem describes a method.

options.text: Informatics
options.rationale: She used data, which is not the same as using technology to manage information or support a decision.

questions.takeaway: EBP looks outward at the literature. QI looks inward at your own data. QSEN stands for Quality and Safety Education for Nurses. Six competencies: patient-centered care, teamwork and collaboration, evidence-based practice, quality improvement, safety, and informatics.
questions.strategy: If the nurse read, it is EBP. If she counted and counted again, it is QI. Re-measuring is the distinguishing feature.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. Key word: best. More than one option may be true, so you are ranking them.
EBP is searching outward for what the research says works best.
Falls are a safety issue, but safety names the goal rather than the method.
She used data, which is not the same as using technology to manage information or support a decision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. She measured her own unit, changed something, and re-measured.

questions.concept: QSEN stands for Quality and Safety Education for Nurses. Six competencies: patient-centered care, teamwork and collaboration, evidence-based practice, quality improvement, safety, and informatics.

questions.topic: Nurse Practice Acts and State Boards

options.text: State Nurse Practice Acts define scope and exist to protect the nurse

options.rationale: A task performed in one state may be outside scope in another.

options.text: State Nurse Practice Acts define scope and exist to protect the public
options.rationale: The act protects the public, not the nurse and not the employer.

options.text: Employers define scope through their own policies and procedures
options.rationale: Agency policy narrows practice within the law; it does not define legal scope.

It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer.
questions.strategy: That purpose clause resolves a whole family of questions. When scope, licensure, or discipline is at issue, the answer serving patient safety is correct.

questions.stem: A unit adopts an artificial intelligence tool that flags clients at risk of deterioration. It alerts on a client whose pulse has risen from 74 to 108 and whose blood pressure has fallen to 94/56. Which statement about the nurse's responsibility is accurate?

options.text: Alerts from the tool may be documented in place of nursing assessment
options.rationale: An alert is not an assessment and cannot substitute for one in the record.

options.text: The nurse should defer to the tool when her assessment disagrees with it
options.rationale: Deferring to a tool over your own findings is the failure mode these systems create. Your assessment stands.

options.text: The nurse remains accountable for assessment and for acting on her own findings
options.rationale: Technology supports judgment and does not replace it. The tool does not carry accountability, you do.

options.text: The tool assumes responsibility for identifying deterioration once implemented
options.rationale: A tool never carries accountability. That stays with the licensed nurse.

questions.takeaway: Technology changes the workflow, never the accountability.
questions.strategy: Any option that moves responsibility from the nurse to a device, a protocol, or another person is wrong on principle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Polarity is positive. No priority key word, so look for the single accurate option.
Deferring to a tool over your own findings is the failure mode these systems create.

questions.stem: A charge nurse assigns work on a medical unit staffed by one RN, one LPN, and one assistive personnel. Client A needs an admission assessment, client B needs insulin teaching, client C is stable and due 0900 oral medications, and client D needs evaluation of an ambulation outcome. Which task is appropriate for the LPN?

questions.stem: A nurse notices that four clients in the past two weeks received scheduled 0800 insulin after 0930. She has reported each delay to the charge nurse and each time was told the unit was short-staffed. Which action best demonstrates a Standard of Professional Performance?

options.text: Stay after her shift to give the insulin herself when the unit is short
options.rationale: Self-sacrificing and it conceals the problem. If she absorbs the gap personally the data disappears and the unit never fixes it.

options.text: Ask the provider to change the insulin to a later administration time
options.rationale: Unsafe. Insulin timing follows meals and glucose, not staffing, and this hands a nursing workflow problem to a provider.

options.text: Continue reporting each late dose to the charge nurse as it occurs
options.rationale: She has already done this four times with the same result. Repeating an action that has not worked leaves the situation exactly where it started.

options.text: Bring the pattern of late doses to the unit practice council with a proposed change
options.rationale: Four late doses in two weeks is a pattern, and patterns are system problems. Quality of practice and leadership are both Professional Performance standards.

questions.takeaway: An individual incident goes to the charge nurse. A pattern goes to the practice council, the policy, or QI.

questions.stem: A nurse runs a colorectal screening clinic, distributing fecal occult blood test kits to adults over 45 who have no bowel symptoms. Three results return positive and she arranges colonoscopy referrals. Which level of prevention does the screening clinic represent?

options.text: Quaternary prevention
options.rationale: Not one of the three levels of prevention.

options.text: Tertiary prevention
options.rationale: Tertiary prevention limits damage and restores function in disease that is already established and symptomatic.

options.text: Secondary prevention
options.rationale: Secondary prevention detects disease at an early stage in people without symptoms, so treatment can begin sooner. Screening is its clearest example.

options.text: Primary prevention
options.rationale: Primary prevention acts before disease exists, through immunization, health education, or risk reduction. Screening does not prevent the disease from developing.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents onset. Secondary detects early in people without symptoms. Tertiary limits damage in established disease.
questions.strategy: Ask whether the disease already exists and whether the person has symptoms. Screening a symptom-free population is always secondary prevention, wherever it takes place.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Adults with no bowel symptoms.
Screening detects rather than prevents onset.
Nothing is established or symptomatic yet.
There are three levels, not four.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: detection before symptoms is secondary prevention.

questions.concept: Primary prevention prevents onset. Secondary prevention detects disease early. Tertiary prevention limits damage and restores function in established disease. These are distinct from the levels of care, which describe where in the system the care is delivered.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses fall risk for a 79-year-old admitted after tripping at home. options.text: Decreased muscle strength and balance
options.rationale: Age-related changes common risk factors, along with slow reflexes.

options.text: Recent weight gain
options.rationale: Weight gain alone is not among the fall risk factors. Reduced strength, vision problems, prior falls, vitamin D deficiency, and dementia are.

options.text: A previous fall
options.rationale: A previous fall is the single strongest predictor of another one, because whatever caused the first is usually still there.

options.text: Living with a spouse who can assist
options.rationale: Available assistance reduces risk rather than raising it.

options.text: Adequate hydration
options.rationale: Reversed. Dehydration causes dizziness and confusion and raises risk.

options.text: Dementia or Alzheimer disease
options.rationale: Cognitive impairment affects judgment and awareness of hazards.

questions.takeaway: Falls are multifactorial: strength and balance, vision, cognition, nutrition, hydration, and previous falls.
questions.strategy: Watch for the reversal. Adequate hydration is protective; dehydration is the risk factor, and reading quickly turns one into the other.

options.text: Infection
options.rationale: Not one of the six.

options.text: Immobility
options.rationale: Mobility matters and is part of the 4 Ms, not the I in SPICES.

options.text: Incontinence
options.rationale: SPICES is sleep disorders, problems with eating or feeding, incontinence, confusion, evidence of falls, and skin breakdown.

questions.takeaway: SPICES: sleep, problems eating, incontinence, confusion, evidence of falls, skin breakdown. SPICES screens older adults: Sleep disorders, Problems with eating or feeding, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown.
questions.strategy: Distractors for acronym items are usually real concepts from the same area. Recall the expansion rather than judging which word fits best.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for one letter of the tool.
Mobility belongs to the 4 Ms.
Not part of the tool.
A goal, not a screening item.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Incontinence is abnormal at any age and is screened for deliberately.

questions.concept: SPICES screens older adults: Sleep disorders, Problems with eating or feeding, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown.

questions.stem: A nurse notes an 83-year-old has eaten less than a quarter of each meal for four days, says food tastes of nothing, and eats alone in her room. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Request an order for a nutritional supplement to replace the calories she is missing
options.rationale: May become part of the plan, but not before the cause is understood.

options.text: Assess for causes such as decreased taste and smell, dental problems, constipation, fatigue, and loneliness
options.rationale: Poor intake in older adults has many possible reasons, and the intervention depends on which one applies.

options.text: Document the intake and reassess in one week to see whether the pattern continues
options.rationale: Delays action while nutritional status declines.

options.text: Encourage the client to eat more at each meal
options.rationale: It is established directly that this is not enough. Telling a client to eat more without knowing why does not work.

questions.takeaway: Understand why the client is not eating before you intervene.
questions.strategy: Look past the option that restates the goal. Encourage more intake names the outcome, not the nursing action that achieves it.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Key word best, with poor intake as the finding.
Restates the goal without addressing the cause.
Intervenes before assessing.
Monitors without acting.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B, which covers the contributing factors.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old becomes drowsy and difficult to rouse 40 minutes after receiving hydromorphone 1 mg orally, a dose he has tolerated previously. His daughter mentions he has a glass of whisky most evenings. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Older adults metabolize alcohol more quickly, so intoxication is less likely
options.rationale: Reversed. Metabolism slows with age.

options.text: Substance use resolves as people age out of it and becomes less relevant over time
options.rationale: Explicitly contradicted. This is called the invisible epidemic and contradicts the assumption.

options.text: Substance use is only a concern in clients with a documented history
options.rationale: The premise of screening is that it is missed, not that it is already known.

options.text: Aging slows how the body breaks down alcohol and drugs, so effects arrive faster and last longer
options.rationale: One of the three drivers, alongside life stress and multiple medications.

questions.takeaway: Do not assume substance use disappears with age. Slowed metabolism, life stress, and polypharmacy all contribute. Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.
questions.strategy: Options built on assumptions about a group are usually wrong, especially when they are the assumption as a problem.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Opposite pair, look closely

steps.detail: The question tests an assumption about aging.
The invisible epidemic exists because this assumption is false.
States the physiology backwards.
Only is an absolute and it defeats screening.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Faster onset and longer duration mean the same drink has a bigger effect.

questions.concept: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old takes lisinopril 10 mg, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and furosemide 40 mg, plus ibuprofen, acetaminophen, a herbal sleep supplement, and a stool softener. Which definition does this meet?

options.text: Taking any medication prescribed by more than one provider
options.rationale: Multiple prescribers is a risk factor for duplication, not the definition of polypharmacy.

options.text: Taking five or more medications at the same time, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements
options.rationale: The definition, and the inclusion of over-the-counter products and supplements is the part clients and nurses most often overlook.

options.text: Taking three or more prescription medications daily, regardless of any other products
options.rationale: Below the threshold. Polypharmacy begins at five.

options.text: Taking medications that require cutting tablets in half to achieve the ordered dose
options.rationale: A concern within polypharmacy, but not the definition.

questions.takeaway: Five or more medications at once, counting over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.
questions.strategy: When an option adds a qualifier that widens the definition correctly, it is often the answer. Here the qualifier is that non-prescription products count.

strategies: Favor qualifiers
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The question asks for the definition, not a related risk.
Three is below the threshold.
Describes a contributing factor.
Describes a dosing concern within polypharmacy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Supplements are not regulated the same way as prescriptions, which is why they count.

questions.concept: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.

questions.stem: A nurse visits a family whose 86-year-old relative has recently moved in with them. They ask what they should expect as she ages and what should prompt a call. Which statement by a family member indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If she becomes confused suddenly, I should call, because that is not normal aging."
options.rationale: Accurate. Sudden confusion is a red flag and delirium is potentially reversible.

options.text: "Her skin will get thinner and drier, and that is expected."
options.rationale: Accurate. Reduced skin resilience and moisture are expected integumentary changes.

options.text: "If she starts leaking urine, that is just part of getting older."
options.rationale: Urinary incontinence is not an expected change of aging. It is common in older adults and it is assessed rather than accepted, because the causes are often treatable.

options.text: "She may need more light to read than she used to."
options.rationale: Accurate. Sensory changes of aging include reduced acuity in lower light.

questions.takeaway: Expected changes are gradual. Incontinence and sudden confusion are not expected at any age.
questions.strategy: The trap is that the wrong statement sounds compassionate. Accepting incontinence as aging is what stops anyone looking for the cause.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skin, vision, and reaction time are expected.
Incontinence is abnormal at any age.
Sudden confusion is correctly identified as not normal.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: incontinence is assessed, not accepted.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old living alone takes eight medications including furosemide 40 mg each morning and zolpidem 10 mg at bedtime. She has fallen twice in six weeks, both times at night. Which observation most warrants further teaching?

options.text: The client cannot open the bottles and asks a neighbor to do it each week
options.rationale: Physical barriers cause missed doses in clients who understand their regimen perfectly. Ability to open bottles, use pill planners, and measure liquids is part of the assessment.

options.text: The client uses a weekly pill organizer filled at the start of each week
options.rationale: An intervention that reduces risk.

options.text: The client reads the label with reading glasses
options.rationale: Using glasses is an adaptation that supports safe administration.

options.text: The client keeps a written list of medications and brings it to appointments
options.rationale: Supports accuracy and helps with reconciliation.

questions.takeaway: Much of medication safety in older adults is physical rather than cognitive.
questions.strategy: Three of these options are adaptations that reduce risk. Find the one describing a barrier, not a strategy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which finding increases risk.
Glasses support safe reading.
An organizer reduces error.
A list supports reconciliation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Dependence on a neighbor to open bottles means doses are missed when the neighbor is away.

questions.scenario: An 82-year-old has been in a rehabilitation unit for three weeks following a hip fracture. Review the functional record.
questions.stem: An 82-year-old has been in a rehabilitation unit for three weeks after a hip fracture. The nurse reviews the functional record, which tracks ambulation, meals eaten, weight, and assistance with dressing across the admission. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The client is progressing as expected for her age
options.rationale: Every measure is moving the wrong way. Age does not explain a three-week decline.

options.text: The client is experiencing functional decline and requires comprehensive assessment
options.rationale: Declining mobility, intake, weight, and self-care together suggest a geriatric syndrome, which involves multiple factors and requires comprehensive assessment.

options.text: The client should be discharged since rehabilitation has plateaued
options.rationale: This is not a plateau, it is a decline, and discharging without assessment abandons the problem.

options.text: The weight loss is the only finding requiring follow-up
options.rationale: Isolating one measure misses that four are moving together, which is the point of the trend.

questions.takeaway: When several measures decline together, think geriatric syndrome and assess comprehensively.
questions.strategy: Trend items reward reading across rows as well as down columns. One declining measure is a finding; four declining together is a pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All four measures worsen across three weeks.
Decline is not expected progress.
A decline is not a plateau.
Four measures are moving, not one.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Poor intake, weight loss, and reduced mobility feed each other.

questions.stem: A home health nurse teaches an 81-year-old about fall prevention after two falls in the past six weeks. The client describes the changes she plans to make around the house and to her routine. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will move the rugs out of the hallway."
options.rationale: Accurate. Scatter rugs are an environmental hazard.

options.text: "I will ask about taking my water pill earlier in the day."
options.rationale: Accurate. Diuretic timing drives the night-time toileting when falls happen.

options.text: "I will replace the bulb at the top of the stairs."
options.rationale: Accurate. Adequate lighting, especially at night, is a intervention.

options.text: "I will stay in bed more so I do not risk falling again."
options.rationale: Immobility causes deconditioning, which weakens the strength and balance that prevent the next fall. The answer to fall risk is more safe movement, not less movement.

questions.takeaway: The answer to fall risk is more safe movement, not less.
questions.strategy: Reducing activity feels like the safe choice and it produces the weakness that causes the next fall. Watch for options that reduce risk by reducing life.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement to correct.
Rugs, diuretic timing, and lighting are all correct.
One statement buys safety with deconditioning.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: bed rest is not fall prevention.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old is moving from the home she has lived in for forty years into an assisted living facility. Since arriving three days ago she has been anxious, mildly confused in the evenings, and has asked repeatedly when she is going home. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Maintain the client's usual routines where possible and include them in decisions
options.rationale: Relocation is a major life stressor involving loss of familiar surroundings, change in routine, loss of control, and separation from relationships. Maintaining routine and including the client restores some control.

options.text: Explain that anxiety after a move is normal and will pass
options.rationale: Dismisses the experience and offers nothing.

options.text: Limit visitors for the first week so the client can settle
options.rationale: Increases isolation at the moment connection matters most.

options.text: Request a sedative to manage the anxiety until she settles into the new surroundings
options.rationale: Medication for an environmental and emotional problem, and sedatives increase fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Relocation stress is treated with routine, inclusion in decisions, and orientation, not with medication.
questions.strategy: When the cause of distress is a loss of control, look for the option that gives some control back.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: The stressor is a move, with anxiety and mild confusion.
Deepens the separation from relationships.
Normalizes without helping.
Adds fall risk and treats the wrong problem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Promote orientation as well.

questions.stem: An older adult has had a gradual decline in memory and the ability to manage finances over three years, with no change in alertness. Which condition does this pattern suggest?

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: Losing the ability to manage finances is a functional decline, not an expected change.

options.text: Dementia
options.rationale: Progressive, chronic cognitive decline over years, with alertness preserved.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Depression presents with mood changes, withdrawal, and loss of interest rather than a three-year decline in instrumental function.

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: Delirium is acute and fluctuating, with inattention and altered consciousness. Nothing here is acute.

questions.takeaway: Delirium is acute and fluctuating. Dementia is progressive and chronic. Depression is mood, withdrawal, and loss of interest. Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.
questions.strategy: Sort the three Ds by time course first. Onset separates them faster than symptom lists do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three years, gradual, alertness unchanged.
Delirium is acute with altered consciousness.
No mood or interest changes are described.
Loss of independent function is not expected aging.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Progressive decline interfering with function is dementia.

questions.concept: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an 84-year-old admitted two days ago with a hip fracture. The daughter reports her mother became confused overnight and does not recognize the room. Which conclusion by the nurse is correct?

options.text: Confusion is expected at this age and requires reassurance only
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis. Treating a new change as normal aging is the error to avoid.

options.text: The daughter should be asked to stay overnight to reorient her mother
options.rationale: Family presence may help, but it does not investigate why the change happened.

options.text: Sudden confusion is a red flag requiring assessment for an underlying cause
options.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag. Hospital-acquired delirium is common two to three days after admission, and infection, poor oxygenation, medications, and acute illness are contributing factors.

options.text: The confusion indicates the onset of dementia and should be documented as a new baseline
options.rationale: Dementia is progressive and chronic. An overnight change is acute and fits delirium.

questions.takeaway: Expected age-related changes are gradual. Sudden change is a red flag and gets investigated. Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives you a time frame, use it. Years suggests aging or dementia. Hours or days suggests an acute cause.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Onset is overnight, on day two of a hospital admission.
Attributes a sudden change to age.
Dementia does not begin overnight.
Comforting, but it skips finding the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C. Think delirium and investigate the cause.

questions.concept: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and potentially reversible, with altered consciousness. Dementia is chronic and progressive with clear consciousness. Depression develops over weeks with intact consciousness.

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 86-year-old after a fall at home. On assessment she finds thin dry skin, slower reaction time during transfers, and reduced hearing for high-pitched sounds. Her daughter reports her mother became confused overnight. Which findings require further nursing assessment rather than being attributed to normal aging? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sudden confusion
options.rationale: A red flag. Expected changes are gradual.

options.text: Slower reaction time
options.rationale: Listed as a change that may occur with normal aging.

options.text: A new unexplained fall
options.rationale: A red flag, and a fall is always a clinical clue.

options.text: Changes in sensory perception
options.rationale: Listed as a change that may occur with normal aging.

questions.takeaway: Gradual changes are expected with aging. Sudden confusion and a new unexplained fall are not, and both need assessment rather than attribution to age.
questions.strategy: Sort by how fast it appeared. Anything sudden or new is assessed; anything gradual and symmetrical is usually expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two findings are gradual and two are new.
Slower reaction time and sensory change are expected with aging.
Overnight confusion and a fall at home.

elimination.verdict: A and C are selected: both appeared suddenly.

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 81-year-old using the 4 Ms framework. He takes nine medications, scores 22 of 30 on cognitive screening, walks 20 feet with a frame, and states his priority is returning to his allotment. Which element does his stated priority represent?

options.text: Reviewing the client's medication list for duplication
options.rationale: That is Medication.

options.text: Asking the client what goals are most important to them for this admission
options.rationale: What Matters is the client's goals and preferences, and it is placed first in the framework deliberately.

options.text: Screening for delirium, dementia, and depression using a validated cognitive tool
options.rationale: That is Mentation.

options.text: Assessing gait and transfer safety, which determines how much assistance he requires
options.rationale: That is Mobility.

questions.takeaway: The 4 Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility. What Matters comes first. The 4 Ms framework for age-friendly care: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility.
questions.strategy: Each distractor here is one of the other Ms. Match the action to the right M rather than judging which is most important.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question names one specific M.
Medication.
Mentation.
Mobility.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. patient-centered care means asking what matters to this person.

questions.concept: The 4 Ms framework for age-friendly care: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old is transferred to a restorative care setting after hospitalization for pneumonia. She walked independently before admission and now needs assistance. She is expected to regain her previous level of function. What is the goal of this care?

options.text: Sustaining a need that is not expected to change
options.rationale: That describes continuing care.

options.text: Diagnosing and treating a new illness that has developed during the admission
options.rationale: Secondary care.

options.text: Regaining function lost during the illness so she can return to her previous level
options.rationale: Restorative care aims at recovery, as distinct from continuing care which sustains a need that will not end.

options.text: Preventing illness before it occurs so that hospitalization is avoided altogether
options.rationale: Preventive care.

questions.takeaway: Restorative care aims at recovery. Continuing care sustains. Restorative care aims at regaining function after illness or injury. Continuing care sustains a need that is not expected to end.
questions.strategy: The expected trajectory decides it. Ask whether the goal is regaining something or sustaining someone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Expected to regain her previous level.
Continuing care sustains.
Treatment and prevention.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: restorative care aims at recovery, as distinct from continuing care which sustains a need that will not end.

questions.concept: Restorative care aims at regaining function after illness or injury. Continuing care sustains a need that is not expected to end.

questions.stem: During an admission assessment, a caregiver answers every question directed at the older adult and becomes irritated when the nurse asks to speak with the client alone. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Speak with the client privately and assess for signs of abuse or neglect
options.rationale: The nurse's role is to observe, assess, ask questions, document, and report. Private assessment is how the client is given the chance to speak.

options.text: Ask the caregiver to explain the client's living arrangements in detail
options.rationale: Continues gathering information through the person who may be the source of harm.

options.text: Document that the caregiver is attentive and involved in the client's daily care
options.rationale: Reframes a red flag as a strength. A caregiver controlling communication is a warning sign.

options.text: Report the caregiver to adult protective services immediately without further assessment
options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters, but reporting follows assessment. One behavior alone is not yet a finding.

questions.takeaway: A caregiver controlling communication is a red flag. Assess the client privately.
questions.strategy: When someone is speaking for the client, the answer is usually to create a private opportunity for the client to speak.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: The behavior described appears on the red flag list.
Recasts a warning sign as a positive.
Keeps the caregiver as the source of information.
Skips the assessment step.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Report according to requirements once you have assessed.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that contribute to this client's risk of falling.
questions.takeaway: Falls are multifactorial: previous falls, medications, toileting, vision, and the environment.
questions.strategy: Two findings in this note are protective rather than hazardous. Read each for whether it raises or lowers the chance of a fall. Two findings reduce rather than create risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings raise risk.
Grab bars and family contact.
Medication, toileting, and environment interact at night.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s4.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Home visit. Client is 84, lives alone in a two-story house. Daughter visits weekends. Since the last visit six weeks ago the client has fallen twice, once on the stairs and once at night going to the bathroom. Reports getting up three to four times nightly to void. Takes a nightly sedative, a morning diuretic, an antihypertensive, two over-the-counter analgesics, a herbal sleep supplement and a stool softener. Reports cutting one tablet in half because the dose seemed high. Wears bifocals. Scatter rugs throughout the hallway. Burned-out bulb at the top of the stairs. Grab bars present in the bathroom. Weight down 4 kg since the last visit. VS: T 36.6 C; HR 76; BP lying 142/84, standing 118/68.

segments.text: Two falls in the past six weeks
segments.rationale: A previous fall is the strongest predictor of another, because whatever caused the first is usually still there.

segments.text: Nightly sedative and a morning diuretic
segments.rationale: The two specified medication classes for fall risk. One slows reflexes and clouds judgment, the other drops pressure on standing.

segments.text: Getting up three to four times nightly to void
segments.rationale: Night-time toileting in poor light is when falls happen, and the diuretic timing is driving it.

segments.text: Scatter rugs and a burned-out bulb at the top of the stairs
segments.rationale: Correct environmental hazards, and the location of the bulb makes it the worst possible placement.

segments.text: Grab bars present in the bathroom
segments.rationale: A safety measure already in place, so it reduces risk rather than creating it.

segments.text: Daughter visits at weekends
segments.rationale: Social contact and support. It does not itself create fall risk.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: A fall is a clinical clue. Ask why the client fell.
questions.strategy: Every contributor in this note can be changed. Options that relocate her or restrict her fluids treat the fall as a fixed fact.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Five contributors present at once.
Decides before assessing.
Risks dehydration and misses the timing.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: The client's situation is best described as [[1]], and the nurse's first action is to [[2]].

options.text: multifactorial fall risk
options.rationale: Previous falls, two fall-risk medication classes, nocturia, bifocals, and environmental hazards all present together.

options.text: a single environmental hazard
options.rationale: The rugs and the bulb matter and they are one contributor among several.

options.text: an expected consequence of aging
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis, and every contributor here is modifiable.

options.text: a neurological emergency
options.rationale: Nothing in the note describes acute neurological change.

options.text: assess gait, balance, vision, toileting, and the home environment
options.rationale: A fall is a clinical clue. The assessment looks for the modifiable reasons behind it rather than treating the fall as the whole event.

options.text: recommend she move to assisted living
options.rationale: A placement decision before anyone has established what is causing the falls.

options.text: advise her to stop drinking fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls, and it does not address the diuretic timing.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: For each proposed action, determine whether it is INDICATED or NOT INDICATED for this client.
questions.takeaway: The answer to fall risk is more safe movement, not less movement. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Two actions here reduce her risk by reducing her life. Both create deconditioning or overstep scope. One proposed action reduces falls by reducing movement. Consider what that costs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rugs, lighting, medications, and toileting.
Outside nursing scope and irrelevant to falls.
Deconditioning worsens the underlying problem.

elimination.verdict: Four actions are indicated and two are not.

rows.text: Secure or remove the scatter rugs
rows.rationale: A effective intervention, and the hallway is where she walks at night.

rows.text: Replace the bulb at the top of the stairs
rows.rationale: Adequate lighting especially at night is specified, and the top of a staircase is the worst place for darkness.

rows.text: Review the medication list with the provider, including the over-the-counter products
rows.rationale: She takes seven products including a sedative and a diuretic, and polypharmacy counts non-prescription items.

rows.text: Advise her to stop taking the stool softener without discussing it
rows.rationale: Discontinuing a medication is outside nursing scope and it addresses nothing in her fall risk.

rows.text: Discuss moving the diuretic to the morning and earlier if possible
rows.rationale: Diuretic timing drives the nocturia that has her walking at night.

rows.text: Recommend she remain in bed at night and use a bedpan
rows.rationale: Immobility causes deconditioning, which weakens the strength and balance that prevent the next fall.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home
questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: For each finding at the follow-up visit, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with the first visit, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: A plan can be working on most measures while one continues to worsen and another appears for the first time.
questions.strategy: Four rows improved and it would be easy to stop reading. The two that matter clinically are the ones that did not. One finding has worsened and one has no baseline. Both matter more than the four that improved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five measures were recorded at the first visit.
Weight is still falling.
Acuity was never assessed.

elimination.verdict: Four improved, one declined, one new finding.

questions.baseline: First visit: two falls in six weeks, voiding three to four times nightly, scatter rugs present, standing BP 118/68 from lying 142/84, weight down 4 kg.

rows.text: No falls in the past six weeks
rows.rationale: Down from two.

rows.text: Voiding once nightly
rows.rationale: The diuretic was moved to the morning.

rows.text: Rugs removed and stair bulb replaced
rows.rationale: Both specified hazards addressed.

rows.text: Standing BP 128/76 from lying 138/82
rows.rationale: The orthostatic drop has narrowed from 24 points to 10 after the medication review.

rows.text: Weight down a further 2 kg
rows.rationale: Continued unintended weight loss, and it was already falling at the first visit. Nutrition is a fall risk factor through weakness and vitamin D and calcium status.

rows.text: Reports her vision has become blurred in the past week
rows.rationale: Her bifocals were noted at the first visit but acuity was never assessed, so there is no baseline. New blurred vision requires assessment in its own right.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with recurrent falls at home

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: Two fall-risk medication classes acting at night, producing the trip she takes in the dark.
questions.strategy: Several contributors are real. Rank by what can change this week and what was present at the moment she fell.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: At night, going to the bathroom.
The diuretic, taken in the morning but acting through the evening.
The staircase and the weekend support cannot change this week.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: Of the contributors identified, the one the nurse can address soonest with the greatest effect is [[1]], and the reason is [[2]].

options.text: the timing of the diuretic and the nightly sedative
options.rationale: Both are fall-risk medication classes and both act at night, which is when she fell.

options.text: the two-story layout of the house
options.rationale: A structural feature that cannot be changed quickly.

options.text: the weekend-only family support
options.rationale: A support gap rather than a direct cause of the falls.

options.text: they produce the night-time toileting in poor light where the falls happened
options.rationale: The diuretic drives the nocturia and the sedative slows her reflexes when she gets up.

options.text: medication changes require no discussion with the provider
options.rationale: Adjusting or stopping a medication sits with the prescriber.

options.text: her age is the main contributor

Stopping a product is the prescriber's.
