chapters.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Clients

questions.stem: A nurse educator explains that care for LGBTQ+ clients is framed by two concepts drawn from the ANA Code of Ethics, with sexuality and gender identity treated as interrelated. Which two concepts are these?

options.text: patient-centered care and health equity
options.rationale: The two priority concepts, with sexuality and gender identity and expression as interrelated concepts.

options.text: Safety and infection control
options.rationale: Important elsewhere, not the framing concepts here.

options.text: Mobility and nutrition
options.rationale: Priority concepts belonging to older adult care.

options.text: Perfusion and gas exchange
options.rationale: Physiological concepts unrelated to this framing.

questions.takeaway: patient-centered care and health equity, framed by the ANA Code of Ethics. Four distinct concepts: sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation. None predicts another. A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles all members of a profession accept. The Code of Ethics for Nursing rests on advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality.
questions.strategy: Priority concept items reward recognizing which framework a concept belongs to. Two belong to different frameworks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for this framing.
Belongs elsewhere.
Belongs to older adult care.
Physiological concepts.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. The ANA Code frames it: compassion, respect for dignity, and regard for the worth of every client.

questions.concept: Four distinct concepts: sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation. None predicts another. A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles all members of a profession accept. The Code of Ethics for Nursing rests on advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality.

questions.stem: A clinic finds that several LGBTQ+ clients have not returned after an initial visit, and two describe feeling judged by staff. The nurse manager reviews the evidence on why this population experiences worse health outcomes than the general population. Which factor is a contributor?

options.text: A reluctance among providers to prescribe medication
options.rationale: Not a contributing factor.

options.text: Lower rates of health insurance in all LGBTQ+ populations
options.rationale: Not one of the drivers.

options.text: A biological predisposition to chronic disease
options.rationale: Not a cause. The disparities are driven by how care is delivered and experienced.

options.text: Lack of LGBTQ+ affirmation in health care, which discourages people from using services
options.rationale: Occurs alongside bias and discrimination during care and heterocentric policies. Care avoided is care not received.

questions.takeaway: The disparities come from bias, heterocentric policies, and lack of affirmation, not from anything intrinsic to clients.
questions.strategy: When a stem asks about a health disparity, look for a system or care-delivery cause rather than a client-level one.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for a contributor.
Locates the cause in the client rather than the system.
Not a contributing factor.
Not a contributing factor.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Avoidance of care is itself an outcome of non-affirming environments.

questions.stem: A teenager arrives at a clinic and the intake form asks for mother's name and father's name. The receptionist reacts visibly when the teenager explains they have two mothers. Which understanding does this illustrate?

options.text: Front desk staff are not part of the care team
options.rationale: The opposite. Their interaction shaped the client's experience of the whole visit.

options.text: Harm often happens before the clinical encounter begins
options.rationale: A heterocentric form combined with a visible reaction exposed the client in a waiting room, before any clinician was involved.

options.text: Documentation requirements must take priority over client comfort
options.rationale: The form could be written differently without losing any information.

options.text: The teenager should have completed the form differently
options.rationale: Places responsibility on the client for a form that did not fit their family.

questions.takeaway: The form and the front desk are part of the care. Harm can happen before a nurse is involved.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes a non-clinical interaction, ask what it reveals about the system rather than about the individuals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The events occur at intake, before any clinical encounter.
The form can be revised without losing data.
Reception staff shape the client experience.
Blames the client for the form.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Use forms that ask for parent or guardian names, and take information without visible reaction.

questions.stem: A nurse feels uncomfortable caring for a transgender client and asks to be reassigned. The unit is short-staffed and no colleague is free to swap. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask a colleague to take the assignment instead
options.rationale: Avoidance, and it leaves the client with whichever nurse is available rather than with competent care.

options.text: Avoid discussing anything related to gender during the encounter
options.rationale: Omits relevant assessment and models discomfort.

options.text: Reflect on the personal biases and assumptions behind the discomfort, and seek education
options.rationale: Self-reflection is a domain: examine assumptions, cultivate accountability, and commit to self-awareness and growth, alongside educating yourself.

options.text: Ask the client to explain their identity so the nurse can learn
options.rationale: Places the burden of education on the client during their own care.

questions.takeaway: Self-reflection first, then education. Not avoidance, and not asking the client to teach you.
questions.strategy: Discomfort in a nurse is answered by self-examination and learning. Options that transfer the work to the client or a colleague are wrong.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: The nurse's discomfort is the finding.
Avoids rather than addresses.
Makes the client the teacher.
Omits assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C, which pairs self-reflection with ongoing education.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to care for a client scheduled for gender-affirming surgery and reviews the range of procedures that fall under that heading, recognizing that transitioning is individualized and no client has all of them. Which procedures are included in the range of gender-affirming surgeries? Select all that apply.

options.text: Masculinizing chest reconstruction, also called top surgery
options.rationale: Masculinizing chest reconstruction sits within the range of gender-affirming surgeries, and no client has all of them since transitioning is individualized.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting
options.rationale: A cardiac procedure unrelated to gender-affirming care.

options.text: Cholecystectomy
options.rationale: Gallbladder surgery, unrelated to gender-affirming care.

options.text: Genital surgical procedures, also called bottom surgery
options.rationale: Genital surgical procedures are one option in the range, and many transgender clients never have them.

options.text: Appendectomy
options.rationale: An abdominal procedure unrelated to gender-affirming care.

options.text: Gynecologic surgery
options.rationale: Gynecologic surgery belongs to the range, and a client who has had it may still require screening based on remaining anatomy.

questions.takeaway: The range spans gynecologic, chest, genital, and facial procedures. Not every client has any of them. Gender-affirming care is recognized as medically necessary rather than cosmetic. Transitioning is individualized and no client has every procedure in the range.
questions.strategy: One clearly unrelated option in a select-all is a gift. Take it out and evaluate the rest against the correct list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which procedures fall in the correct range.
A cardiac procedure, unrelated to gender affirmation.

elimination.verdict: A, D and F are selected.

questions.concept: Gender-affirming care is recognized as medically necessary rather than cosmetic. Transitioning is individualized and no client has every procedure in the range.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 31-year-old transgender man about his ongoing health screening before discharge. He takes testosterone, has had chest reconstruction, and retains a cervix. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "My chest surgery is relevant to how you plan my care after this procedure."
options.rationale: Accurate. Surgical history affects positioning and assessment.

options.text: "Not everyone who is transgender has the same surgeries."
options.rationale: Accurate. Transitioning is individualized and no client has every procedure in the range.

options.text: "Since I take testosterone, I do not need cervical screening any more."
options.rationale: Screening follows the anatomy that is present, not the gender marker or the hormone regimen. Testosterone does not remove the organ or the risk.

options.text: "I still need cervical screening because I have a cervix."
options.rationale: Accurate. Anatomy determines screening.

questions.takeaway: Screen the anatomy that is present. Hormone therapy does not remove an organ or its risk.

Treat each option as true or false

questions.stem: A nursing student uses the terms sex, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation as though they mean the same thing. Which statement reflects correct understanding of these four concepts?

options.rationale: All four concepts vary independently. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three.

options.text: Sexual orientation is determined by sex assigned at birth
options.rationale: No such relationship exists.

questions.takeaway: Four separate concepts. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other three. Four distinct concepts: sex assigned at birth, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation. None predicts another.

questions.stem: A nursing student caring for a client with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria asks whether gender-affirming care means surgery, and whether it is elective. The nurse explains what the term actually covers and how it is regarded clinically. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.rationale: It involves a wide range of services including mental health care, medical care, and social services.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old arrives for a scheduled colonoscopy. The chart lists a legal name he does not use and a gender marker that does not match how he presents. He has not returned for two previous appointments. Which action is appropriate?

questions.stem: A midwifery unit reviews why same-sex and transgender parents report poorer birthing experiences than other families using the same service. options.rationale: Bias during care shapes whether a parent is treated as a parent, and it is a documented driver of poorer birthing outcomes.

options.text: Universal access to affirming postpartum care
options.rationale: Access is inconsistent, which is part of why outcomes are poorer.

options.rationale: Length of stay is not among the contributors to poorer reported experiences.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old three months into hormone therapy under specialist supervision asks the nurse what benefit to expect beyond physical changes. Which statement is accurate?

questions.stem: A nurse finds the unit's intake forms offer only male and female, and staff have had no training on affirming language. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: The difference is a matter of personal style with no clinical consequence
options.rationale: Caring behaviors affect trust, disclosure, and whether a client reports symptoms, all of which have clinical consequences.

options.text: Caring involves both what nurses do and how they do it, and the how shapes the client's experience
options.rationale: the central claim, and it is why caring is taught alongside technical skill rather than instead of it.

options.text: The first nurse was more efficient and therefore delivered safer care
options.rationale: Speed is not safety, and nothing in the stem suggests a safety difference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The measurements are stated to be the same.

questions.stem: A nurse discusses professional boundaries with a colleague after a client asked for her personal phone number at discharge. The colleague describes how she handles requests from clients and families. Which statement by the colleague indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If a client asks for my personal number after discharge, refusing would seem cold."
options.rationale: Declining warmly and explaining the professional boundary is the appropriate response. Personal contact creates an obligation inside a professional relationship.

options.text: "Sitting down with a client who is crying is a real nursing intervention."
options.rationale: Accurate. Presence is being physically and emotionally available.

options.text: "Advocating for a family member to stay overnight can be appropriate."
options.rationale: Accurate. Advocacy explores what the request means rather than applying the rule reflexively.

options.text: "Sharing my own family's illness at length moves the focus onto me."
options.rationale: Accurate. Self-disclosure at length shifts the focus from the client.

questions.takeaway: Caring is warm and bounded. Declining warmly and explaining why maintains both.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement treats a boundary as unkindness. The test is whose needs the action serves.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
Personal contact serves the relationship, not the care.

questions.stem: A nurse sits with a client who has just been told her treatment has not worked. The client falls silent, then says she does not know what to tell her children. Which nurse responses open the conversation rather than closing it? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Silence gives her room to continue, and presence is being physically and emotionally available.

options.text: "Tell me what worries you most about that conversation."
options.rationale: An open invitation that follows her rather than directing her.

options.text: "It sounds as though telling them feels harder than the news itself."
options.rationale: Names the feeling, which is what therapeutic communication does.

options.text: "Children are more resilient than we give them credit for."
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it closes the subject she has just opened.

options.text: "You should tell them as soon as possible."
options.rationale: Giving advice, which replaces her judgment with the nurse's.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic communication opens the conversation rather than closing it, and it names feelings. Presence is being physically and emotionally available to a client, and sitting down is what signals you are not about to leave.
questions.strategy: Reassurance and advice both feel helpful and both end the exchange. That is why they are the standard wrong answers.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: A specific fear about her children.
It dismisses the fear.
It replaces her judgment.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options are kind actions that all involve leaving or redirecting. Several unselected options are kind and involve leaving.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: She is crying and not answering.
It closes the conversation.
Deferring and handing on both remove you.

options.text: Sit down with her and remain available without filling the silence
options.rationale: Being physically and emotionally available. Sitting signals you are not about to leave.

options.rationale: Follows her rather than directing her, and it opens the conversation rather than closing it.

chapters.title: Caring for Clients with Chronic Illness

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 68-year-old newly diagnosed with heart failure before discharge. He describes what he expects over the coming months and how he plans to manage at home. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Most of managing this happens at home, in between my clinic appointments."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why self-management support matters.

options.text: "Once my swelling and breathlessness settle, I will be back to how I was before."
options.rationale: Chronic illness is managed rather than cured. Symptoms can improve while the condition and its effects on roles and daily life continue.

options.text: "Giving up my allotment has affected me as much as the symptoms themselves have."
options.rationale: Accurate. Chronic illness affects roles and self-perception, not only the body.

options.text: "I will weigh myself every morning and report any sudden gain to the clinic."
options.rationale: Accurate, and weight gain is an early marker of fluid retention.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it, and chronic illness is managed rather than cured.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement expects resolution. Chronic means the condition persists even when the symptoms do not.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken expectation.
Back to how I was assumes resolution.
Monitoring, self-management, and role loss are all accurate.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: chronic illness is managed, not resolved.

questions.stem: A practice nurse is planning the year's work for clients with long-term conditions and wants to focus on preventing complications rather than responding to them. She reviews which activities fall within the nursing role. Which nursing actions support health promotion and prevention for clients with chronic illness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Screening for diseases
options.rationale: Screening finds disease before symptoms appear, which is when intervention changes the trajectory rather than managing damage.

options.text: Treating each acute episode as it presents
options.rationale: Episodic treatment is the approach chronic care redesign moves away from.

options.text: Promoting adherence
options.rationale: Adherence determines whether a plan has any effect, and promoting it means finding the barrier rather than repeating the instruction.

options.text: Discouraging clients from asking questions about their condition
options.rationale: Undermines self-management, which depends on the client understanding their condition.

options.text: Limiting client questions to scheduled appointments
options.rationale: Restricting questions undermines the self-management being built.

options.text: Encouraging appropriate screening and prevention efforts
options.rationale: Encouraging screening extends the nurse's role beyond the individual visit into prevention at a population level.

questions.takeaway: Screening, education, adherence, and self-management education. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: A distractor that reduces the client's understanding is always wrong where self-management is the goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which actions support prevention.
Reduces the understanding self-management requires.

elimination.verdict: A, C and F are selected.

questions.scenario: A 77-year-old with heart failure, arthritis, and type 2 diabetes attends clinic monthly. The family attributes recent changes to getting older.
questions.stem: A 77-year-old with heart failure, arthritis, and type 2 diabetes attends clinic monthly. The nurse reviews three months of records showing weight, reported fatigue, ankle swelling, and walking distance. The family attributes the changes to getting older. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The changes are consistent with normal aging in a client of this age
options.rationale: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness, which is exactly why this explanation is rejected.

options.text: The pattern suggests worsening heart failure and requires assessment and provider notification
options.rationale: Rising weight, increasing fatigue, new ankle swelling, and falling exercise tolerance together indicate fluid retention.

options.text: The weight gain reflects improved nutritional intake
options.rationale: Weight gain with edema and reduced tolerance is fluid, not nutrition.

options.text: The reduced walking distance is explained by arthritis alone
options.rationale: Arthritis does not explain the weight gain or the edema. Attributing everything to one condition is the multimorbidity trap.

questions.takeaway: Overlapping conditions mask each other. Read the measures together rather than assigning each to a diagnosis. Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.
questions.strategy: In multimorbidity, the temptation is to explain each finding with a different existing condition. Ask instead what single process explains all of them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, fatigue, edema, and tolerance all move together across three months.
Age does not explain a three-month progressive change.
Weight with edema is fluid.
Arthritis explains one row, not four.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Fluid retention explains every row at once.

questions.concept: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviewing her medical unit notes that nearly every older client is treated for more than one long-term condition at once. Which implication follows for how care is organized?

options.text: The most recently diagnosed condition should take priority over the others
options.rationale: Recency is not clinical priority.

options.text: Chronic conditions should be addressed only after acute problems resolve
options.rationale: They interact, and deferring them worsens the acute picture.

options.text: Each condition should be managed by a separate specialist team independently
options.rationale: Produces conflicting plans and duplicated appointments.

options.text: Care is planned around the person rather than a single disease pathway
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is the normal case in older adults, and single-disease pathways conflict when several apply at once.

questions.takeaway: Multimorbidity is the normal case in older adults, which is why care is organized around the person. Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.
questions.strategy: Options treating conditions as separable are the pattern here. They interact, which is the whole point.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Most clients have several conditions at once.
Separate teams produce conflicting plans.
Recency and sequencing are not priority.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: multimorbidity is the normal case in older adults, and single-disease pathways conflict when several apply at once.

questions.concept: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions, and it is the normal case in older adults rather than the exception.

questions.scenario: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has missed two clinic appointments, reports taking medications only when he remembers, smokes 15 cigarettes daily, and says he does not understand what his blood pressure readings mean. He lives alone and works two jobs.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting from the choices below.

options.text: Assess adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, and lifestyle
options.rationale: The specified assessment priorities for clients with chronic illness.

options.text: Provide self-management education, including what his readings mean and how to respond
options.rationale: Self-management education builds the capability he uses between visits, which is where chronic illness is lived.

options.text: Arrange daily home nursing visits indefinitely
options.rationale: Creates dependence rather than capability, and does not address understanding.

options.text: Tell him non-adherence will lead to complications and document the warning
options.rationale: Warning is not education, and blame does not build self-management.

options.text: Ask his family to take over his medications
options.rationale: He lives alone, and removing him from his own care is not indicated.

options.text: A client with chronic disease requiring self-management support and health promotion
options.rationale: Combines the adherence, tobacco, and health literacy findings with the model's self-management focus.

options.text: A client in acute hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario describes acute decompensation.

options.text: A client requiring immediate hospitalization
options.rationale: No acute indication is present.

options.text: A client who has declined all treatment
options.rationale: He is taking medications inconsistently, which is not refusal.

options.text: Blood pressure and glycemic control over time
options.rationale: The measures that show whether self-management is improving.

options.text: Understanding, checked through teach-back
options.rationale: He states he does not understand his readings, so confirmed understanding is the parameter that matters.

options.text: Serum amylase
options.rationale: Not relevant to these conditions.

options.text: Daily temperature
options.rationale: Not a monitoring priority here.

options.text: Visual acuity weekly
options.rationale: Eye examinations are important in diabetes but not as a weekly monitoring parameter.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness care builds capability. Assess adherence and lifestyle, then teach for self-management. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. Teach-back asks the client to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.
questions.strategy: Two action options treat the client as the problem rather than the partner. Warning and taking over both fail for the same reason.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Inconsistent adherence plus low health literacy in chronic disease.
Creates dependence instead of capability.
Neither builds self-management.

elimination.verdict: Actions A and B, condition A, parameters A and B.

questions.concept: Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. Teach-back asks the client to explain the plan in their own words. It confirms understanding rather than confirming that teaching was delivered.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse his glucose readings range from 180 to 320 mg/dL and he does not know what to do about any of them, so he has stopped checking. He takes metformin when he remembers. Which nursing action best supports self-management?

options.text: Asking the family to take over medication administration to reduce his burden
options.rationale: Removes the client from their own care without an assessed need.

options.text: Arranging daily nursing visits indefinitely so the monitoring is done reliably
options.rationale: Creates dependence rather than capability.

options.text: Providing a detailed schedule the client must follow exactly
options.rationale: Directive rather than supportive, and it does not build the client's capacity to manage.

options.text: Teaching the client to recognize and respond to changes in their own symptoms
options.rationale: Self-management education builds the client's ability to manage the condition between visits, which is where most chronic illness is lived.

questions.takeaway: Self-management education builds the client's capability, because they manage the condition between visits. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.
questions.strategy: In chronic illness items, the answer usually increases the client's capacity rather than doing the task for them.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Key word best, with self-management as the goal.
Directive, not capacity-building.
Creates dependence.
Removes the client from their own care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: self-management education builds the client's ability to manage the condition between visits, which is where most chronic illness is lived.

questions.concept: Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with multiple sclerosis tells the nurse she has stopped attending the book club she has belonged to for years because she is embarrassed by her tremor, and that she no longer feels like the person her friends knew. Her tremor is unchanged on her current treatment. Which concept does this best illustrate?

options.text: Chronic illness
options.rationale: Chronic illness is the personal focus, meaning the emotional and social experience. Withdrawing from a social group because of how the condition feels is illness, not disease.

options.text: Comorbidity
options.rationale: Refers to an additional condition alongside a primary one.

options.text: Chronic disease
options.rationale: Chronic disease is the medical focus: the clinical process in the body, diagnosed and lasting a year or longer.

options.text: Multimorbidity
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is managing two or more concurrent chronic conditions.

questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: When a stem describes what a condition does to someone's life rather than to their body, the answer is illness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The finding is social withdrawal driven by embarrassment.
Disease is the biological process.
Only one condition is described.
No second condition is mentioned.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. The tremor is disease; the empty chair at the book club is illness.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A community nurse assesses a family caregiver during a home visit. She is 68, has cared for her husband with dementia for two years, lives with him, and manages his personal care alone. Which factors place a family caregiver at risk for poor health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Providing care for more than one year
options.rationale: Caregiving past a year moves the demand from a temporary effort to a sustained one, and the health effects accumulate with duration.

options.text: Having respite care available weekly
options.rationale: Respite reduces caregiver strain rather than raising risk.

options.text: Caring for someone with Alzheimer disease or dementia
options.rationale: Dementia care carries constant supervision and behavioral demands, which is why it is singled out from other caregiving.

options.text: Sharing the caregiving role with three siblings
options.rationale: Shared caregiving reduces the burden carried by any one person.

options.text: Living within walking distance of a clinic
options.rationale: Proximity to services eases caregiving rather than raising risk.

options.text: Providing care for a family member with significant needs
options.rationale: Significant needs mean the physical and time demands are high, which limits the caregiver's own sleep, activity, and health care.

questions.takeaway: Five caregiver risk factors, and they stack. Consider the caregiver in the care plan.
questions.strategy: One option in this set describes support rather than burden. That is the exclusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which factors create risk.
Respite relieves burden rather than adding to it.

elimination.verdict: A, C and F are selected.

questions.stem: A community health nurse notices that several clients with asthma live in the same poorly maintained housing complex and that local air quality data show elevated pollutant levels. She considers what falls within her professional role beyond treating each client. Which action reflects the nurse's role in relation to public policy and chronic disease?

options.text: Limiting practice to individual client care only, since policy sits outside nursing
options.rationale: Excludes prevention and population-level awareness.

options.text: Avoiding any discussion of health policy with clients under all circumstances at all
options.rationale: Health education about prevention and screening is explicitly part of the role.

options.text: Recognizing environmental factors that influence health and using reputable information sources
options.rationale: Occurs alongside awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, providing health education, and encouraging screening and prevention.

options.text: Endorsing specific political candidates to clients who ask about health policy
options.rationale: Outside the professional role and not what policy awareness means.

questions.takeaway: Know the policies, recognize environmental influences, use reputable sources, teach, and encourage screening.
questions.strategy: Policy items reward the option describing professional awareness and education rather than advocacy for a position.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks about the nurse's role.
All circumstances is absolute and contradicts health education.
Outside the professional role.
Only excludes prevention work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: occurs alongside awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, providing health education, and encouraging screening and prevention.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with COPD is discharged after his third admission this year. His saturation is 90% on room air, he will use home oxygen at 2 L, and he cannot coordinate his inhaler. Which nursing action best reflects chronic care?

options.text: Schedule a follow-up appointment and end nursing involvement at the point of discharge
options.rationale: Ends coordination at the moment self-management begins.

options.text: Coordinate with the client, family, caregivers, and the health care team
options.rationale: Care often includes clients, families, caregivers, and a team spanning physical, occupational, and speech therapy and specialty physicians.

options.text: Refer the client to a single specialist for ongoing management of everything
options.rationale: Narrows care to one discipline.

options.text: Provide written discharge instructions to the client before he leaves the unit
options.rationale: Necessary but insufficient. Chronic illness care extends past the individual and past a single handout.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness care is a team effort that includes the family and caregivers.
questions.strategy: Key word best. All four options are things someone might do; the answer is the one that matches the model of care.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Discharge planning for a chronic condition.
A handout alone does not coordinate care.
Narrows to one discipline.
Withdraws coordination too early.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: care often includes clients, families, caregivers, and a team spanning physical, occupational, and speech therapy and specialty physicians.

questions.stem: A nurse visits a 68-year-old who has cared for her husband with dementia at home for two years. She describes how she is managing and what she plans to do about her own health. Which caregiver statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Caring for someone with dementia is harder than most people realize."
options.rationale: Accurate. Dementia care carries constant supervision and behavioral demands.

options.text: "As long as I am coping, my own appointments can wait."
options.rationale: Caregiving past a year, being 65 or older, dementia care, living with the care recipient, and high needs are risk factors for the caregiver's own health. Deferring her own care is how that risk becomes illness.

options.text: "Living with him means there is no point in the day when I am able to stop."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is a risk factor.

options.text: "I should ask about respite before I reach the point of not coping."
options.rationale: Accurate. Respite arranged early is more useful than respite arranged in crisis.

questions.takeaway: Caregiver risk factors compound. Deferring your own health care is how sustained caregiving becomes illness.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is the one every caregiver says. Coping is not the same as being well.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
Duration, age, dementia, living together, high needs.
Coping now does not protect health later.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: her own care does not wait for things to settle.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 61-year-old with a blood pressure of 176/98 who smokes 20 cigarettes daily, has missed four clinic appointments, and whose A1C is 9.4%. Which assessment is most important for planning his care?

options.text: Surgical history and anesthesia tolerance
options.rationale: Perioperative concerns rather than chronic illness assessment.

options.text: Immunization status and travel history, since both affect long-term risk
options.rationale: Relevant elsewhere, not the priorities.

options.text: Adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and lifestyle
options.rationale: The specified assessment priorities for clients with chronic illness.

options.text: Range of motion, reflexes, and gait only, since function drives chronic outcomes
options.rationale: A physical subset that omits the behavioral and lifestyle areas specified.

questions.takeaway: Adherence, symptoms, tobacco, alcohol, and lifestyle.
questions.strategy: The list mixes clinical and behavioral areas. An option containing only physical findings is too narrow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the assessment priorities.
Only narrows to physical findings.
Not the correct set.
Perioperative rather than chronic.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the assessment priorities for clients with chronic illness.

questions.stem: A nurse educator asks which elements belong to the framework used to organize care for long-term conditions. Which is a component of the Chronic Care Model?

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: One of the six components, alongside community resources, the health system, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems.

options.text: Acute care triage
options.rationale: Sorts clients by urgency of presentation rather than organizing long-term care.

options.text: Emergency preparedness
options.rationale: An organizational function rather than one of the six components.

options.text: Infection surveillance
options.rationale: Belongs to infection control rather than chronic condition management.

questions.takeaway: Six components: community, self-management support, health system, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems. The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.
questions.strategy: The model is built around supporting the client between visits, so components that sound acute or episodic are wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One component of the model.
Sorts clients by urgency of presentation rather than organizing long-term care.
Belongs to infection control rather than chronic condition management.
An organizational function rather than one of the six components.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: one of the six components, alongside community resources, the health system, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems.

questions.concept: The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.

questions.stem: Two clients were diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis in the same year. One works full time with pain rated 2 of 10 on stable medication. The other has left work and rates her pain 7 of 10. Which statement explains this difference?

options.text: Both clients should follow the same care plan for the sake of consistency
options.rationale: Disease-centered care, which is the approach being argued against.

options.text: The second client's condition is more advanced and needs no further assessment
options.rationale: May be true or not, and either way it substitutes assumption for assessment.

options.text: One of the two clients is not adhering to the treatment plan as it was prescribed
options.rationale: Assumes a cause the stem does not support and blames the client for a difference in disease effect.

options.text: Effects and limitations vary between clients with the same condition
options.rationale: No two clients are the same, which is why care is patient-centered rather than disease-centered.

questions.takeaway: Same diagnosis, different lives. Assess the person, not the label.
questions.strategy: Options that blame the client or standardize care are usually wrong in chronic illness items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Same condition, different function.
Blames the client without evidence.
Assumes rather than assesses.
Disease-centered rather than patient-centered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: no two clients are the same, which is why care is patient-centered rather than disease-centered.

questions.scenario: Two clients on the same unit have rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed the same year. One works full time and manages independently. The other requires assistance with dressing and has stopped driving.
questions.stem: Which nursing conclusions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Physical effects may vary between clients with the same chronic illness
options.rationale: Stated directly, along with the point that functional limitations vary.

options.text: Individual assessment is essential because no two clients are the same
options.rationale: The reason care is patient-centered rather than disease-centered.

options.text: The second client is likely not adhering to the treatment plan
options.rationale: Blames the client for a difference attributable to variation in disease effect.

options.text: Care should be patient-centered rather than disease-centered
options.rationale: patient-centered care follows from the fact that the same diagnosis produces different effects in different people, so the plan starts from the person rather than the disease.

options.text: Both clients should follow the same care plan for consistency
options.rationale: Disease-centered care, which is what this objective argues against.

options.text: Psychosocial needs including depression and isolation should be assessed in both
options.rationale: Psychosocial needs, and the second client's loss of driving raises isolation risk.

options.text: The first client requires no further assessment because she is functioning well
options.rationale: Current function does not remove the need for assessment, and chronic illness is experienced privately.

questions.takeaway: Same diagnosis, different lives. Assess the person, not the label.
questions.strategy: Three wrong options here standardize care, blame the client, or skip assessment. All three recur.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identical diagnosis, very different function.
Blames the client without evidence.
Disease-centered rather than patient-centered.
Good function does not remove assessment need.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with heart failure and arthritis attends clinic reporting fatigue that has worsened over six weeks. Her weight is up 3 kg since her last visit and she has stopped walking to the corner shop. Her daughter says this is just getting older. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.text: Agree with the family, since fatigue of this kind is expected at his age
options.rationale: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness, which is the reason not to accept this explanation.

options.text: Reassure the family that the fatigue is unrelated to his underlying heart failure
options.rationale: Factually wrong and closes off assessment.

options.text: Assess for causes including medication side effects and changes in the chronic conditions
options.rationale: Overlapping symptoms are a specified challenge, and medication side effects are specifically confused with normal aging.

options.text: Recommend increased rest and reassess in a month to see whether it settles
options.rationale: Delays assessment of a new symptom in a client with two chronic conditions.

questions.takeaway: Age-related changes can mask chronic illness. New symptoms get assessed, not attributed.
questions.strategy: This is the same principle as other material's age is not a diagnosis, appearing in a chronic illness context. This same distinction separates a clinical process from how a person lives with it.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: A new symptom with two chronic conditions present.
Attributes a new symptom to age.
Fatigue is a recognized feature of heart failure.
Delays assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: overlapping symptoms are a specified challenge, and medication side effects are specifically confused with normal aging.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse that his father had it too, so there was nothing he could have done. He works twelve-hour shifts, eats mostly takeaway food, and has not exercised in years. Which factors are described as contributing to chronic disease?

options.text: Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors including tobacco, alcohol, and nutrition
options.rationale: The three specified categories, and genetics interacts with the others rather than acting alone.

options.text: Infectious exposure in early childhood that predisposes the person to later disease
options.rationale: Not one of the categories.

options.text: Lifestyle factors only, since behavior is what the client is able to change
options.rationale: Excludes genetics and environment.

options.text: Genetic factors only, since family history determines who develops the condition
options.rationale: Genetics is one of three specified categories.

questions.takeaway: Genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors, interacting rather than acting separately.
questions.strategy: Options containing only are almost always wrong when a condition is multifactorial.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The question asks what contributes to chronic disease.
Only excludes two categories.
Only excludes two categories.
Not among the factors.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the three specified categories, and genetics interacts with the others rather than acting alone.

questions.stem: A clinic is redesigning how it cares for clients with long-term conditions, having found that most problems arise between visits rather than during them. The team reviews the framework built around planned rather than reactive chronic care. Which are components of the Chronic Care Model? Select all that apply.

options.text: Community
options.rationale: Community resources extend care beyond the clinic, which matters because chronic illness is lived mostly outside health care settings.

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: Self-management support builds the client's capability, since they manage the condition between visits and that is where most of it happens.

options.text: Acute rehabilitation
options.rationale: A care setting rather than a component of the chronic care framework.

options.text: Delivery system design
options.rationale: Delivery system design determines how visits, follow-up, and team roles are arranged so chronic care is planned rather than reactive.

options.text: Emergency department throughput
options.rationale: A measure of acute service flow rather than a component of chronic care.

options.text: Emergency preparedness
options.rationale: An organizational function rather than a component of chronic care.

questions.takeaway: Community, self-management support, health system, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems. The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.
questions.strategy: Five of the six are offered. Recognize the one that is the outlier rather than trying to rank importance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks which options belong to the model.
Not among the six components.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: The Chronic Care Model organizes long-term condition care through community resources, the health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, and clinical information systems. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require the nurse's attention at this visit.
questions.takeaway: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness. Assess new symptoms rather than attributing them.
questions.strategy: The family's explanation is deliberately included. It tells you what to teach, and it is not itself a finding. One finding is the family's interpretation rather than a clinical finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings have moved over three weeks.
Existing diagnoses are context.
A teaching cue rather than a clinical finding.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s4.

questions.nursesNote: 1130: Client is 77, attends clinic with heart failure, type 2 diabetes and arthritis, all diagnosed eight years ago. Over the past three weeks his weight is up 3 kg and he reports new ankle swelling. Walks 90 meters before stopping, down from 300 meters. Has stopped attending the allotment he has tended for 20 years. States he takes his medication only when he remembers. Family attributes the changes to getting older. VS: T 36.8 C; HR 96; RR 20; BP 138/84; SpO2 93% on room air.

segments.text: Weight up 3 kg with new ankle swelling over three weeks
segments.rationale: Fluid retention, and the combination with reduced exercise tolerance points at worsening heart failure.

segments.text: Walks 90 meters before stopping, down from 300 meters
segments.rationale: A measurable fall in exercise tolerance over the same period.

segments.text: Has stopped attending the allotment he has tended for 20 years
segments.rationale: Chronic illness affects roles and self-perception, and social withdrawal is a psychosocial need.

segments.text: Takes medication only when he remembers
segments.rationale: Adherence is a assessment priority, and it may explain the deterioration.

segments.text: Diagnosed with heart failure and type 2 diabetes eight years ago
segments.rationale: Background history rather than a finding requiring attention now.

segments.text: Family attributes the changes to getting older
segments.rationale: Their explanation, and it is a cue about understanding rather than a clinical finding.

questions.caseTitle: Living with multiple chronic conditions

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: Disease is the clinical process. Illness is how the person lives it.
questions.strategy: Both halves of this client are in the note. The swelling is disease; the allotment he no longer visits is illness.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Swelling and walking distance are measurable.
The allotment is what the condition has cost him.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: His ankle swelling and reduced walking distance are examples of [[1]], and his withdrawal from the allotment is an example of [[2]].

options.text: chronic disease
options.rationale: The medical focus: the clinical process occurring in the body.

options.text: chronic illness
options.rationale: Illness is the personal experience, not the physical sign.

options.text: multimorbidity
options.rationale: Managing two or more concurrent conditions, which he has, and it is not what these findings are.

options.text: chronic illness
options.rationale: The personal focus: the emotional and social experience of living with the condition.

options.text: chronic disease

questions.caseTitle: Living with multiple chronic conditions

questions.stem: Which 2 assessments are the priority at this visit?
questions.takeaway: Assessment priorities in chronic illness: adherence, symptom management, tobacco, alcohol, and lifestyle.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. The two that matter are the ones that could change what happens next.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Inconsistent medication.
Swelling and exercise tolerance.
History and preferences do not change this visit.

options.text: Adherence, including why he takes his medication inconsistently

questions.caseTitle: Living with multiple chronic conditions

questions.stem: For each finding six weeks later, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with the first visit, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: Compare each finding against its own baseline. Physical improvement does not automatically restore the illness experience.
questions.strategy: The allotment row is the point. Four physiological measures improved and the thing that mattered to him has not. One finding is unchanged and it is the one the client would notice most.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five findings were recorded at the first visit.
The allotment is still empty.
His caregiving role was never assessed.

questions.baseline: First visit: weight up 3 kg with ankle swelling, walked 90 meters, stopped attending the allotment, taking medication only when remembered, SpO2 93%.

rows.text: Weight down 3 kg with no ankle swelling
rows.rationale: The fluid retention has resolved.

rows.text: Walks 250 meters before stopping
rows.rationale: Up from 90 meters.

rows.text: Uses a weekly pill organizer and reports taking every dose
rows.rationale: Adherence addressed with a practical aid.

rows.text: SpO2 96% on room air
rows.rationale: Up from 93%.

questions.caseTitle: Living with multiple chronic conditions

questions.stem: The nurse plans this visit. Which 2 actions address what is driving his deterioration?
questions.takeaway: Find the modifiable cause and report the trend. Accepting the change as aging is the error.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options accept, accommodate, or label rather than investigate.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Three weeks of weight gain, swelling, and falling tolerance.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an 80-year-old who managed independently until this admission and now needs help with bathing, dressing, and walking 20 feet. Her hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL and she has lost 3 kg. Which statement about functional status is accurate?

options.text: Functional status refers only to the physical ability to walk without assistance
options.rationale: Too narrow. It includes physical, psychological, cognitive, and social domains.

options.text: A decline in function is usually linked to illness and its chronicity
options.rationale: Which is why a decline prompts a search for a cause rather than acceptance as aging.

options.text: Functional decline in an older adult is expected and does not require intervention
options.rationale: Interventions focus on maintaining, restoring, and maximizing functional status.

options.text: Functional status is assessed only at discharge, when placement is being decided
options.rationale: Baseline function is needed on admission to recognize any change.

questions.takeaway: Function spans physical, psychological, cognitive, and social domains, and decline points at illness rather than age.

Only walking is too narrow.

Only at discharge loses the baseline.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with advanced dementia becomes distressed each afternoon, saying she must leave to collect her children from school. Staff have repeatedly corrected her and told her the children are adults, and her agitation has increased each time. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Acknowledge the feeling behind the statement and redirect gently
options.rationale: Validation is used where the client cannot be reoriented. You respond to the emotion rather than correcting the fact.

options.text: Leave her alone until the episode passes, so she is not further distressed
options.rationale: Abandons a distressed client.

options.text: Reorient her to the date and explain her children are adults
options.rationale: Reality orientation suits a client who can be reoriented, and repeated correction has already increased her distress.

options.text: Agree that she should go and offer to walk her to the door
options.rationale: Deception, and it sets up a further distressing moment when she cannot leave.

questions.takeaway: Reality orientation for a client who can be reoriented. Validation where she cannot.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you correction has already failed, which is what selects validation over orientation. One option would be correct for a different client. Read what has already been tried.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Repeated correction increased agitation.
Orientation has already failed.
Deception and abandonment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: validation is used where the client cannot be reoriented.

questions.topic: Red flags in an older adult
questions.stem: The nurse admits an 84-year-old from home following a fall. She assesses the skin, cognition, continence, senses, and mobility, and speaks with the daughter about recent changes. Highlight the findings that require further nursing assessment.

segments.text: Client is alert and oriented to person, place, and time.
segments.rationale: A normal baseline, and it is the reference point against which any later change is measured.

segments.text: Skin is thin and dry with reduced elasticity.
segments.rationale: An expected integumentary change of aging.

segments.text: Reports new difficulty controlling urine over the past two weeks.
segments.rationale: Urinary incontinence is abnormal at any age. It is common in older adults and it is not expected.

segments.text: Skin has lost resilience and moisture since her last visit two years ago.
segments.rationale: Her deck names loss of skin resilience and moisture as an expected integumentary change of aging.

segments.text: Daughter reports her mother has fallen twice in the past month with no identified cause.
segments.rationale: A new unexplained fall is a red flag, and a fall is always a clinical clue.

segments.text: Reports needing more light to read than she did a year ago.
segments.rationale: An expected sensory change of aging.

segments.text: Has lost 5 kg since her last clinic visit three months ago.
segments.rationale: Unintended weight loss is not an expected change and points at nutrition, illness, or a functional problem.

segments.text: Slower reaction time noted during transfer.
segments.rationale: An expected change of aging.

questions.takeaway: Expected changes are gradual. Anything new, sudden, or unexplained is assessed.
questions.strategy: Read each sentence for the words new, unexplained, or a stated time frame. Those move a finding out of the expected column. Several findings are expected changes of aging. Under plus and minus scoring a wrong highlight subtracts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Do not highlight as you go; several findings are deliberately normal.
Gradual is expected, recent change is not.
Both are common in older adults and neither is expected.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a colleague there is no point teaching an 88-year-old about her new 5 mg warfarin dose because she will not retain it. The client scores 28 of 30 on cognitive screening and manages her own finances. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Reality orientation

options.text: Reminiscence

options.text: Ageism

options.text: Functional decline
options.rationale: A measurable change in the ability to perform daily activities.

questions.takeaway: Ageism is discrimination by age, and nurses must first assess their own attitudes toward older adults and toward their own aging. Ageism is assuming capability, preference, or prognosis from a person's age rather than assessing the individual.

options.text: Malnutrition

options.rationale: Healing is slower in older adults, not faster.

options.rationale: Appetite typically falls during hospitalization rather than rising.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old repeatedly asks the nurse to repeat questions and answers inconsistently. The television is on and two staff are talking in the doorway. She wears hearing aids that are at home. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reduce the background noise, face her directly, and speak clearly without shouting
options.rationale: Correct adaptations for hearing impairment. Shouting distorts speech rather than clarifying it.

options.text: Speak louder so she can hear you over the television in the room
options.rationale: Shouting distorts, and the television can simply be turned off.

options.text: Document that she is confused and report the change in condition to the provider
options.rationale: Attributes a sensory problem to cognition, which is a consequential error in an older adult.

options.text: Ask her family to answer on her behalf so the assessment can be completed
options.rationale: Bypasses a client who can communicate with adaptation.

questions.takeaway: Reduce noise, face the client, do not shout. Sensory change is not confusion. A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional torts cause harm through the nature of the act. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known the care was substandard.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a family about their 84-year-old relative's sudden confusion, which began overnight three days after hip surgery. The family asks what is happening and what should be done. Which family statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "An infection can show up as confusion before she runs a fever."
options.rationale: Accurate. In older adults the classic signs are often absent.

options.text: "Her confusion started overnight, so her dementia must be getting worse."
options.rationale: Dementia is chronic and progressive over years. A change occurring overnight is delirium until proven otherwise, and delirium has a cause that is often reversible.

options.text: "The pain medication she started yesterday could be part of what is happening."
options.rationale: Accurate. Medications are a contributor to delirium.

options.text: "Tying her hands down would probably make her more agitated than she is now."
options.rationale: Accurate. Restraints worsen delirium and agitation and are a last resort.

questions.strategy: Onset is the discriminator. Anything that appears overnight cannot be a chronic progressive process.

Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Overnight rules out dementia.
Infection and medication are both specified.
Restraints worsen the condition.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: overnight onset means delirium, not dementia.

options.rationale: Immediately checkable, immediately correctable, and the most rapidly dangerous of the four.

options.text: A developing infection
options.rationale: Common, reversible, and it presents as confusion in older adults, often without a high fever.

questions.stem: For each nursing action, determine whether it is a HIGH, INTERMEDIATE, or LOW priority for this client now.
questions.takeaway: Set priorities high, intermediate, and low using the ABCs and Maslow, and consider this client's unique situation. Maslow's hierarchy ranks needs from physiological, through safety, love and belonging, and esteem, to self-actualization. It is a priority-setting tool alongside the ABCs. The ABCs rank airway, breathing, and circulation as the first priorities, and they are the first priority-setting tool to apply.
questions.strategy: Pain control here is intermediate rather than low precisely because it serves the breathing goal. Rank by what it enables, not by the category it falls in. One action is not itself a breathing intervention but directly enables one.

rows.rationale: Gas exchange is failing, and the ABCs place breathing at the top.

rows.rationale: The infection is driving the deterioration, and delay allows it to continue.

rows.text: Controlling his chest pain so he can breathe deeply and cough
rows.rationale: Important, and it serves the respiratory goal rather than competing with it. Unrelieved pain is why he will not sit forward.

rows.rationale: Appropriate before discharge and not while he is acutely unwell.

rows.rationale: A comfort measure with no bearing on his current problems.

segments.rationale: Retention is a possibility requiring assessment, and six hours is long enough to act on.

questions.topic: When outcomes are not fully met
questions.stem: A client has not met the outcome of ambulating 50 feet with a walker by day three. He walked 15 feet once and rates his pain 7 of 10 on movement. Which actions does the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess the client for new or overlooked data
options.rationale: And the reported pain is exactly the kind of data that may have been missed.

options.text: Reconsider whether the nursing diagnosis or priority is still accurate
options.rationale: Correct. If pain is the barrier, the priority problem may be pain rather than mobility.

options.text: Adjust the goals, outcomes, or the target timeframe
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Select new or additional interventions
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Record the outcome as not met and close the problem
options.rationale: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data and the process loops. Closing the problem ends the cycle rather than continuing it.

questions.takeaway: When outcomes are not fully met: reassess, reconsider the diagnosis, adjust the outcome or timeframe, and select new interventions. A nursing diagnosis classifies the client's response to illness and is what registered nurses treat independently. Nurses treat responses, not diseases.

steps.detail: An outcome partially met, with a possible reason.

questions.stem: An outcome stated the client would maintain a urine output above 30 mL/hr. Over the past six hours his output has been 45, 38, 32, 28, 22, and 18 mL. Which conclusion does the nurse record?

options.text: Not met, and the downward trend requires escalation

options.rationale: The hourly values are the evaluative measure the outcome specified.

options.text: Partially met, since three of six hours reached the target
options.rationale: Counting hours ignores which three, and the three that failed are the most recent.

options.rationale: Averaging conceals the trend. The outcome specified an hourly minimum, not a mean.

questions.takeaway: Read the direction, not the average. A trend falling through a target is worse than a single low value.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Falling every hour, and below target for the last three.

The failing hours are the most recent ones.

questions.topic: Met, partially met, or not met

options.rationale: The outcome was specific and observable, so it could be evaluated.

options.text: Not met, because he required prompting for one step of the procedure

questions.takeaway: Met, partially met, or not met. Recording which step failed is what makes the next intervention specific.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates four outcomes at the end of a shift: pain below 4 of 10, oxygen saturation above 92%, an independent dressing change, and understanding of a new medication. Which principle guides her choice of evaluative measure?

questions.stem: For each finding two days later, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with day three, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: Compare each finding against its own baseline. An outcome that was already met and remains met is unchanged, not improved.
questions.strategy: The dressing row is the discrimination. Still able is not the same as better, and recording it as improvement would misrepresent the plan. One outcome was already met and remains met. Consider whether that is improvement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings were recorded on day three.
The dressing change was correct then and now.
Mood was never assessed.

elimination.verdict: Three improved, one unchanged, one new finding.

questions.baseline: Day three: ambulated 20 feet, pain 8/10 during the attempt, dressing change demonstrated correctly, sacral skin non-blanching.

rows.text: Ambulated 55 feet with a walker
rows.rationale: Up from 20 feet, and beyond the original target.

rows.text: Rates pain 3 out of 10 during ambulation with scheduled analgesia
rows.rationale: Down from 8, which is why she walked further.

rows.text: Sacral skin blanches on pressure
rows.rationale: The stage 1 injury has resolved with pressure relief.

rows.text: Performs the dressing change independently
rows.rationale: She demonstrated it correctly on day three as well, so the outcome remains met rather than having improved further.

rows.text: Reports feeling low and tearful about going home alone
rows.rationale: Mood and her feelings about discharge were not assessed on day three, so there is no baseline. It requires assessment and may affect the discharge plan.

questions.caseTitle: Evaluating and revising the plan

questions.stem: Two of the four outcomes were not met. Which 2 actions does the nurse take?
questions.takeaway: Reassess, reconsider the diagnosis, adjust the outcome or timeframe, then select new interventions.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Four wrong options lower the standard, close the plan, or repeat what failed.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Mobility and pain, with one likely causing the other.
Discontinuing and replacing.
Neither responds to the data.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Reassess for new or overlooked data before changing any intervention
options.rationale: And the reported pain is the kind of data that may have been missed.

options.text: Reconsider whether pain, rather than mobility, is now the priority problem
options.rationale: If pain is the barrier the priority diagnosis may need to change before the interventions do.

options.text: Discontinue the mobility outcome entirely
options.rationale: Removes a legitimate goal rather than addressing why it was not reached.

options.text: Replace the outcome with one she has already achieved
options.rationale: Lowers the standard to match the result.

options.text: Record both outcomes as not met and close the plan
options.rationale: Evaluation data becomes new assessment data and the process continues.

options.text: Continue the current interventions unchanged for another 48 hours
options.rationale: Repeats an approach that has already failed twice.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: Met, partially met, or not met, with the data that supports the conclusion.
questions.strategy: Unbroken and intact are not the same. Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 pressure injury.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Correct twice, unprompted, is met.
The outcome said intact.
Extent does not soften an unmet standard.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: For the dressing change outcome the nurse records [[1]], and for the skin outcome she records [[2]].

options.text: met, supported by two correct return demonstrations
options.rationale: Return demonstration is the evidence a psychomotor outcome requires, and she performed it correctly twice.

options.text: partially met, since she needed no prompting
options.rationale: Needing no prompting is what met looks like.

options.text: unable to evaluate, since the outcome was subjective
options.rationale: A return demonstration is directly observable.

options.text: not met, since non-blanching redness means the skin is not intact
options.rationale: The outcome specified intact skin, and a stage 1 pressure injury does not meet it.

options.text: met, since the skin is unbroken
options.rationale: Intact is not the same as unbroken. Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 injury.

options.rationale: Extent does not convert an unmet outcome into a partial one when the standard was intact skin.

questions.stem: A nurse has twice paged the provider about a client whose blood pressure has fallen from 128/74 to 88/52 over four hours and who is now increasingly drowsy. Neither page was returned. Which tool does she use next?

options.text: The five rights of delegation
options.rationale: Belongs to delegation.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: Graded escalation language: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue. Each step raises the stakes explicitly.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: The broader teamwork framework CUS belongs to, with pillars of communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support.

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: The right tool for the first call and the wrong one for the third. Repeating a report that has already failed changes nothing.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports. CUS escalates. SBAR structures a report: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The recommendation is the part most often dropped. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: When a stem says you already reported and nothing happened, the answer is escalate, not report again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two reports have already failed.
Repeating the same tool changes nothing.
A framework, not a moment-to-moment tool.
Wrong domain.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: graded escalation language: I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue.

questions.concept: SBAR structures a report: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. The recommendation is the part most often dropped.
