questions.stem: A manager introduces a new fall prevention protocol written entirely by the leadership team and circulated by email. Six weeks later an audit shows it is rarely followed, although staff report they are aware of it. Which factor most likely explains this?

options.text: The protocol was too short a document to be taken seriously by staff
options.rationale: Length does not determine adoption.

options.text: Nurses on the unit lack the training to follow it
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem suggests a knowledge gap, and assuming one locates the failure in the staff.

options.text: The nurses delivering the care did not participate in writing it
options.rationale: Shared governance exists because staff follow protocols they helped create, and adoption falls when they do not.

options.text: Audits are unreliable measures of what actually happens in practice
options.rationale: An audit finding is data, not an explanation to dismiss.

questions.takeaway: Shared decision-making is why protocols get followed. Adoption follows participation. Shared governance means the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why protocols they helped write get followed.
questions.strategy: Options locating the failure in the staff are the pattern here. The stem tells you who wrote it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Leadership alone.
Length and audit reliability.
No knowledge gap described.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: shared governance exists because staff follow protocols they helped create, and adoption falls when they do not.

questions.concept: Shared governance means the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why protocols they helped write get followed.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to delegate vital signs on a stable client to assistive personnel so she can complete an admission assessment. She wants the delegation to be safe and defensible. Place the steps of delegation in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Determine whether the task is appropriate to delegate
options.rationale: Right task. Some activities never move, including assessment, evaluation, teaching, and unstable clients.

options.text: Determine whether the client's condition is stable and appropriate for delegation
options.rationale: Right circumstance. A stable situation with a predictable outcome is required, and this is where most delegation questions are decided.

options.text: Confirm the person is competent and qualified to perform the task
options.rationale: Right person. Having watched is not the same as being competent.

options.text: Give clear instructions, expectations, and what must be reported back
options.rationale: Right directions and communication. A delegation without a reporting threshold is incomplete.

options.text: Supervise, follow up on the outcome, and evaluate the result
options.rationale: Right supervision and evaluation, and it is the step most often skipped.

questions.takeaway: Task, circumstance, person, directions, supervision. The last one is the one people drop.
questions.strategy: Read the client, not just the task. A delegable task on an unstable client stays with the RN. Handing off the task feels like the end. It is the fourth of five steps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Whether the task can be delegated at all comes first.
Supervision and evaluation close the process.
Circumstance, then person, then directions.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, E.

questions.stem: A nurse, a physical therapist, and a dietitian meet about a client whose weight has fallen 5 kg and who walks 20 feet with assistance. Each contributes to one shared plan. Which benefit does this collaboration provide?

options.text: Higher staff satisfaction and lower moral distress
options.rationale: Correct. Empowering environments support both client outcomes and staff wellbeing.

options.text: Reduced need for interprofessional communication on the unit
options.rationale: Collaboration increases communication rather than reducing it.

options.text: Elimination of the need for delegation between members of the team
options.rationale: Delegation remains a core leadership competency.

options.text: Fewer opportunities for professional development
options.rationale: Professional development is a Magnet standard and part of an empowering environment.

questions.takeaway: A culture of autonomy, quality, and collaboration raises satisfaction and lowers moral distress. Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with. Moral distress is knowing what is right and being prevented from doing it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which of two defensible positions is right.
questions.strategy: Moral distress is knowing what is right and being blocked from doing it. Environments that increase autonomy reduce the blocking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The outcome of an empowering culture.
Each describes something being reduced or eliminated that the culture actually supports.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: specified directly.

questions.concept: Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with. Moral distress is knowing what is right and being prevented from doing it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which of two defensible positions is right.

questions.stem: A hospital is introducing interprofessional rounding, with the whole team reviewing each client together at the bedside. Staff are asked to prepare by reviewing the competencies that make team practice work. Which are the four interprofessional competencies? Select all that apply.

options.text: Values and ethics
options.rationale: Values and ethics establish that team members share a commitment to the client rather than to their own discipline's priorities.

options.text: Roles and responsibilities
options.rationale: Knowing each discipline's roles prevents both duplication and the assumption that someone else has done it.

options.text: Communication
options.rationale: Communication is a competency because most team failures are communication failures rather than knowledge failures.

options.text: Teamwork
options.rationale: Teamwork covers how the group functions under pressure, which is when coordination usually breaks down.

options.text: Financial stewardship
options.rationale: Not one of the four.

questions.takeaway: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, teamwork, supported by interprofessional rounding. The four interprofessional competencies are values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.
questions.strategy: Four of the five are, so identify the outlier rather than ranking importance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The four interprofessional competencies.
Not among the four.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: The four interprofessional competencies are values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.

questions.stem: A new graduate asks who decides the values and direction that shape nursing practice across an entire organization, as opposed to who manages a shift or who regulates the profession. Who sets the nursing philosophy for an organization?

options.text: The Joint Commission, which accredits the organization
options.rationale: Sets accreditation standards.

options.text: The charge nurse on each unit
options.rationale: Manages the shift rather than setting organizational philosophy.

options.text: The State Board of Nursing, which regulates licensure
options.rationale: Regulates licensure and practice, not one organization's philosophy.

options.text: The nurse executive, often the chief nursing officer
options.rationale: And the philosophy shapes the practice environment beneath it.

questions.takeaway: The nurse executive, often the CNO, sets the nursing philosophy.
questions.strategy: Sort by scope: shift, organization, state, or accreditation. Only one operates at organizational level.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Organizational nursing philosophy.
Shift-level.
External regulators.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: specified directly, and the philosophy shapes the practice environment beneath it.

questions.stem: A unit is organized so that an RN leads a group of staff who together deliver care to a set of clients during a shift, with the RN directing and supervising the work. Which model is this?

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: An RN leads a team delivering care to a group of clients, directing and supervising the work.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: One RN is responsible for a client across the admission.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Coordinates care across settings and beyond discharge.

options.text: Functional nursing
options.rationale: Divides work by task, with each person performing one task for all clients.

questions.strategy: Sort the models by what gets assigned: a client, a group, a task, or a trajectory.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A group of clients to a team for a shift.
One client across an admission.
Across settings, and by task.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: an RN leads a team delivering care to a group of clients, directing and supervising the work.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to call the provider about a postoperative client whose condition has changed over the past four hours. She reviews her findings and must decide what to lead with. Highlight the three highest priority findings to emphasize to the provider.

segments.text: Blood pressure has fallen from 122/74 to 88/52 over four hours
segments.rationale: A downward trend in perfusion pressure, and trends outrank single values.

segments.text: Client reports the room is too warm
segments.rationale: A comfort issue, not a priority to report.

segments.text: Heart rate has risen from 82 to 124
segments.rationale: Compensatory tachycardia accompanying the falling pressure, and the two together suggest hypovolemia.

segments.text: Dressing has a small amount of dried drainage from this morning
segments.rationale: Old, dried, and small. Expected postoperatively.

segments.text: Client is increasingly difficult to rouse
segments.rationale: A change in level of consciousness, and altered mentation with falling pressure signals decompensation.

segments.text: Client has not had a bowel movement since surgery two days ago
segments.rationale: Worth addressing and not among the three highest priorities.

segments.text: Family asks when the client can have visitors
segments.rationale: Not a clinical finding.

questions.takeaway: Report the trend, not the isolated number, and lead with perfusion and mentation.
questions.strategy: When a stem asks for a fixed number of findings, rank rather than select. Two options may be real concerns and still not make the top three. Some unselected findings are still worth addressing later.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Three findings describe a change over time; the rest are static.
Circulation and level of consciousness outrank elimination and comfort.
Exactly three are requested, so a fourth selection costs you.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s3, and s5.

questions.stem: A charge nurse reviews delegation with a new graduate who has been assigning tasks to assistive personnel for the first time. The new graduate describes what she delegated during the shift and how. Which statement by the new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I need to say what readings should be reported back to me."
options.rationale: Accurate. Right directions and communication includes the reporting threshold.

options.text: "The initial admission assessment is one task that cannot be delegated."
options.rationale: Accurate. It establishes the baseline others judge against.

options.text: "Vital signs are routine, so they can go to assistive personnel on any client."
options.rationale: The task is delegable and the client decides it. An unstable client with an unpredictable outcome stays with the RN however routine the task appears.

options.text: "Contact precautions change the PPE worn, not who may provide the care."
options.rationale: Accurate. Isolation status does not alter scope.

questions.takeaway: Read the client, not just the task. Four things never move: initial assessment, evaluation, teaching, and unstable clients.
questions.strategy: A delegable task on an unstable client is not delegable. The stability of the client is the deciding variable.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The task is routine; the client may not be.
Reporting threshold, initial assessment, and PPE are correct.
Any client is the word that makes it wrong.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: the client's stability decides it.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old is discharged after a stroke with a rehabilitation bed arranged, home oxygen at 2 L, four new medications, and a swallowing assessment pending. Which role coordinates his care across these settings?

options.text: Shared governance
options.rationale: Staff participation in unit decisions, not a care delivery model.

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: A staffing structure within one unit.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Someone coordinates care across settings and over time, with attention to outcomes and resource use.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: One RN following a client within the admission, not across settings.

questions.takeaway: If the stem crosses settings or agencies, think case management. Case management coordinates a client's care across settings and over time, including beyond discharge.
questions.strategy: Staffing models operate inside a unit. Case management is the one that reaches past discharge.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three different settings after discharge.
Both are unit staffing structures.
A governance structure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: someone coordinates care across settings and over time, with attention to outcomes and resource use.

questions.concept: Case management coordinates a client's care across settings and over time, including beyond discharge.

questions.stem: A nurse works a shift on a medical unit. She is assigned five clients, decides the order in which to see them, telephones a provider to question an order she believes is unsafe, and later answers for a task she delegated that was not completed correctly. Match each situation with the concept it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse is assigned five clients and is expected to complete their assessments and medications this shift
items.rationale: What you are supposed to do, meaning your job duties. It points at the work.

items.text: A nurse decides to ambulate a client before completing routine charting, based on her clinical judgment
items.rationale: Freedom to make independent choices within your scope, without waiting to be told.

items.text: A nurse calls the provider to question an order she believes is unsafe
items.rationale: Legal power to act, and it explicitly includes the power to question an order.

items.text: A nurse answers for a delegated task that was not completed correctly under her supervision
items.rationale: Answering for outcomes. It does not transfer even when the task does.

questions.takeaway: Responsibility is what you have. Autonomy is deciding. Authority is the power to act. Accountability is answering for it. Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.
questions.strategy: These four are tested as a set. Sort by direction: at the work, at the decision, at the power, or back at you. These four sit inside decentralization and shared governance. Sort them by what each one points at.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An assignment of clients is responsibility.
Choosing the order of care is autonomy.
Questioning an order is authority.
Answering afterward is accountability.

questions.concept: Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.

questions.stem: Staff nurses review three months of their own fall data, write a new prevention protocol, and present it to the manager, who adopts it. Which concept does this demonstrate?

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Answering for the outcomes of your own actions.

options.text: Shared governance
options.rationale: The nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why such protocols are followed.

options.text: Delegation
options.rationale: The transfer of a task to another person.

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Coordinating a client's care across settings and over time.

questions.takeaway: Shared governance is about who participates. Decentralization is about how far down decisions are pushed. Shared governance means the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why protocols they helped write get followed.
questions.strategy: These two appear together often. Ask whether the stem is about participation or about the level at which a decision is made.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staff nurses writing the protocol they will use.
The transfer of a task to another person.
Coordinating a client's care across settings and over time.
Answering for the outcomes of your own actions.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the nurses who deliver care participate in the decisions that govern it, which is why such protocols are followed.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse is planning assignments for a team of one RN, one LPN/LVN, and one assistive personnel.
questions.stem: For each task, click to specify which staff members may appropriately perform it. Each task may be appropriate for more than one.

rows.text: Obtaining vital signs on a stable client
rows.rationale: Routine data collection on a stable client sits within every scope.

rows.text: Performing the initial admission assessment
rows.rationale: Establishes the baseline others judge against and cannot be delegated.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the RN has already begun
rows.rationale: The LPN assists with implementation of a defined plan. Initiating teaching remains the RN's.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a client met the goal in the care plan
rows.rationale: Evaluation requires interpretation.

rows.text: Assisting a stable client with bathing and grooming
rows.rationale: Within every scope, though it is usually delegated.

rows.text: Administering an intramuscular medication
rows.rationale: Within LPN scope in many states, and medication administration varies with education and the state nurse practice act.

rows.text: Assessing a client whose condition has become unstable
rows.rationale: An unstable client with an unpredictable outcome stays with the RN.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: Four things never move: initial assessment, evaluation, teaching, and unstable clients.

steps.detail: The RN may perform every task listed.
Initial assessment, evaluation, and the unstable client.
Reinforcing teaching yes, initiating no.

questions.stem: A nurse manager explains that the unit's practice model treats clients and families as partners rather than as recipients of care, and that the model rests on four specific elements. options.text: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, and collaboration

options.text: Situation, background, assessment, recommendation

SBAR.
Interprofessional competencies.
TeamSTEPPS pillars.

questions.stem: A new graduate says she does not see herself as a leader because she manages no one. Her preceptor explains that leading her own client care requires a specific set of learnable skills used every shift. Which skills does this describe?

options.text: Policy writing and chairing committees within the organization
options.rationale: Governance activities, not the ground-level set.

options.text: Budgeting, staffing, and scheduling for the unit as a whole
options.rationale: Management functions rather than the bedside leadership skills specified.

options.text: Research design and statistical analysis
options.rationale: Not the skills.

options.text: Clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication
options.rationale: Correct, with team communication delivered through SBAR, CUS, and TeamSTEPPS. Leadership skills are learnable and practical, not abstract.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ground-level skills for leading your own client care.
Management functions.
Neither is the correct set.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: specified directly, with team communication delivered through SBAR, CUS, and TeamSTEPPS.

questions.concept: The LEARN model structures a cross-cultural encounter: Listen to the client's perception, Explain your own, Acknowledge differences, Recommend a plan, Negotiate agreement. questions.stem: A charge nurse assigns work to assistive personnel. Client A awaits discharge after an uncomplicated appendectomy. Client B's blood pressure has fallen from 122/70 to 92/58 over three readings. Client C is on contact precautions with a healing wound. Client D is afebrile on routine antibiotics. Which client's vital signs should NOT be delegated?

options.text: A client whose blood pressure has fallen across the last three readings
options.rationale: A trend is not a stable situation. You take these yourself because you need the number as it exists, along with what you notice while taking it.

options.text: A client on contact precautions with a healing surgical wound
options.rationale: Isolation status changes the PPE worn, not who may take a vital sign.

options.text: A client receiving routine intravenous antibiotics who is afebrile
options.rationale: Stable and predictable.

options.text: A client awaiting discharge after an uncomplicated appendectomy
options.rationale: Stable with a predictable outcome.

questions.stem: A hospital preparing a Magnet application must demonstrate that its nursing practice environment meets the program's standards. A staff nurse asks what will actually be assessed. Which response is accurate?

options.rationale: Magnet assesses the practice environment rather than individual performance.

options.text: Structures and processes, including shared decision-making and leadership

options.text: Physician satisfaction scores and medical outcome data
options.rationale: Nursing-sensitive outcomes reflect nursing care, which is what the program measures.

options.text: Compliance with state licensing inspections only
options.rationale: Licensing is a separate regulatory requirement rather than a recognition program.

steps.detail: The practice environment as a whole.

Nursing-sensitive outcomes reflect nursing care.
Licensing is a separate regulatory process.

questions.concept: The Magnet Recognition Program and nursing-sensitive outcomes are how nursing quality is measured, as distinct from medical outcomes.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to delegate several tasks to assistive personnel and wants to be sure she is meeting each of the conditions that make a delegation safe and defensible. Which are among the five rights of delegation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Right task
options.rationale: Is this task appropriate to delegate?

options.text: Right to refuse the assignment
options.rationale: The right to refuse belongs to the ten rights of medication administration. It is not one of the five rights of delegation.

options.text: Right person
options.rationale: Is the person competent and qualified?

options.text: Right documentation
options.rationale: Documentation matters and is not one of the five. This is a right of medication administration, which is a different framework.

options.text: Right directions and communication
options.rationale: Clear instructions, expectations, and what to report.

options.text: Right documentation of the outcome

questions.stem: A nurse believes a client needs unhurried discharge teaching on four new medications. She has six clients, two admissions pending, and 25 minutes before he leaves. She knows what good care requires and cannot deliver it. Which term describes her experience?

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: You know what is right and something outside you prevents it. The barrier is staffing and time.

options.text: Ethical dilemma
options.rationale: Requires that you do NOT know what is right, because two defensible options pull against each other. Here nothing is unclear.

options.text: Values conflict
options.rationale: Would mean her values clash with someone else's.

options.text: Negligence
options.rationale: A legal term requiring a breach of the standard of care.

questions.takeaway: One question separates them: do you know what is right? No means dilemma. Yes, and you are blocked, means moral distress. Moral distress is knowing what is right and being prevented from doing it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which of two defensible positions is right.
questions.strategy: Phrases like the nurse believes or the nurse knows signal that the right action is already clear, which points at moral distress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She knows what is right, so it is not a dilemma.
No competing values between people are described.
No breach of the standard of care has occurred.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Unaddressed moral distress drives burnout.

questions.concept: Moral distress is knowing what is right and being prevented from doing it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which of two defensible positions is right.

options.text: Conceal the medication in food so the client receives the dose
options.rationale: Removes consent entirely and is never acceptable, however compassionate the intent.

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: So the plan can be reconsidered.

options.rationale: Noncompliant is a judgment. Documentation must be factual: what was refused and what the client said.

options.text: Document the refusal and the client's stated reason
options.rationale: The factual entry that belongs in the record.

questions.takeaway: Confirm understanding, notify the provider, and document factually. Not to change the client's mind.

questions.stem: A competent 78-year-old with a written advance directive declining intubation develops a saturation of 84% and rising carbon dioxide. His daughter demands intubation. Which ethical principle guides the nurse?

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: The competent client decides. Confirming understanding first is what makes it autonomy rather than abandonment.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: The most dangerous distractor in ethics. Doing what you believe is good for a competent person who has refused it is not beneficence, it is a violation of autonomy.

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Keeping promises and commitments, which is not what is here.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Concerns fair distribution of resources, and no allocation question is present.

questions.takeaway: Beneficence never overrides autonomy for a competent client. Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with.
questions.strategy: When a competent client has stated a wish, autonomy usually wins. Look for the option that names the client's authority.

questions.stem: A care team disagrees with a family about continuing aggressive treatment for a client with an advance directive requesting comfort measures. Place the following actions in the correct order the nurse should take to work toward resolution, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Gather all relevant clinical, social, and spiritual information about the situation
options.rationale: You cannot reason about a situation you have not described. Gathering comes after recognizing there is an ethical question and before values are sorted.

options.text: Recognize that the situation involves an ethical problem, not just a clinical one
options.rationale: Nothing else can happen until the problem is ethical. Treated as purely clinical, the disagreement gets managed rather than resolved.

options.text: Clarify the values and key ethical principles and relationships involved
options.rationale: With the facts assembled, name whose values are in play and which principles collide. Here autonomy and beneficence pull against each other.

options.text: List the possible actions that could be taken to address the disagreement
options.rationale: Options are generated only after the values are clear, otherwise you are choosing between actions without knowing what you are optimizing for.

options.text: Develop and implement a plan that addresses the identified problem
options.rationale: Acting comes last, and it addresses the problem as defined rather than the surface disagreement.

questions.takeaway: Recognize it as ethical, gather information, clarify values, list options, then act. An ethical dilemma involves two defensible positions grounded in different principles, where nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested. An advance directive documents a client's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.
questions.strategy: Ordered-response items reward finding the first and last step before sorting the middle. Recognition almost always opens a process and implementation almost always closes it.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Recognizing the problem as ethical must precede everything.
Implementing a plan is the only action step.
Information, then values, then options. Each depends on the one before it.

elimination.verdict: B, A, C, D, E.

rows.rationale: An action taken to produce benefit.

rows.rationale: Refraining in order to prevent foreseeable harm.

rows.rationale: The client decides, and understanding was confirmed.

rows.rationale: Stopping to prevent tissue injury.

questions.takeaway: Acting to help is beneficence. Refraining to prevent injury is nonmaleficence. The client deciding is autonomy. Scarcity is justice. questions.stem: A nurse reviews the chart of a client with advanced illness whose family disagrees with the plan of care. The record contains laboratory values, routine care entries, a written directive, and notes about the disagreement. Highlight the findings that indicate an ethical problem rather than a purely clinical one.

segments.text: Client has a written advance directive requesting comfort measures only
segments.rationale: A documented decision. On its own it is a clinical fact to follow, not a conflict.

segments.text: Adult daughter has asked staff to continue aggressive treatment against the directive
segments.rationale: Two defensible positions grounded in different principles, autonomy and beneficence.

segments.text: Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL
segments.rationale: A laboratory value requiring clinical judgment, not ethical reasoning.

segments.text: A staff nurse has told the client's family that the directive can be ignored if they insist
segments.rationale: Misinformation that undermines the client's documented autonomy.

segments.text: Client received scheduled analgesia at 0800
segments.rationale: Routine care.

segments.text: Team members disagree about whether the client's quality of life justifies further treatment
segments.rationale: Quality of life is contested because it is culturally shaped, individually defined, and largely unmeasurable.

segments.text: Client is unresponsive and cannot participate in the discussion
segments.rationale: A clinical fact that raises the stakes and is not itself the ethical problem.

questions.takeaway: Recognizing that a situation involves an ethical problem is the first step in working toward resolution.
questions.strategy: An ethical problem exists where defensible positions conflict or where someone's documented autonomy is at risk. A difficult clinical fact is not the same thing. Several findings are clinically significant without being ethical problems. Highlight only the ethical ones.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two parties wanting different things on principled grounds.
Misinformation about a directive threatens the client's decision.
Laboratory values and routine care are clinical, not ethical.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s2, s4, and s6.

questions.stem: Two clients need the unit's only negative-pressure room. One has suspected tuberculosis with a three-week cough and a temperature of 38.1 C. The other is neutropenic with a white cell count of 0.6. Which ethical principle guides the decision?

options.text: Fidelity
options.rationale: Fidelity is keeping promises and commitments, which is not what a decision about allocating a scarce room turns on.

options.text: Beneficence
options.rationale: Would describe doing good for one client, but the question is how to choose between two.

options.text: Justice
options.rationale: Fairness in the distribution of a scarce resource, allocated on clinical risk rather than on who advocated loudest.

options.text: Autonomy
options.rationale: Would apply if a client were making a decision, and neither is.

questions.takeaway: Justice questions almost always involve scarcity. One bed, one room, limited staff, triage.
questions.strategy: Look for two claimants and one resource. That structure names the principle before you read the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two clients, one room.
The question is allocation, not care of one.
No promise and no client decision.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: fairness in the distribution of a scarce resource, allocated on clinical risk rather than on who advocated loudest.

questions.stem: A family asks the nurse not to tell a client about a new cancer diagnosis. The client has asked the nurse three times what the tests showed. What is the nurse's BEST action?

options.text: Agree to the family's request to protect the client
options.rationale: Abandons the client's autonomy and makes you party to withholding information they have requested.

options.text: Document the family's request and take no further action
options.rationale: Records the problem and leaves the client exactly where they were.

options.text: Tell the client the diagnosis directly
options.rationale: Well-intentioned and outside your role. Disclosure of a diagnosis belongs to the provider.

options.text: Explore the family's concerns and notify the provider
options.rationale: Neither agrees to the deception nor steps outside your scope. Exploring usually surfaces fear, and the provider is the one who discloses.

questions.takeaway: When a family asks you to withhold information, the answer is rarely yes or no. It is explore, then involve the provider.
questions.strategy: Two options here are the obvious poles. The answer is almost always the one that works the problem rather than resolving it in either direction. More than one action may eventually be needed. Select the action that is both within scope and responsive to the client.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word BEST, and the client has asked repeatedly.
Violates the client's autonomy and makes you party to withholding information he has requested.
Outside nursing scope.
Documents without acting.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: neither agrees to the deception nor steps outside your scope.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews four staff actions from the past week: an error reported immediately, a workstation logged out before leaving the room, a client's wishes relayed to a provider despite family objection, and a stated return time kept exactly. Match each nursing action with the ethical or legal term it BEST demonstrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A nurse discovers a medication error, immediately notifies the provider and manager, and completes an occurrence report
items.rationale: Accountability is answering for your own actions. Owning the error and reporting it is the definition in practice.

items.text: A nurse steps away from a shared workstation and logs out of the record before administering a medication in another room
items.rationale: Protecting information from those without a need to know. An open record under your login exposes data and attributes anything done next to you.

items.text: A nurse contacts the primary provider to relay a client's wish for comfort care despite family objections
items.rationale: Advocacy promotes care that reflects the client's wishes. It points outward at the client, even when others disagree.

items.text: A nurse says, "I will be back in 20 minutes with your next dose," and returns at the stated time
items.rationale: Responsibility is following through on what you accepted. Keeping a stated commitment is the everyday form of it.

questions.takeaway: Accountability points back at you, responsibility points at the work, advocacy points at the client, confidentiality protects the information.
questions.strategy: Matching items are answered by direction. Ask where each action points before reaching for a definition. Two of these terms are frequently confused. Decide whether the action answers for the past or delivers on the present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Backward at yourself, at the work, outward at the client, or at the information.
Logging out is unambiguously confidentiality.
Each term is used once, so the last pairing is fixed by elimination.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to give metoprolol 50 mg orally. The client's apical rate is 44, down from 62 this morning, and his blood pressure is 96/54. She withholds the dose and notifies the provider. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.text: Autonomy, the client's right to make his own decisions
options.rationale: The pair-mate and the trap. Beneficence is acting to do good; this nurse withheld an action.

options.text: Fidelity, keeping promises and honoring commitments made
options.rationale: Keeping promises and commitments, which is not what is here.

options.text: Nonmaleficence
options.rationale: The nurse refrained in order to prevent harm. A rate of 44 with a drug that slows the heart is foreseeable injury.

options.text: Justice, the fair distribution of benefits and burdens
options.rationale: Fairness in allocation.

questions.takeaway: Ask whether the nurse acted or refrained. Adding something is beneficence; withholding to prevent injury is nonmaleficence. Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm. Beneficence is the duty to act for the client's benefit.
questions.strategy: When both principles appear as options, the verb in the stem decides it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Withholds is the key word.
Beneficence requires an action taken.
Neither truth-telling nor allocation is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the nurse refrained in order to prevent harm.

questions.concept: Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid causing harm. Beneficence is the duty to act for the client's benefit.

questions.stem: A disagreement about the goals of care for a client with advanced illness cannot be resolved between the team and the family. Both positions are defensible, no law has been broken, and the discussion has stalled after two meetings. Which resource does the nurse recommend?

options.text: The charge nurse, who oversees the unit that shift
options.rationale: Manages the shift, not the ethical question.

options.text: The multidisciplinary ethics committee
options.rationale: The body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in client care. Multidisciplinary matters, because the point is several perspectives on one hard case.

options.text: Risk management, which reviews incidents and hazards
options.rationale: Prevents harm and financial loss from liability, and is problem-focused rather than values-focused.

options.text: The State Board of Nursing, which regulates licensure
options.rationale: Handles licensure and discipline and enforces the standard of care. Legal, not philosophical, and it is the trap worth understanding.

questions.takeaway: Ethical course of action means the ethics committee. Discipline or licensure means the Board. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Sort by what the body does. One writes standards, one advises on a case, one disciplines licensees, one manages liability.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An unresolved values disagreement in client care.
A staffing role.
Discipline and licensure.
Liability prevention.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in client care.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A care team is struggling to agree on a plan for a client with a severe chronic illness because members disagree about the client's quality of life. Which statements help explain why consensus on this term is difficult to reach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Community and cultural values shape definitions of quality, and these values shift over time
options.rationale: Quality of life is socially constructed, so the standard itself moves between groups and across decades.

options.text: A person's individual life experiences influence how they personally define quality of life
options.rationale: Two people with identical function can rate their lives very differently based on what they have lived.

options.text: Elements such as meaningful work and family relationships are difficult to measure objectively
options.rationale: The components that matter most to people resist measurement, which is why teams cannot simply check them.

options.text: Whether a person is employed is the single objective measure that should determine quality of life
options.rationale: Reduces a contested multidimensional concept to one variable, and employment status says nothing about meaning.

options.text: Outcomes that cannot be easily quantified are difficult to evaluate using standard statistical methods
options.rationale: Unmeasurable outcomes cannot be compared across clients, which is part of why evidence does not settle the disagreement.

questions.takeaway: Quality of life is contested because it is culturally shaped, individually defined, and largely unmeasurable.
questions.strategy: The wrong option in a quality-of-life item is usually the one offering a single objective substitute for the whole concept. One option offers a simple measurable substitute for a complex concept. That is the distractor pattern here.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: The question asks why consensus is hard, so correct options explain difficulty.
Single and should determine are both absolutes, and employment is not a proxy for meaning.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse educator discusses ethical reasoning with staff after a conflict between a family and the team over an advance directive. Staff describe how they think about codes, dilemmas, and distress. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "An ethical dilemma means two defensible positions, not that someone is behaving badly."
options.rationale: Accurate. Both positions rest on real principles.

options.text: "Moral distress is knowing what is right and being prevented from doing it."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is distinct from a dilemma.

options.text: "The ethics committee is the body that helps determine a course of action."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is consulted when a dilemma arises in client care.

options.text: "If I disagree with a provision of the code of ethics, it does not bind me."
options.rationale: A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles that all members of a profession accept. Disagreeing with a provision does not release you from it.

questions.takeaway: All members of a profession accept the code. You do not opt in selectively.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement treats a professional code as a personal position. That distinction is the whole point of having a code.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
All members accept it.
Dilemma, distress, and the committee are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: disagreement does not release you.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate an ethical or legal problem requiring the nurse's action.
questions.takeaway: Recognizing that a situation involves an ethical problem is the first step in working toward resolution. An advance directive documents a client's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.
questions.strategy: Two findings here are clinically significant without being ethical problems. The orders are correct and the vital signs fit the plan. Two findings are clinically significant and are not ethical problems.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two parties wanting different things on principled grounds.
Misinformation about a directive threatens his decision.
The orders and the vital signs are not problems.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s4.

questions.nursesNote: 1600: Client is 79, admitted four days ago with advanced heart failure. Written advance directive in the record requesting comfort measures only, signed two years ago and witnessed. Client became unresponsive this morning. Two adult children present and insisting that everything be done, stating they will hold the nurse responsible if their father dies. Provider has written orders consistent with the directive. A staff nurse has told the family the directive can be set aside if they insist. Charting from the previous shift reads "family difficult and unrealistic." VS: T 36.4 C; HR 58 and irregular; RR 10; BP 84/50; SpO2 88% on 4 L.

segments.text: Family insisting on full treatment against a written advance directive
segments.rationale: Two defensible positions grounded in different principles: the family's beneficence against the client's autonomy. That is an ethical dilemma.

segments.text: A staff nurse telling the family the directive can be set aside if they insist
segments.rationale: Misinformation that undermines the client's documented autonomy, and it will make the conflict worse.

segments.text: Charting that reads "family difficult and unrealistic"
segments.rationale: A judgment rather than a factual entry. Documentation records what was said and done.

segments.text: Family stating they will hold the nurse responsible
segments.rationale: Pressure directed at the nurse. It does not change what the client decided, and the nurse needs support to withstand it.

segments.text: Provider orders consistent with the advance directive
segments.rationale: Correct practice. The orders match the client's documented decision.

segments.text: Heart rate 58 and irregular with SpO2 88% on 4 liters
segments.rationale: Clinical findings consistent with the client's condition and his comfort-focused plan, rather than an ethical problem.

questions.caseTitle: Conflict at the end of life
questions.concept: An advance directive documents a client's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: A written directive speaks for the client when the client cannot. Family preference does not override it. Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with. An ethical dilemma involves two defensible positions grounded in different principles, where nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested.
questions.strategy: The family's threat is deliberate pressure. It does not change what the client decided and it does not make the nurse's response colder.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Autonomy against beneficence, both defensible.
Overrides his own decision.
Wrong body for a care decision.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: The situation is best described as [[1]], and the nurse should [[2]].

options.text: an ethical dilemma between the client's autonomy and the family's beneficence
options.rationale: Two defensible positions, each grounded in a real principle. Nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested.

options.text: moral distress in the nurse
options.rationale: Would require the nurse to know what is right and be blocked from it. Here the orders and the directive agree, so she is not blocked.

options.text: a legal violation by the family
options.rationale: Disagreeing with a directive is not itself unlawful.

options.text: follow the directive and the current orders while supporting the family, and request an ethics consultation
options.rationale: The directive is the client's own decision and carries legal weight. The ethics committee is the body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in client care.

options.text: provide resuscitative measures because the family has demanded them
options.rationale: Overrides the client's documented decision on the basis of family preference.

options.text: contact the State Board of Nursing for direction
options.rationale: The Board handles licensure and discipline. It does not advise on a client's care decisions.

questions.caseTitle: Conflict at the end of life
questions.concept: Autonomy is the client's right to make their own decisions about their care, including decisions the team disagrees with. An ethical dilemma involves two defensible positions grounded in different principles, where nobody is behaving badly and the right action is contested.

questions.stem: Reviewing the record, the nurse finds the entry "family difficult and unrealistic" and a set of vital signs charted on the wrong client earlier in the shift. Which 2 actions should she take?
questions.takeaway: Single line, label it, initial and date. Never erase, and never reference an occurrence report in the chart. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed. An occurrence report is a risk management tool for identifying hazards. It is not part of the medical record and must never be referenced in the chart.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options either destroy the original or pull a risk management document into the legal record. One wrong option concerns a document that does not belong in the chart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A judgmental entry and a misfiled set of observations.
Correction fluid and deletion both conceal.
It stays outside the record.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Correct the wrong-client entry by drawing a single line through it, labeling it, and initialing and dating it
options.rationale: The original must remain readable. Obliterating or erasing suggests concealment.

options.text: Document the family's stated concerns factually rather than as a characterization
options.rationale: Documentation is factual and specific. What they said and what was discussed belongs in the record; a judgment does not.

options.text: Use correction fluid to remove the wrong-client entry
options.rationale: Never erase, black out, or use correction fluid. The original entry must remain readable.

options.text: Delete the previous nurse's entry about the family
options.rationale: You do not alter another clinician's entry. You add your own factual documentation.

options.text: Chart that an occurrence report was completed about the misfiled entry
options.rationale: The occurrence report is a risk management tool and is not part of the medical record.

options.text: Leave the wrong-client entry in place and note the correct information elsewhere
options.rationale: Leaves inaccurate data in a client's record where someone may act on it.

questions.caseTitle: Conflict at the end of life
questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed. An occurrence report is a risk management tool for identifying hazards. It is not part of the medical record and must never be referenced in the chart.

questions.stem: For each proposed action, determine whether it is INDICATED or NOT INDICATED at this point.
questions.takeaway: Recognize it as ethical, gather information, clarify values, list options, then act.
questions.strategy: Two proposed actions treat a values conflict as paperwork or as something to hand to someone else. One proposed action treats a disagreement about values as an administrative problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The conflict is specified and unresolved.
An objection is not revoked administratively.
Avoidance resolves nothing.

elimination.verdict: Four actions are indicated and two are not.

rows.text: Request a multidisciplinary ethics committee consultation
rows.rationale: The body that determines an ethical course of action when a dilemma arises in client care, and the discussion has stalled.

rows.text: Gather the clinical, social, and spiritual information about the situation
rows.rationale: The second step of the process. You cannot reason about a situation you have not described.

rows.text: Correct the colleague's misinformation with the family
rows.rationale: They have been told the directive can be set aside, and that will shape every conversation until it is addressed.

rows.text: Ask the family to sign a form withdrawing their objection
rows.rationale: Their objection is not a document to be revoked, and it treats a values conflict as an administrative one.

rows.text: Continue comfort measures as the directive and orders specify
rows.rationale: Comfort measures only is an active plan, and it remains the client's documented decision.

rows.text: Transfer the client to another nurse to avoid the conflict
rows.rationale: Avoidance leaves the family without support and the dilemma unresolved.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: Recognize it as ethical, gather information, clarify values, list options, weigh them, act, evaluate.
questions.strategy: The step people skip is gathering. A dilemma feels like it needs a decision, and it needs a description first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recognition has already happened.
Gathering the information.
Both come later or belong elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: Having recognized the ethical problem, the nurse's next step is to [[1]], and the step that follows is [[2]].

options.text: gather the clinical, social, and spiritual information about the situation
options.rationale: The second step. You cannot reason about a situation you have not described.

options.text: decide which principle outranks the other
options.rationale: Principles are weighed after the information and the values have been gathered.

options.text: act on the position with the strongest legal backing
options.rationale: Acting comes near the end, after options have been listed and weighed.

options.text: clarify the values held by everyone involved
options.rationale: The family's position rests on values, and naming them is what makes the conflict workable.

options.text: document the disagreement in the client's record
options.rationale: The record holds clinical facts, not an account of an interprofessional dispute.

options.text: transfer the client to another nurse
options.rationale: Avoidance leaves the family unsupported and the dilemma unresolved.

questions.stem: For each finding two days after the ethics consultation, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with the original situation, or whether it is a NEW FINDING.
questions.takeaway: Some things should not change. Comfort measures only was the correct plan on day one and on day three.
questions.strategy: The unchanged row here is the success, not the failure. A plan that was right at the start stays right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings were recorded originally.
The plan was correct throughout.
Chaplaincy and the nurse's own experience.

elimination.verdict: Three improved, one unchanged, two new findings.

questions.note: One unchanged finding reflects a correct plan rather than a stalled one.

rows.text: The family understands the directive and has withdrawn the objection
rows.rationale: The misinformation has been corrected and the conflict has resolved.

rows.text: The colleague's misinformation has been addressed directly and privately
rows.rationale: The source of the escalation has been removed.

rows.rationale: The documentation meets the standard.

questions.stem: A home health nurse notes multiple bruises in various stages of healing on the head, abdomen, and posterior legs of a nonambulatory 8-month-old infant. The caregiver states the bruises are from the infant rolling off the couch a few times. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Discuss the situation with a colleague for a second opinion before acting
options.rationale: Delays a mandated report. The standard is reasonable suspicion, not certainty.

options.text: Report the reasonable suspicion of abuse to the appropriate child protective authority
options.rationale: Nurses are mandated reporters. A nonambulatory infant cannot produce bruises in varied stages across those sites, so the explanation is not plausible and the threshold for reporting is met now.

options.text: Confront the caregiver about the inconsistency in the explanation he gave
options.rationale: Risks the child's safety by alerting a possible perpetrator, and it is not the nurse's role to investigate.

options.text: Document the findings in detail and complete a full physical assessment
options.rationale: Essential and not first. Documentation supports the report; it does not substitute for making it.

questions.takeaway: Mandated reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and it is not delayed for confirmation.
questions.strategy: The detail that decides this is nonambulatory. An infant who cannot move independently cannot self-inflict bruises in multiple stages across several body regions. Documentation is essential, but consider which action is legally mandated FIRST given a nonambulatory infant with these findings.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word FIRST, with a nonambulatory infant and an implausible explanation.
Documentation supports but does not replace the report.
Investigation is not the nurse's role and may endanger the child.
Reasonable suspicion is the threshold, so no second opinion is required.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: nurses are mandated reporters.

questions.stem: A client in skeletal traction develops pale, cold toes with decreased sensation. The nurse becomes occupied with another client's emergency and never documents or reports the finding. Two days later the leg requires amputation. Which statements correctly describe a breach of duty in this situation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Failure to document the change in neurovascular assessment findings
options.rationale: Documentation is part of the standard of care, and an undocumented finding is invisible to everyone who follows.

options.text: Failure to notify the provider about a significant change in condition
options.rationale: The change required an order to act on, and the omission is the direct link to the harm.

options.text: Failure to provide discharge teaching about cast care
options.rationale: Not relevant to this injury. The client is in traction and the harm occurred during the admission.

options.text: Failure to recognize and act on early signs of impaired circulation
options.rationale: A reasonably prudent nurse recognizes pale, cold, insensate toes as neurovascular compromise.

options.text: Failure to complete an occurrence report for the other client's emergency
options.rationale: Unrelated to this client's harm and not a breach of duty toward him.

questions.takeaway: Breach of duty means conduct fell below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do, and it must connect to the harm. The standard of care is what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Not the best nurse, and not the nurse's own opinion.
questions.strategy: Two options here describe real nursing responsibilities that are not connected to this client's injury. Relevance to the harm is what makes an omission a breach. Two options describe nursing responsibilities that are real but unconnected to this client's harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The harm is amputation from unrecognized circulatory compromise.
Cast care teaching is unrelated to a client in traction.
Concerns a different client.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and D are selected.

questions.concept: The standard of care is what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances. Not the best nurse, and not the nurse's own opinion.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old is confused and pulling at her intravenous line, which she has dislodged once. Her temperature is 38.3 C, her saturation is 91%, and she received oxycodone two hours ago. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Raise all four side rails so she cannot get out of the bed unassisted
options.rationale: Four raised side rails constitute a restraint, which students frequently do not realize.

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints to stop her pulling at the intravenous line
options.rationale: Restraints are a last resort and can worsen confusion and agitation.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative so she will settle overnight
options.rationale: Adds to the medication burden that may be causing the confusion.

options.text: Assess for the cause of the confusion and try least restrictive measures
options.rationale: Confusion has a cause, and infection, hypoxia, medications, and dehydration are all reversible. Least restrictive intervention comes first.

questions.takeaway: Least restrictive intervention first, and four raised side rails count as a restraint. Restraints are a last resort requiring an order, after least restrictive measures have been tried. They worsen delirium and agitation.
questions.strategy: Three of these options are restraints or chemical restraint in different clothing. Only one assesses.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Key word FIRST, with confusion of unknown cause.
Both are restraints.
Chemical restraint, and it may worsen the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: confusion has a cause, and infection, hypoxia, medications, and dehydration are all reversible.

questions.concept: Restraints are a last resort requiring an order, after least restrictive measures have been tried. They worsen delirium and agitation.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing annual compliance training and is asked which law governs how client information is stored, accessed, and shared, as distinct from the law defining what she may do as a nurse. Which federal statute governs the privacy and security of protected health information?

options.text: The Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Requires that clients be informed of their right to make advance directives, which is a different federal statute.

options.text: The Good Samaritan law
options.rationale: Protects voluntary aid at an emergency scene.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, which sets the privacy and security standards for protected health information.

options.text: The Nurse Practice Act
options.rationale: A state statute defining scope of practice.

questions.takeaway: HIPAA governs privacy and security of health information. The Nurse Practice Act is state law defining scope. A Nurse Practice Act is state law overseen by the State Board of Nursing. It defines scope of practice and exists to protect public health, safety, and welfare, not to protect the nurse or the employer. HIPAA is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. It provides rights to clients over their health information and sets privacy and security standards.
questions.strategy: Sort by level: federal statute, state statute, or a protection. Option A is a real federal statute addressing a different right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Privacy and security of health information.
State law on scope.
Emergency aid protection.
Advance directives, not privacy.

questions.stem: A nurse manager investigates four incidents on her unit in one month. Which actions constitute a breach of client confidentiality? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accessing the record of a family member on another unit out of curiosity
options.rationale: A privacy violation carrying federal penalties and board discipline. Being related to the client grants no access.

options.text: Applying physical restraints without an order and without following agency policy
options.rationale: Restraining a client without an order and outside agency policy is an intentional act causing harm, so it carries criminal exposure as well as licensure action for breaching the standard of care.

options.text: Reporting a reasonable suspicion of child abuse to the appropriate authority
options.rationale: A legally protected and mandated action. Good-faith reporting carries immunity.

options.text: Falsifying documentation of vital signs to avoid appearing behind
options.rationale: Fraudulent record-keeping is criminal and is grounds for licensure action.

options.text: Completing a routine occurrence report after a minor fall with no injury
options.rationale: A risk management process functioning as intended, not sanctionable conduct.

questions.takeaway: Privacy breaches, unauthorized restraint, and falsified records carry both criminal and licensure consequences. Mandated reporting is protected.
Occurrence reports are routine risk management.

options.text: "Reasonable suspicion is the threshold for a mandated report, rather than proof."

options.text: "I should reference the occurrence report in the client's chart."

questions.stem: A new graduate asks her preceptor what she can do to protect herself legally, having heard that nurses are frequently named in claims. The preceptor explains that the strongest protection is something she already does every shift. Which nursing action most reduces legal risk?

options.text: Documenting care accurately, completely, and at the time it is provided

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews three reported events: a client burned by a heating pad left on too long, a client discussed by name in a lift where another passenger recognized her, and a client harmed by care the nurse should have known was substandard. Match each event with the term it BEST illustrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A client is burned by a heating pad left on too long
items.rationale: A tort is a civil wrong: a wrongful act or omission of care made against a person or property. This is the standard example.

items.text: A nurse discusses a client by name in a lift and another passenger recognizes her
items.rationale: A quasi-intentional tort. You did not mean to cause harm and you did, through the nature of the act itself.

items.text: A client is harmed by care the nurse knew or should have known was substandard
items.rationale: An unintentional tort. Harm arises where the person inflicting it knew, or should have known, that the care fell below standard.

questions.takeaway: A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional means you did not mean harm and caused it. Unintentional means you knew or should have known the care was substandard. strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Disclosure in a lift causes harm through the act itself.
Knew or should have known is the unintentional tort wording.
Each term is used once.

A tort is a civil wrong. Quasi-intentional torts cause harm through the nature of the act. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known the care was substandard.

questions.stem: A nurse observes a colleague repeatedly documenting assessments she did not perform. She has raised it with the colleague directly and nothing has changed. The colleague tells her that reporting it would damage the unit. Which action is correct?

options.text: Take no further action, since she has already raised it with the colleague directly

options.rationale: An assessment recorded but never performed means decisions are being made on data that does not exist. Direct discussion has already failed, so the concern escalates.

options.rationale: The record is for clinical facts about the client, not for observations about a colleague.

options.text: Discuss it with other staff to see whether they have noticed the same thing
options.rationale: Talks about a colleague rather than reporting through the proper channel.

The record is for clinical facts about the client.

questions.stem: An order reads heparin 25,000 units subcutaneously every 12 hours for a 70 kg client. The usual prophylactic dose is 5,000 units. The prescriber is unavailable and the dose is due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Follow the chain of command to clarify the order before administering
options.rationale: The nurse must determine that an order is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the condition, and within scope. When it is not, you clarify before acting.

options.text: Administer the dose since the provider wrote the order
options.rationale: The most important wrong answer. Carrying out an incorrect order makes the error yours as well; the provider's responsibility does not erase yours.

options.text: Ask another nurse to administer it instead, since she is uncomfortable
options.rationale: Transfers the risk to a colleague and changes nothing about the order.

options.text: Refuse to give the medication and say nothing further to the prescriber
options.rationale: The client goes untreated and no one knows why.

questions.takeaway: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment.

questions.stem: A client admitted with a hemoglobin of 6.4 g/dL has a written advance directive declining blood products. He is alert and oriented. His spouse tells the nurse he did not mean it and asks her to proceed with the transfusion. Which action is correct?

options.text: Gather more information, including whether a power of attorney or directive exists
options.rationale: Both extremes act before the facts are known. A documented advance directive or a health care power of attorney converts the spouse's claim into a legally binding one.

options.text: Contact the hospital ethics committee before taking any further action on the order
options.rationale: Appropriate later if a genuine conflict remains, and it is not the first step in a hemorrhage.

options.text: Withhold the transfusion based on the spouse's statement about his beliefs
options.rationale: Acts on an unverified report of the client's wishes. A spouse does not automatically hold decision-making authority.

options.text: Administer the blood as ordered since the client has not personally refused
options.rationale: Ignores credible evidence about the client's values and treats silence as consent.

questions.takeaway: Verify decision-making authority before acting on a surrogate's report of what a client would want. An advance directive documents a client's own decisions about future care and speaks for them when they cannot. Family preference does not override it.

Both act on an incomplete picture, in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A nurse gives metoprolol 50 mg to a client whose apical rate is 48 without checking the hold parameter. He becomes symptomatic with a rate of 38 and requires transfer. Which legal concept does this illustrate?

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent, which is absent.

options.text: Negligence only
options.rationale: Not wrong so much as imprecise. Negligence is the broad category, and when a licensed professional commits it in that role the specific term is malpractice.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Covers acts such as breaching confidentiality, where harm was not intended but resulted from the nature of the act.

options.text: Malpractice
options.rationale: Negligence committed by a professional acting in that role. Duty existed, the armband check was omitted, conduct fell below the standard, and harm followed.

questions.takeaway: Malpractice is the professional species of negligence. Name a licensed professional in the stem and the answer is malpractice. Negligence is failing to act as a reasonable nurse would in similar circumstances. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm, judged against what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances.
questions.strategy: The standard is what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the same geographical area.

steps.detail: A licensed nurse acting in that role, with harm resulting.
Correct but not the specific term.
Neither intent nor a quasi-intentional act is present.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: negligence committed by a professional acting in that role.

questions.concept: Negligence is failing to act as a reasonable nurse would in similar circumstances. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm. Malpractice is professional negligence causing harm, judged against what a reasonable nurse with similar training would have done in similar circumstances.

questions.stem: A nurse admits a 76-year-old for elective surgery and asks whether he has documented his wishes about future care. He says his daughter will decide if anything goes wrong, but has signed nothing. Which statements about advance directives are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Family standing does not override a documented directive, and this is the assumption that creates the conflicts requiring ethics committees.

questions.stem: A nurse asks her manager which body of law defines what she may legally do as a nurse and which defines the duty she owes an individual client. She has been told that agency policy also governs her practice. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Statute defines scope through the practice act; common law establishes duty

options.rationale: Scope is set by statute.

options.text: Agency policy carries the same force as statute within the organization

questions.stem: A client scheduled for surgery is unable to describe the procedure and asks the nurse what will be done. The consent form is unsigned. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask another nurse to witness the signature
options.rationale: Witnesses a consent you know is not informed.

options.text: Have the client sign and document that teaching will follow
options.rationale: Reverses the order and records a consent obtained without understanding.

options.text: Explain the procedure so the consent can be signed
options.rationale: Generous and outside your role. Explaining the procedure belongs to the provider, and doing it yourself produces a signature on an explanation the provider never gave.

options.text: Stop the process and contact the provider
options.rationale: The nurse verifies that the client is competent, that the signature is voluntary, and that the client understands what the provider explained. Not understanding means the third condition has failed.

questions.takeaway: Confusion or not understanding is a stop signal, not a teaching opportunity. Informed consent requires three conditions: a competent client, given voluntarily, who understands what the provider explained. The nurse witnesses that understanding.

Explaining is the provider's role.
Both proceed with a consent known to be uninformed.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she has administered a scheduled medication to the wrong client. He is alert, asymptomatic, and the drug was not one he takes. She must respond before continuing her round. Place the following actions in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: Assess the client for effects of the medication given

options.rationale: The provider needs to know in order to prescribe monitoring or treatment.

options.text: Implement any prescribed monitoring or treatment
options.rationale: Acting on the orders that result from the notification.

options.text: Document the medication given, the assessment, and the provider notification in the record
options.rationale: The clinical facts belong in the record. Note that you document what happened, not that a report was filed.

options.text: Complete an occurrence report according to agency policy
options.rationale: A risk management tool, completed after the client is safe, and it is not part of the medical record.

questions.takeaway: Client first, provider second, treatment third, then the record, then the occurrence report. An occurrence report is a risk management tool for identifying hazards. It is not part of the medical record and must never be referenced in the chart.

Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Assessing the client outranks any administrative action.
The occurrence report is a systems tool and comes last.
Notify, treat, then document the clinical facts.

questions.stem: An off-duty nurse stops at the scene of a car crash and provides care until paramedics arrive. She receives no payment and acts within what she knows. Afterward she asks her manager what legal protection applies. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: She is fully protected regardless of what she does, since the situation was an emergency

options.text: Her nurse practice act does not apply outside her place of employment, so no standard governs her

Her license travels with her.
Regardless is absolute.
