questions.stem: A nurse completes an occurrence report after a client's minor fall with no injury. A colleague tells her she should not have filed it because it will be used against her, and asks whether it belongs in the chart. Which statement about the occurrence report is correct?

options.text: It is used to identify problems and take corrective action

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that support a concern for elder mistreatment.
questions.takeaway: Red flags: unexplained injury, poor hygiene, unmet needs, fearfulness, inconsistent explanations, a caregiver controlling communication, and financial concerns.

questions.nursesNote: 1015: Home health visit. Client is 79, lives with her adult son. Since the last visit five weeks ago she has lost 6 kg. Wearing clothing soiled with urine. Bruising noted on both upper arms in a grip pattern and on the left flank, in differing stages of healing. Client flinches when her son moves closer and looks to him before answering. Son answers every question directed at her and states she has been refusing to eat. His account of the arm bruising changes twice during the visit. Client's monthly pension has been withdrawn in full each month with no receipts for groceries or medication. Prescribed antihypertensive bottle is full and dated seven weeks ago. VS: T 36.2 C; HR 96; BP 158/92; SpO2 97%.

segments.text: Bruising on both upper arms in a grip pattern and on the flank, in differing stages
segments.rationale: Unexplained injuries are a specified red flag, and the bilateral grip pattern with varied ages is not consistent with a single accidental cause.

segments.text: Clothing soiled with urine and 6 kg weight loss
segments.rationale: Poor hygiene and unmet basic needs are red flags and both point toward neglect.

segments.text: Client flinches when her son moves closer
segments.rationale: Fearfulness is a red flag.

segments.text: Son answers every question and his account changes twice
segments.rationale: A caregiver controlling communication and inconsistent explanations are both specified red flags.

segments.text: Pension withdrawn in full each month with no receipts
segments.rationale: Financial abuse is one of the four specified types.

segments.text: Blood pressure 158/92
segments.rationale: Consistent with an untaken antihypertensive. It is a consequence to address rather than a red flag in itself.

segments.text: Client lives with her adult son
segments.rationale: A living arrangement. It is context, and it is not a finding.

questions.stem: A nurse hands over a client whose blood pressure has fallen from 130/80 to 96/58 across the shift, with a urine output of 20 mL over the past two hours. The oncoming nurse has four other clients and has not met him. Which handoff report best supports continuity?

questions.stem: A nurse documents a set of vital signs taken at twenty minutes past midnight. The unit records all times in the 24-hour clock. How is this time written?

That is 1:20 a.m., an hour later.

options.rationale: The occurrence report is not part of the medical record.

options.text: take no further action, since the entry has been struck
options.rationale: The correct client's record still has no entry for that time.

questions.caseTitle: Documentation and privacy at handover

questions.stem: A client is admitted following a house fire and remains in hospital for several days. The nurse observes an initial surge in heart rate and blood pressure, a period where the vital signs settle while the client remains under strain, and later a decline in her physical condition. Place the stages of the general adaptation syndrome in the correct order, from FIRST to LAST.

options.text: The body recognizes a stressor and activates the fight-or-flight response
options.rationale: Alarm. The sympathetic nervous system activates, producing increased heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, and blood glucose, plus sweating, muscle tension, dilated pupils, increased alertness, and decreased digestion.

options.text: The body attempts to adapt and stabilize while the stressor continues
options.rationale: Resistance. Vital signs may return toward normal while resources are being consumed, which is why a client can look stable and still be depleting.

options.text: Adaptive resources are depleted and physiological functioning declines
options.rationale: Exhaustion. When the stressor persists beyond the body's capacity to adapt, illness and organ effects follow.

questions.takeaway: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Resistance is where a client looks fine and is spending reserves. The general adaptation syndrome has three stages: alarm with sympathetic activation, resistance where the body adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion when adaptive resources are depleted.
questions.strategy: The stage most often misread is resistance, because normalized vital signs are mistaken for recovery. A client in the resistance stage may have near-normal vital signs. Stability is not the same as recovery.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recognition and sympathetic activation open the response.
Depletion closes it.
Adaptation while the stressor continues.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C. Alarm activates the sympathetic response, resistance adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion follows when adaptive resources run out.

questions.concept: The general adaptation syndrome has three stages: alarm with sympathetic activation, resistance where the body adapts while the stressor continues, and exhaustion when adaptive resources are depleted.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a colleague has become irritable, is making uncharacteristic errors, and has stopped talking about work at home. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Avoid discussing the feeling with colleagues to remain professional
options.rationale: Isolation worsens the response, and dialogue with colleagues is a support.

options.text: Recognize this as a possible stress response and seek support and coping strategies
options.rationale: Emotional numbing after repeated exposure to others' trauma is consistent with secondary traumatic stress, and coping and resilience can be built.

options.text: Continue working and expect the feeling to pass with experience
options.rationale: Untreated secondary traumatic stress accumulates rather than resolving.

options.text: Request transfer to a unit with no acutely ill clients
options.rationale: Avoidance may be part of a plan and does not by itself address the response.

questions.takeaway: Secondary traumatic stress is a recognized occupational response, and resilience is built rather than assumed.
questions.strategy: Any option that normalizes, avoids, or isolates a stress response in a nurse is wrong. nurse wellbeing is part of the content.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Emotional numbing after months of trauma exposure.
Normalizes without addressing.
Avoidance alone.
Isolation worsens it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: emotional numbing after repeated exposure to others' trauma is consistent with secondary traumatic stress, and coping and resilience can be built.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old admitted after a workplace injury reports difficulty sleeping, constant worry about lost income, and that the unit noise makes it worse. He asks the nurse what can be done. Which nursing interventions support a client managing stress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching relaxation techniques
options.rationale: Relaxation techniques act on the physiological arousal itself, which is why they help even when the stressor cannot be changed.

options.text: Requesting a sedative so the client sleeps tonight
options.rationale: Medicates the symptom without addressing what is producing it.

options.text: Assessing the environment for noise, privacy, and safety
options.rationale: Environmental cues are part of the assessment.

options.text: Advising the client to avoid thinking about the stressor
options.rationale: Suppression is not coping, and it removes the opportunity to work the problem.

options.text: Collaborating with the health care team and support system when appropriate
options.rationale: Collaboration brings in resources the nurse does not hold alone, and the support system is a factor in coping capacity.

options.text: Reassessing sleep, anxiety, pain, appetite, concentration, and safety
options.rationale: Correct in evaluation, and each is a marker of whether coping is improving.

questions.takeaway: Interventions build coping and the environment supports it. Evaluation reassesses the markers.
questions.strategy: Any option telling a client not to think about something is wrong. Avoidance is not an effective coping strategy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Interventions supporting stress management.
Suppression removes the chance to cope.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E and F are selected.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old is admitted with chest pain that proves non-cardiac. His troponin is negative and his ECG is normal, but he tells the nurse he has not slept since being told his job is ending in six weeks. Which type of crisis is this?

options.text: Developmental crisis
options.rationale: Triggered by normal life transitions such as retirement or becoming a parent.

options.text: Situational crisis
options.rationale: Provoked by external events such as a job loss, a crash, or serious illness.

options.text: Secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Stress from repeated exposure to others' trauma.

options.text: Adventitious crisis
options.rationale: An unplanned, rare, catastrophic event such as a natural disaster.

questions.takeaway: Developmental follows a life transition. Situational follows an external event. Adventitious is catastrophic and rare. A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.
questions.strategy: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Sort by what triggered it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An external event affecting one person.
Job loss is not a normal expected transition.
Not rare or catastrophic in scale.
Not exposure to another's trauma.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: provoked by external events such as a job loss, a crash, or serious illness.

questions.concept: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old admitted after losing her home in a flood has a pulse of 108, a blood pressure of 146/88, and has not slept for three nights. She tells the nurse she has nowhere to go. Which priority does the nurse address first?

options.text: Collaborating with the support system
options.rationale: Appropriate when relevant, and it follows safety.

options.text: Setting time frames that match the setting
options.rationale: A planning detail, not the priority.

options.text: Prioritizing safety
options.rationale: Safety comes first in planning, and expressed hopelessness makes it the immediate concern.

options.text: Setting realistic patient-centered outcomes
options.rationale: Part of planning and not the first consideration when hopelessness has been expressed.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize safety first, then realistic outcomes, client involvement, collaboration, and time frames.
questions.strategy: When a stem includes hopelessness, worthlessness, or any statement about not going on, safety moves to the front regardless of what else is in the options. All four options are part of planning. Select the one that must come FIRST given what the client has expressed.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Hopelessness has been expressed.
All are legitimate planning steps that come after safety.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: safety comes first in planning, and expressed hopelessness makes it the immediate concern.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for four clients on a medical unit, each responding to a difficult situation in a different way. She recognizes that these unconscious responses are protecting each person from something they cannot yet face. Match each client behavior with the defense mechanism it BEST illustrates. Each term is used only once.

items.text: A client with a new cancer diagnosis says the laboratory must have mixed up the samples
items.rationale: Refusing to accept a painful reality. It protects the person from information they cannot yet absorb.

items.text: A client angry about his own smoking history accuses the nurse of being judgmental
items.rationale: Attributing your own feeling to someone else.

items.text: A hospitalized adult begins asking a parent to make all her decisions and speak for her
items.rationale: Returning to behavior from an earlier developmental stage under stress.

items.text: A client who can no longer play sports after an injury devotes himself to coaching
items.rationale: Making up for a perceived deficit by excelling in another area.

questions.takeaway: Denial, projection, dissociation, regression, compensation. Defense mechanisms are unconscious and not automatically unhealthy. Defense mechanisms are unconscious and not automatically unhealthy: denial, projection, dissociation, regression, and compensation.
questions.strategy: Match by what the mechanism does with the feeling: refuses it, relocates it, retreats from it, or redirects it. Dissociation is the fifth mechanism and does not appear here. Detaching from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rejecting the diagnosis outright is denial.
Assigning your own feeling to another is projection.
Adult behaving as a child is regression.
Redirecting into another area is compensation.

questions.concept: Defense mechanisms are unconscious and not automatically unhealthy: denial, projection, dissociation, regression, and compensation.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old describing an assault tells the nurse that during the event she felt she was watching from the ceiling. Her pulse is 96 and her responses are flat. Which defense mechanism does this describe?

options.text: Dissociation
options.rationale: Detaching from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings. It commonly appears during and after trauma.

options.text: Denial
options.rationale: Refusing to accept a reality, and she is not refusing that it happened.

options.text: Projection
options.rationale: Attributing one's own feeling to another person.

options.text: Compensation
options.rationale: Excelling in one area to offset a deficit in another.

questions.takeaway: Dissociation is detachment from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings. Defense mechanisms are unconscious and not automatically unhealthy: denial, projection, dissociation, regression, and compensation.
questions.strategy: The phrase watching it happen to someone else is the signature. It is detachment rather than refusal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Detachment from the experience itself.
She acknowledges the event occurred.
Neither involves detachment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: detaching from thoughts, feelings, or surroundings.

questions.concept: Defense mechanisms are unconscious and not automatically unhealthy: denial, projection, dissociation, regression, and compensation.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews several client situations during a shift.
questions.stem: A nurse reviews several client situations during a shift, each involving a different pattern and duration of stress. Some describe a single recent event, others describe strain that has continued for years, and in some the client's usual coping has stopped working. For each situation, click to specify which concepts it supports. Each situation may support more than one.

rows.text: A client feels tense before a scheduled family meeting this afternoon
rows.rationale: Short-term stress from an immediate event, and it resolves when the event passes.

rows.text: A client has managed housing instability and debt for three years
rows.rationale: Ongoing stress persisting over time, and it is what produces allostatic load.

rows.text: A client loses his job of twenty years and says his usual ways of coping no longer work
rows.rationale: The event itself is acute, and the failure of previous coping makes it a crisis. It is situational because an external event provoked it.

rows.text: A client's home is destroyed by flooding and she cannot see a way forward
rows.rationale: An external event producing an immediate stress response, with coping that has stopped working.

rows.text: A caregiver has supported a spouse with dementia for four years and now reports exhaustion
rows.rationale: Persistent over time. It becomes a crisis only if previous coping methods stop working.

rows.text: A client describes years of financial strain that recently became unmanageable after an eviction notice
rows.rationale: Long-standing stress that has reached a turning point where coping no longer works.

questions.constraint: Each column must have at least one response selected.
questions.takeaway: A crisis is defined by coping that has stopped working, not by the size of the event. A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.
questions.strategy: The rows that map to two columns are the ones where an event and a failure of coping occur together. Look for language about coping no longer working. Each column must have at least one response selected, and a crisis can accompany either acute or chronic stress.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Afternoon versus years separates acute from chronic.
That phrase is what adds the crisis column.
A crisis can sit on top of either acute or chronic stress.

elimination.verdict: Two rows acute only, two chronic only, and two carrying the crisis column alongside another.

questions.concept: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.

questions.stem: A client whose home burned down three weeks ago has a pulse of 104, a blood pressure of 138/86, respirations of 20, and trembling hands. She reports she cannot stop feeling on edge. Which stage does this reflect?

options.text: Any highly stressful event
options.rationale: Not every stressful event overwhelms coping.

options.text: A turning point when previous coping methods no longer work
options.rationale: The defining feature is the failure of what used to work, not the size of the event.

options.text: A psychiatric emergency requiring hospitalization
options.rationale: Some crises require that and the term is broader.

options.text: A permanent inability to cope
options.rationale: A crisis is a turning point, not a permanent state.

questions.takeaway: What makes it a crisis is that the person's usual coping has stopped working. A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.
questions.strategy: Two people can face the same event and only one is in crisis, which is why the definition rests on coping rather than on the event.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The definition is being asked for.
Stressful is not the same as overwhelming.
Too narrow.
A turning point implies change is possible.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the defining feature is the failure of what used to work, not the size of the event.

questions.concept: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental follows a life transition, situational follows an external event, adventitious is catastrophic and rare.

questions.scenario: The nurse assesses a client admitted for observation who appears distressed.
questions.stem: A nurse assesses a client admitted for observation who appears distressed. She records both what he reports and what she observes, and must separate the two before writing her note. For each cue, indicate whether it is SUBJECTIVE or OBJECTIVE data.

rows.text: "I have not slept properly in two weeks."
rows.rationale: The client's own report about sleep, and only he can supply it.

rows.text: Tearful during the admission interview
rows.rationale: An observed behavior.

rows.text: "I do not know how I am going to manage."
rows.rationale: A statement about coping.

rows.text: Heart rate 104 and hands trembling
rows.rationale: Measured and observed.

rows.text: Hair unwashed and clothing soiled
rows.rationale: Observed hygiene, a specified objective cue.

rows.text: Rates his anxiety as 8 out of 10
rows.rationale: A rating scale still records the client's perception. The number does not make it objective.

questions.takeaway: Subjective cues are what the client says about stress, fear, coping, sleep, pain, support, and safety. Objective cues are affect, behavior, vital signs, restlessness, crying, withdrawal, hygiene, and appetite.
questions.strategy: The trap is a rating scale. A number attached to a perception is still subjective, because only the client can supply it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: If only the client can know it, it is subjective.
8 out of 10 looks measured and is a report.
A quoted statement is always subjective.

elimination.verdict: Three rows subjective, three objective.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and an A1C of 9.2% enrolls in a self-management course, buys a glucose meter, and books a dietitian appointment. Which coping strategy is he using?

options.text: Emotion-focused coping
options.rationale: Managing feelings related to the stressor, such as talking with a friend or using relaxation.

options.text: Regression
options.rationale: A defense mechanism, returning to behavior from an earlier stage.

options.text: Denial
options.rationale: Refusing to accept a painful reality.

options.text: Problem-focused coping
options.rationale: Taking action to change or solve the stressor itself.

questions.takeaway: Problem-focused changes the stressor. Emotion-focused manages the feeling about it. Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Neither is inherently better. Effectiveness depends on the person, the situation, and culture, and on whether the stressor is changeable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is acting on the problem itself.
No feelings are being managed here.
Both are defense mechanisms.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: taking action to change or solve the stressor itself.

questions.concept: Self-management support builds the client's capability, because the client manages the condition between visits where no nurse is present. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 46-year-old about managing stress three weeks after her home was destroyed in a fire. She describes how she has been coping and what she plans to do next. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "How I read a situation affects how hard it hits me."
options.rationale: Accurate. Appraisal is why the same event affects two people differently.

options.text: "If my usual ways of coping stop working, that is worth telling someone about."
options.rationale: Accurate. A crisis is defined by coping that no longer works.

options.text: "The best thing I can do is not think about it until I feel stronger."
options.rationale: Suppression is not coping. It removes the chance to work the problem, and avoidance is not among the effective strategies.

options.text: "Talking with my sister does not change what happened, but it helps me manage it."
options.rationale: Accurate. Emotion-focused coping is the fitting strategy when the stressor cannot be altered.

questions.takeaway: Suppression is not coping. Problem-focused changes the stressor; emotion-focused manages the response to it.
questions.strategy: Any option telling a client not to think about something is wrong.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken strategy.
Not thinking about it is avoidance.
Emotion-focused coping, appraisal, and failed coping are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: avoidance is not a coping strategy.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for two clients admitted with the same diagnosis on the same day. One manages the admission calmly and the other is overwhelmed within hours. The nurse considers what differs between them beyond the diagnosis itself. Which factors influence a person's ability to cope with stress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Age and developmental stage
options.rationale: Age and developmental stage shape what a person has already faced and what resources they have built by this point in life.

options.text: Culture and beliefs
options.rationale: Culture and beliefs shape what counts as a stressor at all, and what responses are acceptable to the person.

options.text: Past experiences
options.rationale: Past experience tells the person whether they have survived something like this before, which affects appraisal directly.

options.text: Height and body build
options.rationale: Not among the factors, and it has no bearing on coping capacity.

options.text: Support system
options.rationale: Correct factor, alongside financial and personal resources.

options.text: Problem-solving skills and personal outlook
options.rationale: Problem-solving skills determine what options a person can see, and outlook determines whether they expect any of them to work.

options.text: Blood type
options.rationale: Unrelated to stress appraisal or coping capacity.

questions.takeaway: Eight factors: age and stage, culture and beliefs, past experiences, health and energy, support system, resources, problem-solving skills, and outlook. Appraisal is how a person interprets the impact of a stressor, which is why the same event affects two people differently.
questions.strategy: Health and energy level is worth remembering, because it explains why a hospitalized client copes less well than the same person would at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factors influencing coping ability.
A physical characteristic unrelated to coping.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E and F are selected.

questions.concept: Appraisal is how a person interprets the impact of a stressor, which is why the same event affects two people differently.

questions.stem: A client who survived a serious motor vehicle collision six months ago reports intrusive memories, difficulty sleeping, and avoidance of driving. He was not physically injured in the crash and asks whether what he is experiencing is real. Which statement about post-traumatic stress disorder is accurate?

options.text: It resolves without intervention within one month in all cases
options.rationale: Absolute, and untreated symptoms can persist for years.

options.text: It develops only in people who were physically injured
options.rationale: Exposure to actual or threatened harm is sufficient, and injury is not required.

options.text: It is a stress response following exposure to actual or threatened harm
options.rationale: It sits within traumatic stress, and symptoms persist beyond the event.

options.text: It is the same as secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Secondary traumatic stress arises from repeated exposure to others' trauma rather than from one's own.

questions.takeaway: PTSD follows exposure to actual or threatened harm. Injury is not required.
questions.strategy: Options containing only, all cases, or always are usually wrong, because stress responses vary by person.

strategies: Eliminate absolutes

steps.detail: An accurate statement about PTSD.
Only who were injured is too narrow.
All cases is absolute.
Conflates two distinct types.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: it sits within traumatic stress, and symptoms persist beyond the event.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old is admitted after a house fire destroyed her home. The nurse assesses her orientation, mood, sleep, vital signs, intake, and contact with family. Highlight the findings that require immediate nursing intervention.

segments.text: Client is alert and oriented to person, place, and time
segments.rationale: A normal finding and a useful baseline.

segments.text: States, "Nothing I do works anymore and I do not see how I get through this"
segments.rationale: Expressed hopelessness with failed coping. Safety is prioritized first in planning.

segments.text: Reports she has not slept in three days
segments.rationale: Sleep loss impairs judgment and coping capacity and is a marker in evaluation.

segments.text: Tearful during the admission interview
segments.rationale: An expected emotional response to a catastrophic loss, and it is an objective cue rather than an emergency.

segments.text: Heart rate 104 and hands trembling
segments.rationale: Consistent with sympathetic activation in the alarm stage, and expected in this situation.

segments.text: Has declined all contact with her sister and her closest friend
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from the support system, which is a factor influencing coping and removes a protective resource.

segments.text: Reports she ate a small meal this morning
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding.

questions.takeaway: Safety first. Expressed hopelessness, sleep loss, and withdrawal from support all require intervention.
questions.strategy: Distinguish an expected stress response from a finding that needs action. Tearfulness after losing a home is expected; hopelessness is not. Some findings are expected stress responses. Highlight only those requiring intervention.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Statements about not getting through are assessed immediately.
Withdrawal removes the support system.
Tearfulness and tachycardia fit the alarm stage.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s2, s3, and s6.

questions.stem: A client admitted in crisis two days ago has attended relaxation sessions and met with the social worker. The nurse must now determine whether the plan has helped. options.rationale: Not a meaningful measure of an individual's coping.

steps.detail: Evaluating a stress management plan.

questions.stem: A client awaiting a transplant that may not come for months tells the nurse she has started a meditation practice and talks daily with a friend. Which coping approach is this?

Neither describes managing feelings.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old who has cared for a spouse with advanced illness for three years reports exhaustion, a resting pulse of 96, and four upper respiratory infections this winter. Which effects of prolonged stress apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reduces the body's immune response
options.rationale: Leaving the body less able to fight pathogens.

options.text: Increases susceptibility to infections
options.rationale: A direct consequence of the reduced immune response.

options.text: Slows the healing process
options.rationale: Which is why chronic stress also appears as a risk factor for infection.

options.rationale: Chronic stress contributes to cardiovascular and metabolic harm, not efficiency.

options.text: Contributes to long-term physical and mental health effects

questions.nursesNote: 1030: Client seen in clinic, self-referred. Reports her home was destroyed by fire eleven days ago. Lost her job two months prior. States "I have always handled things, but nothing I do works anymore and I do not see how I get through this." Reports sleeping about two hours a night for the past week and eating one meal a day. steps.detail: Regulation of the sleep-wake cycle.
Movement and autonomic control.
Involved in sleep, not in regulating the cycle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: sleep regulation involves the hypothalamus, along with hypocretins for wakefulness and REM, prostaglandin, L-tryptophan, and growth factors.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old in long-term care reports poor sleep. She takes a diuretic and four other medications, has osteoarthritis with night-time pain, wears hearing aids she removes at bedtime, and gets up several times to void. Which factors contribute to sleep problems in older adults? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nocturia
options.rationale: Correct risk factor, and it fragments sleep through repeated waking.

options.text: Polypharmacy
options.rationale: Correct risk factor, and several drug classes affect sleep directly.

options.text: Pain
options.rationale: Pain both delays sleep onset and wakes the person repeatedly, and it is frequently under-treated at night.

options.text: Increased total sleep requirement with age
options.rationale: Total sleep requirement does not increase with age. Sleep becomes lighter and more fragmented.

options.text: Deeper slow-wave sleep with advancing age
options.rationale: Slow-wave sleep decreases with age rather than deepening.

options.text: Regular daytime physical activity
options.rationale: Daytime activity improves sleep rather than disrupting it.

questions.takeaway: Nocturia, polypharmacy, pain, comorbidities, and sensory impairment. Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.
questions.strategy: One option reverses the direction of an age-related change. That is the standard distractor pattern in lifespan items.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factors contributing to sleep problems.
Sleep requirement decreases with age rather than increasing.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications, counting prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products together.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses sleep for a client admitted three days ago who reports lying awake for a long time before sleep comes. She asks how long it usually takes him to fall asleep after getting into bed. Which component of the sleep assessment is this?

options.text: Nighttime awakenings
options.rationale: How often the client wakes after falling asleep.

options.text: Sleep latency
options.rationale: The time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is a assessment component.

options.text: Perceived sleep quality
options.rationale: How rested the client feels, which is asked separately.

options.text: Sleep efficiency
options.rationale: The proportion of time in bed actually spent asleep.

questions.takeaway: Assessment covers bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality. Sleep latency is the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is one of the sleep assessment components alongside awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.
questions.strategy: Latency and awakenings point at different problems. Difficulty falling asleep suggests one pattern; repeated waking suggests another, such as nocturia or pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Time taken to fall asleep.
A ratio, not a duration.
Quality and frequency of waking.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is a assessment component.

questions.concept: Sleep latency is the time from getting into bed to falling asleep, and it is one of the sleep assessment components alongside awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease reports he cannot sleep in hospital. He explains that lying flat leaves him breathless, and he has been sitting upright in the chair for most of the night. Which factor most likely contributes to his difficulty sleeping?

options.text: Increased REM sleep in respiratory disease
options.rationale: Not a described feature.

options.text: Reduced need for sleep with chronic illness
options.rationale: Illness increases the need for sleep while making it harder to get.

options.text: Elevated melatonin production
options.rationale: Not a described feature of respiratory disease.

options.text: Positioning needs and breathlessness disrupt sleep
options.rationale: Breathlessness worsens lying flat, so the position that allows sleep and the position that allows breathing work against each other.

questions.takeaway: Illness increases the need for sleep and often makes it harder to get.
questions.strategy: Each disease group disrupts sleep by a specific mechanism. Respiratory is positioning and breathlessness; cardiac is nocturnal angina and apnea; gastrointestinal is nocturnal symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: COPD and difficulty sleeping.
Neither is described.
Reverses the relationship between illness and sleep need.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: specified directly for respiratory disease including COPD and asthma.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old has slept about four hours a night for three weeks since starting a new job. His surgical wound from two months ago has not fully healed, he reports more pain from it than before, and he has had two upper respiratory infections. Which consequences result from inadequate sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: Impaired immune function
options.rationale: And it links sleep to infection risk.

options.text: Impaired wound healing
options.rationale: Correct, alongside the growth hormone mechanism.

options.text: Reduced pain tolerance
options.rationale: And it explains why a poorly slept client reports more pain from the same stimulus.

options.text: Improved concentration through increased alertness
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation impairs function, judgment, and mood rather than improving them.

options.text: Impaired judgment and mood
options.rationale: Judgment and mood decline with sleep loss, which matters clinically because a sleep-deprived client makes poorer decisions about their own care.

questions.takeaway: Poor sleep impairs immunity, healing, pain tolerance, judgment, and mood.
questions.strategy: Reduced pain tolerance is the one worth carrying into practice. The client who slept badly is not exaggerating the same wound the next morning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consequences of inadequate sleep.
States a benefit where it describes impairment.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches sleep hygiene to a 51-year-old who reports taking two hours to fall asleep most nights. She describes her evening routine and what she intends to change. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will keep the same bedtime and wake time, including at weekends."
options.rationale: Accurate. Weekend variation undoes the circadian consistency.

options.text: "I will stop the coffee after dinner and skip the nightcap."
options.rationale: Accurate. Caffeine and alcohol are both specified disruptors.

options.text: "I will exercise during the day but not within an hour or two of bed."
options.rationale: Accurate. Daytime activity helps; activity close to sleep does not.

options.text: "I will stay in bed reading until I feel sleepy enough to drop off."
options.rationale: The bed is reserved for sleep only. Using it for other activities weakens the association between bed and sleep, which is the thing being rebuilt.

questions.takeaway: The bed is for sleep only. Consistent timing, no caffeine or alcohol late, screens off, daytime exercise.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is the thing most people actually do, and it feels productive.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken habit.
Bed for sleep only.
Timing, substances, and exercise are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: reading in bed weakens the association.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that represent modifiable causes of his sleep disruption.
questions.takeaway: Find the treatable causes before reaching for a sleeping tablet.
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether the team could change it this week. Age and the admitting diagnosis are context; timing, pain, light, and interruptions are levers. Two findings are relevant background rather than modifiable causes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four findings describe things the team controls.
Age and the diagnosis cannot be changed.
Diuretic timing, pain, light, and clustering.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s5.

questions.nursesNote: 2130: Client admitted four days ago with community-acquired pneumonia. Reports he has not slept more than two hours at a stretch since admission. Receives furosemide at 2000 daily. Rates incisional-free chest discomfort 6/10 at night, last analgesia 1400. States staff switch on the overhead light at each entry. Wakes three to four times nightly to void. Observed dozing during physiotherapy this afternoon and unsteady walking to the bathroom, requiring a steadying hand. Requests "something to help me sleep." VS: T 37.1 C; HR 88; RR 18; BP 132/76; SpO2 94% on room air.

segments.text: Furosemide administered at 2000
segments.rationale: Diuretic timing drives nocturia. Moving the dose earlier is a change the team can make.

segments.text: Chest discomfort rated 6/10 at night, last analgesia 1400
segments.rationale: Unrelieved pain both delays sleep onset and wakes him, and it is treatable.

segments.text: Overhead light switched on at each entry
segments.rationale: Light suppresses melatonin, and dimming during evening hours is a intervention.

segments.text: Age 68
segments.rationale: Not modifiable. Older adults sleep less and more fragmented, which is expected rather than correctable.

segments.text: Staff enter separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws
segments.rationale: Clustering care reduces interruptions, which is the largest controllable cause of hospital sleep loss.

segments.text: History of pneumonia requiring admission
segments.rationale: The reason he is here. It shapes the picture and is not itself a modifiable sleep cause.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with disrupted sleep in hospital

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: Find and fix the causes before medicating. Nocturia, pain, light, and noise are all modifiable.
questions.strategy: His request for a sleeping tablet is the pull in this case. The answer addresses why he cannot sleep rather than sedating him through it. He has asked for a specific intervention. Consider whether it addresses the cause.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Four causes are identified and all are modifiable.
Falls and confusion risk in an unsteady older adult.
Dismisses a treatable problem.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.sentence: The client is most likely experiencing [[1]], and the nurse's priority is to [[2]].

options.text: sleep deprivation from treatable environmental and physiological causes
options.rationale: Nocturia from diuretic timing, unrelieved pain, light, and interruptions are all identified and all modifiable.

options.text: obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Would require snoring with witnessed apneic episodes, and none is described.

options.text: a parasomnia
options.rationale: Undesirable physical events during sleep, which he does not report.

options.text: an expected age-related change requiring no action
options.rationale: Older adults sleep less, and a new problem with identifiable causes is still assessed.

options.text: address the identified causes before considering a sleep medication
options.rationale: Four modifiable causes are present, and sedating an already unsteady older adult adds fall risk while leaving them in place.

options.text: request a benzodiazepine at bedtime as he has asked
options.rationale: Short-term use only, with falls and confusion the specific risk in older adults, and he is already unsteady.

options.text: reassure him that poor sleep in hospital is normal
options.rationale: Common is not the same as acceptable, and it dismisses a problem with treatable causes.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with disrupted sleep in hospital

questions.stem: The nurse plans interventions for tonight. Which 2 actions should she take FIRST?
questions.takeaway: Remove the reason he wakes and treat the pain that keeps him awake. Both can happen before tonight. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Exactly two are requested. Three wrong options manage the consequences of poor sleep rather than its causes. Some of the others may be appropriate later.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Nocturia and pain are the two acting tonight.
Risks dehydration and misses the timing issue.
Both add risk without addressing the cause.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Discuss moving the furosemide dose earlier with the provider
options.rationale: Removes the reason he wakes, and the timing change can be made before tonight.

options.text: Offer analgesia before he settles and reassess its effect
options.rationale: Unrelieved pain at 6 out of 10 will wake him regardless of any other change.

options.text: Restrict his fluids after noon
options.rationale: Risks dehydration, which causes dizziness and falls in older adults, and it does not address the medication timing.

options.text: Request a benzodiazepine at bedtime
options.rationale: Short-term use only, and it adds fall risk to a client who is already unsteady.

options.text: Place a bed alarm and raise all four side rails
options.rationale: Four raised side rails are a restraint, and neither addresses why he is awake.

options.text: Document that he is requesting a sleep aid and reassess tomorrow
options.rationale: Records the request and changes nothing tonight.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with disrupted sleep in hospital
questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: For each proposed action, determine whether it is INDICATED or NOT INDICATED given this new information.
questions.takeaway: When a plan is working, you continue it and keep measuring. You do not add the intervention it made unnecessary.
questions.strategy: Improvement is the reason not to add sedation, not the reason it has become safe. One proposed action responds to improvement by adding the medication that was previously declined.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Voiding once, pain 2 out of 10, sleeping five hours, still unsteady.
The situation is improving and he remains a fall risk.
The measures are how you know it is still working.

elimination.verdict: Four actions are indicated and two are not.

questions.scenario: Two nights later the furosemide has been moved to 0800 and scheduled analgesia has been added at 2100. The client reports waking once to void, rates his pain 2 out of 10 overnight, and slept about five hours. He remains unsteady on standing and dozed briefly during the morning.

rows.text: Continue the earlier furosemide timing
rows.rationale: Night-time voiding has fallen from four times to one, so the change is working.

rows.text: Cluster nursing care overnight and dim the lights
rows.rationale: Interruptions remain the largest controllable cause, and he still reports being woken by staff.

rows.text: Add a benzodiazepine now that other measures are in place
rows.rationale: He is sleeping longer and remains unsteady. Adding a sedating agent introduces fall risk to a situation that is improving.

rows.text: Continue scheduled night-time analgesia
rows.rationale: His pain fell from 6 to 2 out of 10 with the scheduled dose, which is why he is sleeping.

rows.text: Discontinue the assessment of his sleep now that it has improved
rows.rationale: Sleep quality, latency, and awakenings are the measures that show whether the plan continues to work.

rows.text: Assess his steadiness before each ambulation
rows.rationale: Daytime drowsiness and unsteadiness are both fall risks and both are still present.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with disrupted sleep in hospital

questions.stem: For each finding today, determine whether it reflects IMPROVEMENT, NO CHANGE, or DECLINE compared with admission, or whether it is a NEW FINDING not previously assessed.
questions.takeaway: Compare each finding against its own baseline. A finding never measured before is new information, not a change.
questions.strategy: Two findings are unchanged and one has no baseline at all. Unchanged and new are different answers. One finding has no baseline to compare against, and two are genuinely unchanged rather than improved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five measures were recorded at admission.
Five rows have a baseline; one does not.
Snoring was never assessed.

elimination.verdict: Three improved, two unchanged, one new finding.

questions.baseline: Admission: sleeping two hours at a stretch, waking three to four times nightly, pain 6/10 at night, unsteady on standing, SpO2 94% on room air.

rows.text: Sleeps five to six hours at a stretch
rows.rationale: Up from two hours at a stretch.

rows.text: Wakes once nightly to void
rows.rationale: Down from three to four times.

rows.text: Rates night-time pain 2 out of 10
rows.rationale: Down from 6 out of 10.

rows.text: SpO2 94% on room air
rows.rationale: Identical to the admission value.

rows.text: Remains unsteady on standing
rows.rationale: Unchanged from admission, and it is why sedation remains inappropriate.

rows.text: Reports loud snoring witnessed by his wife during visiting hours
rows.rationale: Snoring was never assessed at admission, so there is no baseline. It is new information requiring evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea rather than a change in a previous measure.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with disrupted sleep in hospital

questions.stem: For each finding, determine whether it is a MODIFIABLE cause, a NON-MODIFIABLE factor, or requires MEDICAL REVIEW.
questions.takeaway: Sort what you can change, what the prescriber changes, and what is simply context.
questions.strategy: Two causes are modifiable and two need an order. Knowing which is which decides whether you act or ask.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clustering and lighting.
Diuretic timing and analgesia.
Age and an existing diagnosis.

elimination.verdict: Two modifiable by nursing, two requiring medical review, two non-modifiable.

questions.scenario: Before the evening round the nurse sorts the identified causes by who can change each one.

rows.text: Staff entering separately for vital signs, medications, and blood draws
rows.rationale: Clustering care is within nursing control.

rows.text: The overhead light switched on at each entry
rows.rationale: Dimming lights during evening hours is a intervention.

rows.text: Furosemide scheduled at 2000
rows.rationale: Changing the timing of a prescribed medication requires the prescriber.

rows.text: Chest discomfort rated 6 out of 10 at night
rows.rationale: Unrelieved pain needs an analgesia review.

rows.text: Age 68
rows.rationale: Older adults sleep less and more fragmented, which is expected.

rows.text: History of hypertension managed with medication
rows.rationale: A stable existing condition rather than a sleep cause.

chapters.title: The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes receives rapid-acting insulin at 0730 in anticipation of breakfast. At 0745 the kitchen reports the trays are delayed by at least 40 minutes. His glucose before the dose was 148 mg/dL. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain a carbohydrate source now, because rapid-acting insulin is already working
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is given with food precisely because its onset is immediate, and a delayed tray creates a low.

options.text: Wait for the tray to arrive and monitor him for symptoms meanwhile
options.rationale: The insulin is acting while he waits, and monitoring does not prevent the fall.

options.text: Hold the next scheduled dose to compensate for the delayed meal
options.rationale: Addresses a future dose while the current one is still working.

options.text: Administer a second dose once the tray arrives
options.rationale: Compounds the problem with more insulin.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting insulin is given with food. A delayed tray after the dose is a hypoglycemic event waiting to happen.
questions.strategy: The timing relationship between insulin type and food is what these questions test, not the numbers themselves.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Dose given, food delayed.
Waiting does not stop the fall.
Future doses and additional insulin.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: rapid-acting insulin is given with food precisely because its onset is immediate, and a delayed tray creates a low.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches foot care to a client with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes whose monofilament testing shows reduced sensation bilaterally. Which client action requires correction?

options.text: Buy new shoes at the end of the day when the feet are largest
options.rationale: Correct. Feet swell through the day, so shoes fitted in the morning are too tight by evening.

options.text: Apply moisturizer to the tops and bottoms of your feet, and between your toes
options.rationale: Moisturizer goes on the tops and bottoms but never between the toes. Trapped moisture in a warm dark space grows fungus.

options.text: Check the water temperature by hand before bathing the feet
options.rationale: Correct. Neuropathy means the client may not feel a scald until the burn has happened.

options.text: Inspect your feet and the soles daily for blisters, redness, or drainage
options.rationale: Correct. Daily inspection catches injury the client cannot feel because of neuropathy.

questions.takeaway: Moisturize the tops and bottoms, never between the toes.
questions.strategy: In a spot-the-error item, three options are correct practice. Verify each against a rule you can name; the one you cannot justify is the answer.

strategies: Negative polarity

steps.detail: Intervenes means find the error. Three statements will be correct.
Daily inspection is standard teaching.
End-of-day shoe fitting accounts for swelling.
Water temperature checking addresses neuropathy.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B. Every foot-care rule traces to neuropathy or to poor circulation and infection risk; moisture between the toes belongs to the second.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes tells the nurse his uncle lost a foot to the disease and asks what he can do to avoid the same outcome. He works long hours on his feet and has never seen a podiatrist. Which teaching points does the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect your feet daily
options.rationale: Neuropathy means injury is not felt, so it must be seen.

options.text: Attend regular eye examinations
options.rationale: Retinopathy can progress to irreversible blindness and is detectable before symptoms appear.

options.text: Keep blood pressure and lipid levels within target ranges
options.rationale: A stated goal of diabetes management, because macrovascular complications are driven by the same vascular damage.

options.text: Go barefoot indoors so the feet can breathe
options.rationale: Never barefoot. An unfelt injury on an insensate foot is how ulcers begin.

options.text: Trim toenails straight across
options.rationale: Reduces ingrown nails, and a podiatrist should do it if neuropathy or thick nails are present.

options.text: Use a heating pad on the feet in cold weather
options.rationale: Explicitly avoided. Neuropathy means the client may not feel a burn.

options.text: Report any wound that is not healing
options.rationale: Impaired healing and immune response turn minor injuries into serious infections.

questions.takeaway: Every foot-care rule traces to one of two deficits: the client cannot feel injury, or the injury will not heal.
questions.strategy: The two false options both involve exposing the foot to something it cannot feel. Once you see the pattern the item resolves quickly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Prevention of complications in a new diagnosis.
Barefoot exposes an insensate foot to injury.
Heating pads risk burns the client will not feel.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G remain, covering feet, eyes, vascular targets, and wound reporting.

questions.stem: A client presents with a glucose of 512 mg/dL, a pH of 7.19, a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L, and deep rapid respirations at a rate of 32. Which finding confirms the nurse's suspicion?

options.text: Shallow, slow respirations with a normal respiratory pattern
options.rationale: The opposite. Respirations are deep and rapid because the lungs are compensating for acidosis.

options.text: Absent ketones in the urine
options.rationale: Ketones are the defining feature of DKA and appear in both urine and serum.

options.text: Serum pH of 7.46, reflecting a compensated metabolic picture
options.rationale: That is alkalosis. DKA produces a pH below 7.3.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with a fruity breath odor
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations blow off carbon dioxide to raise the pH, and the fruity odor is exhaled ketones.

questions.takeaway: Kussmaul respirations are compensation for acidosis, not an airway problem. Treat with insulin and fluids. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Do not reach for oxygen or suctioning when you see deep rapid breathing in DKA. Correcting the acidosis is what stops it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for an expected finding in DKA.
Respirations are deep and rapid, not shallow and slow.
7.46 is alkalotic; DKA is acidotic.
Ketones define the condition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D, which pairs the respiratory pattern with the exhaled ketones.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has a glucose of 486 mg/dL, a pH of 7.22, moderate serum ketones, and deep rapid respirations. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Inject into the same thigh each day so absorption stays predictable
options.rationale: Repeated use of one spot causes lipodystrophy, which makes absorption less predictable, and it does not address the exercise effect.

options.text: Use a site away from the exercising muscle, such as the abdomen
options.rationale: Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb, so injecting into the thigh before walking accelerates the insulin just as activity is lowering the glucose.

options.text: Switch the rapid-acting insulin to bedtime
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin covers a meal, so moving it to bedtime separates it from the food it is meant to match.

options.text: Stop walking until the glucose stabilizes
options.rationale: Activity is part of management. The timing and site are what need adjusting, not the exercise itself.

questions.takeaway: Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb, so site choice matters when activity follows a dose.
questions.strategy: When a stem pairs an injection site with an activity involving that limb, absorption rate is what the question is testing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thigh injection at 0800, brisk walking at 0830.
Repeated use of one spot causes lipodystrophy.
Activity is part of the plan.
Rapid-acting insulin is matched to a meal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: move the injection away from the muscle about to be exercised.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes managed on metformin for eight years is started on insulin. He tells the nurse this means he now has type 1 and that he has failed. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Type 2 becomes type 1 once insulin is required
options.rationale: The two have different causes. Type 1 is autoimmune destruction of beta cells.

options.text: Needing insulin indicates the regimen was not followed
options.rationale: Progression occurs despite good adherence and is not a failure.

options.text: Type 2 may require insulin over time without becoming type 1
options.rationale: Insulin resistance progresses and the pancreas eventually cannot compensate. The diagnosis does not change.

options.text: Insulin in type 2 is used only during hospital admissions
options.rationale: It may be part of long-term management at home.

questions.takeaway: Type 1 has no insulin. Type 2 begins with resistance and adds declining production over time.
questions.strategy: Watch for options that blame the client. They are almost always wrong and they are written to feel plausible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client is asking about mechanism, so the answer should explain one.
The two have different causes.
It may be part of long-term management at home.
Progression occurs despite good adherence and is not a failure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: insulin resistance progresses and the pancreas eventually cannot compensate.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for four clients with type 2 diabetes. One takes acarbose with each meal, one takes a sulfonylurea, one takes metformin alone, and one is on NPH insulin each morning at 0800. Each has asked how to manage a low blood glucose at home.
questions.stem: Which instructions does the nurse give? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client on acarbose should treat a low with glucose tablets rather than table sugar
options.rationale: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors slow carbohydrate absorption, so sucrose will not be broken down in time. Glucose is absorbed directly.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The rule of 15, and it applies to a conscious client with a glucose under 70 who can swallow safely.

options.text: If the glucose is still low after 15 minutes, give another 15 grams and recheck again
options.rationale: Correct. One dose is frequently not enough, which is why the recheck is part of the treatment.

options.text: The client on NPH at 0800 should expect the highest risk of a low in the early morning
options.rationale: NPH given at 0800 peaks a shift and a half later, so the risk window stretches from around noon to 2000.

options.text: The client on metformin alone is at low risk of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Metformin does not stimulate insulin release, so it rarely causes a low unless combined with an agent that does.

options.text: An unconscious client should be given oral carbohydrate immediately
options.rationale: Never put anything in the mouth of a client who cannot protect the airway. That client needs intravenous dextrose or glucagon.

questions.takeaway: Rule of 15, glucose rather than table sugar on acarbose, and nothing by mouth if the client cannot swallow safely. The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious client who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options here reverse a real rule: the NPH peak window and the airway rule. Check the direction of each before selecting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Four clients on different agents, each with a different risk profile.
NPH at 0800 peaks from about noon to 2000, not in the early morning.
Oral carbohydrate requires a client who can protect the airway.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected, covering the rule of 15, the acarbose exception, and the low risk with metformin alone.

questions.concept: The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious client who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with type 2 diabetes is brought in after four days of increasing confusion. Blood glucose is 640 mg/dL, serum ketones are negative, and the pH is normal. His mucous membranes are dry and his heart rate is 108. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis, given the markedly elevated blood glucose
options.rationale: DKA requires ketones and acidosis, and it occurs typically in type 1.

options.text: An expected postprandial rise
options.rationale: No meal produces a glucose of 640 in any client.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: Extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, occurring more often in type 2.

options.text: Hypoglycemia, given the altered mental status on presentation
options.rationale: The glucose is 640 mg/dL.

questions.takeaway: The dividing line between DKA and HHS is ketones, not the glucose number. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: Students sort by how high the sugar is and get it backwards, because HHS runs higher than DKA.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No ketones, normal pH, type 2.
Ketones and acidosis are absent.
Glucose 640 is not low.
Not a postprandial value.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, occurring more often in type 2.
