questions.stem: A 52-year-old attends a screening clinic. He is asymptomatic, has a family history of type 2 diabetes, and his fasting blood glucose two weeks ago was 134 mg/dL. Today's fasting blood glucose is 141 mg/dL. His A1C is 7.2%. Which finding establishes the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

options.text: The absence of symptoms, since type 2 is frequently silent
options.rationale: Type 2 diabetes is frequently silent for years, so having no symptoms neither supports nor excludes the diagnosis.

options.text: Fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two separate occasions
options.rationale: His readings of 134 and 141 are both above 126 and were taken two weeks apart, which meets the diagnostic standard.

options.text: A single fasting blood glucose of 141 mg/dL
options.rationale: Above the threshold and drawn once. Diagnosis requires a fasting value over 126 mg/dL on two occasions, so one reading is not enough.

options.text: An A1C of 7.2%, which is above the target for glycemic control
options.rationale: The A1C reports average glucose over about three months and is used to judge control against a target of under 7%. It tells you his control is above target, not that the diagnosis is established.

questions.takeaway: Fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions establishes the diagnosis. The A1C reports average control over three months, with a target under 7%. The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.
questions.strategy: Separate the value that makes a diagnosis from the value that measures control. Two options here are real diabetes figures used for different purposes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two fasting values two weeks apart, plus an A1C.
One reading above 126 does not meet the standard of two occasions.
A1C measures control against a target, not the diagnostic threshold.
Being asymptomatic is common in type 2 and proves nothing either way.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: both fasting values exceed 126 mg/dL and were taken on separate occasions, which is what the diagnosis requires.

questions.concept: The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.

questions.scenario: A 74-year-old with type 2 diabetes is admitted after four days of increasing confusion. Blood glucose 618 mg/dL, serum ketones negative, serum pH 7.37, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, heart rate 112, blood pressure 96/58.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client.

rows.text: Establish intravenous access for fluid resuscitation
rows.rationale: Severe dehydration is the immediate threat in HHS, and fluid replacement is the priority.

rows.text: Monitor serum potassium during insulin administration
rows.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so the serum level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias.

rows.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis
rows.rationale: There is no acidosis. The pH is 7.37 and ketones are negative.

rows.text: Perform frequent neurological assessment
rows.rationale: Altered mental status is the hallmark of HHS and the marker of whether treatment is working.

rows.text: Encourage independent ambulation to the bathroom
rows.rationale: A confused, hypotensive, dehydrated older adult is a fall risk and needs assistance.

rows.text: Monitor intake and output
rows.rationale: Osmotic diuresis is driving the fluid loss, so output guides replacement.

questions.takeaway: In HHS the priority is fluid, not insulin alone, and there is no acidosis to correct. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: Work matrix rows against the data given. Two rows here are wrong because the client has no acidosis and is unsafe to mobilize alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose over 600, no ketones, normal pH, and signs of volume depletion.
There is no acidosis to correct.
Confusion plus hypotension is a fall risk.

elimination.verdict: The four remaining rows are indicated: fluids, potassium monitoring, neurological checks, and intake and output.

questions.concept: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia, glucose 600 or more, without significant ketones. DKA has ketones and acidosis. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four clients with type 1 diabetes who each had a hypoglycemic episode this week. She wants to identify the cause in each case so the pattern can be prevented rather than simply treated. Which situation is a recognized cause of hypoglycemia?

options.text: A client whose insulin was held because his glucose was 80
options.rationale: Holding insulin at a low-normal reading prevents a fall rather than causing one.

options.text: A client who increased her activity without adjusting her insulin or intake
options.rationale: Increased activity without adjustment is a cause, alongside excess insulin, missed or delayed meals, inadequate carbohydrate intake, and alcohol without food.

options.text: A client who missed a scheduled dose of her prescribed insulin
options.rationale: Missing insulin causes hyperglycemia, and in type 1 it risks ketoacidosis.

options.text: A client who ate a larger breakfast than usual
options.rationale: More carbohydrate raises glucose rather than lowering it.

questions.takeaway: Causes of hypoglycemia: excess insulin or diabetes medication, missed or delayed meals, inadequate carbohydrate, increased activity without adjustment, and alcohol without food.
questions.strategy: Work each option by asking whether it adds insulin effect or removes glucose. Only those two directions cause a low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for a recognized cause of a low.
More carbohydrate raises glucose.
Missing insulin causes hyperglycemia.
Holding insulin at 80 prevents a fall.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: increased activity without adjusting insulin or intake is one of the causes.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes has a glucose of 812 mg/dL, a serum osmolality of 340 mOsm/kg, negative ketones, and is difficult to rouse. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Glucose spills into the urine and draws water with it
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis. Above roughly 180 mg/dL the kidney's reabsorption capacity is exceeded, glucose enters the urine, and being osmotically active it pulls water and electrolytes along.

options.text: High glucose damages the kidneys, causing them to leak fluid
options.rationale: Describes nephropathy, which is a chronic complication developing over years. It does not explain polyuria at the onset of illness.

options.text: Ketones irritate the urinary tract, increasing urgency
options.rationale: Ketones appear in urine but do not cause the polyuria, which occurs in hyperglycemia with or without ketones.

options.text: Insulin deficiency directly stimulates the bladder
options.rationale: Insulin has no direct action on the bladder.

questions.takeaway: Polyuria is osmotic diuresis. It drives the dehydration, which drives the polydipsia.
questions.strategy: The three Ps come from one process. Understanding it means you can reason to any of them rather than memorizing all three.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The question asks for the mechanism, not the consequence.
Nephropathy is a late complication, not the cause of new polyuria.
No such mechanism exists.
Polyuria occurs in HHS, where ketones are absent.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Glucose is osmotically active and takes water with it.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea becomes shaky, diaphoretic, and confused at 1500 after eating little at lunch. The glucose reads 58 mg/dL. He is alert, follows commands, and is swallowing safely. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Start an intravenous dextrose infusion
options.rationale: Also reserved for unsafe swallowing, and it requires access this client does not need.

options.text: Administer intramuscular glucagon from the emergency supply
options.rationale: Reserved for a client who cannot swallow safely. This client can take oral carbohydrate, which is faster and less invasive.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 30 minutes and treat if it has fallen further
options.rationale: Delays treatment of a symptomatic low that can progress to seizures and loss of consciousness.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: The rule of 15. Give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still low.

questions.takeaway: Conscious, glucose under 70, able to swallow: give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes. The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious client who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.
questions.strategy: The route is decided by swallowing, not by how low the number is. Check the stem for whether the client can protect the airway.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word first, and the stem states the client is alert and swallowing safely.
Glucagon is for the client who cannot swallow.
Intravenous dextrose is for the same situation.
Waiting is not a treatment for symptomatic hypoglycemia.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, rechecked in 15 minutes and repeated if still low.

questions.concept: The rule of 15 treats hypoglycemia in a conscious client who can swallow: give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.

questions.stem: A parent brings a 9-year-old to the clinic reporting that she has started wetting the bed again after years of being dry, seems tired all the time, and is drinking constantly. She has lost 3 kg over the past month. Which findings support a possible new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes? Select all that apply.

options.text: New bedwetting after years of being dry at night
options.rationale: Enuresis is polyuria in a child, and it is often what brings the family in.

options.text: Excessive thirst
options.rationale: Polydipsia, the body's response to fluid lost through osmotic diuresis.

options.text: Weight gain over the past month
options.rationale: Weight loss, not gain, accompanies new type 1 diabetes. Without insulin the body breaks down fat and muscle.

options.text: Unusual fatigue and irritability
options.rationale: Both are presenting features in children.

options.text: Dark velvety patches on the neck
options.rationale: Acanthosis nigricans is a sign of insulin resistance and points to type 2, not type 1.

questions.takeaway: In children, look for enuresis, irritability, unusual fatigue, and weight loss alongside the three Ps.
questions.strategy: Two distractors here are correct diabetes findings attached to the wrong type or the wrong direction. Check each against type 1 specifically.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Type 1 in a child, so the pediatric presentation applies.
Type 1 causes weight loss.
Acanthosis nigricans indicates insulin resistance, meaning type 2.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain: the three Ps in pediatric form plus fatigue and irritability.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old is admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis with a glucose of 512 mg/dL and a pH of 7.18. The serum potassium is 5.1 mEq/L and an insulin infusion has just been started. The nurse reviews the orders before continuing. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis more rapidly
options.rationale: Not a routine intervention, and correcting the pH quickly would accelerate the potassium shift the nurse is trying to control.

options.text: Restrict all intravenous fluids until the serum potassium normalizes
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation is a priority in DKA. Withholding it worsens the dehydration.

options.text: Withhold all potassium replacement because the level is elevated
options.rationale: The level is misleading. Acidosis has pushed potassium out of cells while days of osmotic diuresis depleted the total body store.

options.text: Monitor the serum potassium frequently during the insulin infusion
options.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells and correcting the acidosis reverses the shift, so the serum level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias.

questions.takeaway: A normal or high potassium in DKA hides a real deficit that treatment is about to expose. Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: When a stem gives a lab value that looks reassuring in a client whose physiology is shifting, ask what the treatment will do to that value.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Key word priority. Insulin has just been started.
Treats the number as if it reflected total body potassium.
Not routine, and it accelerates the shift.
Fluids are central to DKA management.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D. Potassium replacement runs alongside the insulin, not after it.

questions.concept: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with type 2 diabetes takes a sulfonylurea and a beta blocker for hypertension. He is found at 1500 pale and confused, having eaten little at lunch. He reported no warning symptoms beforehand and says he usually feels shaky when his sugar drops. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: Confusion is an expected effect of the beta blocker
options.rationale: Beta blockers do not typically cause acute confusion, and attributing it to the drug would delay checking the glucose.

options.text: He has developed tolerance to his usual warning symptoms
options.rationale: Tolerance is not the mechanism. The symptoms are being pharmacologically suppressed rather than worn out.

options.text: The beta blocker blunted the adrenaline response that normally warns him
options.rationale: The early warning signs of hypoglycemia are sympathetic: shakiness, sweating, and tachycardia. Beta blockade suppresses them, so the first thing anyone notices may be confusion.

options.text: The sulfonylurea prevents hypoglycemia from occurring in the first place
options.rationale: The opposite. Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release regardless of intake, which is why they cause hypoglycemia on their own.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers blunt the adrenaline response, so a client may lose the early warning of hypoglycemia entirely.
questions.strategy: When a client on a beta blocker presents with confusion and no preceding shakiness, suspect a masked low rather than a different problem.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: He normally feels shaky and this time felt nothing.
Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia rather than preventing it.
Attributing confusion to the beta blocker delays checking the glucose.
The symptoms are suppressed, not tolerated.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: beta blockade suppresses the sympathetic warning signs, so confusion may be the first sign anyone sees.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with type 1 diabetes was found drowsy at her desk after skipping lunch and taking her usual rapid-acting insulin. The nurse assesses her and must distinguish a low glucose from a high one before treating. Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Diaphoresis
options.rationale: A sympathetic response to falling glucose and one of the earliest signs.

options.text: Shakiness
options.rationale: Also sympathetic, and often the first thing the client notices.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with fruity breath
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations and exhaled ketones belong to DKA, which is hyperglycemia.

options.text: Confusion
options.rationale: The brain depends on a continuous glucose supply, so cognition changes early.

options.text: Tachycardia
options.rationale: Part of the same sympathetic response.

options.text: Polyuria and polydipsia
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis requires high glucose. These are hyperglycemic findings.

questions.takeaway: Hypoglycemia is sympathetic activation plus altered cognition. Hyperglycemia is fluid loss plus, in DKA, acidosis.
questions.strategy: Sorting findings by which state produces them prevents the most common error in diabetes items, which is treating one emergency as the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Signs of hypoglycemia specifically.
Kussmaul respirations and fruity breath are DKA findings.
The three Ps require hyperglycemia.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, and E remain. Severe hypoglycemia progresses to seizures and loss of consciousness.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a fifteen-year history of type 2 diabetes reports tingling and numbness in both feet that has developed gradually over the past year. He mentions he no longer feels the water temperature clearly when he bathes. Which complication does the nurse recognize?

options.text: A microvascular complication
options.rationale: Neuropathy is microvascular, alongside retinopathy and nephropathy. Small vessels supply the nerves, the eye, and the kidney.

options.text: An expected change of aging
options.rationale: A specific bilateral sensory change in a client with diabetes warrants assessment, not attribution to age.

options.text: An early sign of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia produces shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and confusion, not a chronic bilateral sensory loss.

options.text: A macrovascular complication
options.rationale: Macrovascular complications involve large vessels: coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke.

questions.takeaway: Micro is small vessels: eyes, kidneys, nerves. Macro is large vessels: heart and brain.
questions.strategy: The prefix tells you which organs are involved. Sorting by vessel size answers most complication items without further recall.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bilateral sensory change in the feet in long-standing diabetes.
Large-vessel disease affects the heart and brain.
A change from baseline is assessed, not attributed to aging.
Wrong symptom cluster and wrong time course.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A. Neuropathy plus poor circulation is why diabetic feet lose limbs.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 24-year-old newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes before discharge. He describes how he plans to manage his insulin, his glucose checks, and his feet at home. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If I am too unwell to eat, I should hold my insulin until I can manage a meal."
options.rationale: Stress hormones raise glucose during illness regardless of intake. Holding insulin in type 1 during illness is a direct route to ketoacidosis.

options.text: "If my glucose is under 70 and I can swallow, I take 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the glucose is rechecked in 15 minutes.

options.text: "Exercise speeds absorption from the limb I inject, so I should think about the site."
options.rationale: Accurate, which is why injecting the thigh before a walk is poor site choice.

options.text: "I will inspect my feet every day and report any sore or change."
options.rationale: Accurate. Reduced sensation means injuries go unnoticed.

questions.takeaway: Insulin continues during illness in type 1. Reduced intake is managed, not by holding the insulin.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is intuitive: no food, no insulin. It is the commonest route into ketoacidosis.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the dangerous belief.
No insulin means uncontrolled fat breakdown and ketones.
Rule of 15, exercise and site, and foot care are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: insulin continues during illness.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require IMMEDIATE follow-up by the nurse.
questions.takeaway: Sudden confusion, fruity breath, tachycardia with a falling pressure, and polyuria together point at a hyperglycemic emergency.
questions.strategy: Separate background history from findings that have changed. Her hypertension and her prescription are context; the confusion and the fruity breath are new. Two findings describe her existing history rather than a change. Under plus and minus scoring a wrong highlight subtracts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three findings are stated to be new or recent.
Existing diagnoses and prescriptions are context.
Confusion, ketones, volume depletion, and polyuria form one picture.

elimination.verdict: Highlight s1, s2, s3, and s6.

questions.nursesNote: 0915: Client presents to clinic accompanied by daughter. Last seen 11 months ago. History of type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 9 years ago and hypertension. Takes metformin twice daily and lisinopril once daily. Daughter reports client has been missing metformin doses for about three weeks since her supply ran out. Client reports increased thirst and passing urine four to five times each night for the past two weeks, and unintentional weight loss of 7 lb (3.2 kg). Reports feeling increasingly tired and "not right" over the past two days. During the interview the client is unsure of the month and believes she is at the hospital; daughter confirms this is new this morning. Skin dry with poor turgor. Breath has a fruity odor. VS: T 100.4 F (38.0 C); HR 112 beats/min; RR 26 breaths/min; BP 98/60 mm Hg; SpO2 97% on room air.

segments.text: New confusion about the month and her location
segments.rationale: A sudden change in mental status, confirmed as new by the daughter. In an older adult this is a red flag and here it accompanies signs of severe hyperglycemia.

segments.text: Fruity breath odor
segments.rationale: Exhaled ketones. In a client with diabetes this indicates fat is being broken down for fuel and ketones are accumulating.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats/min with blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Tachycardia with a low-normal pressure suggests volume depletion, which fits the polyuria, the dry skin, and the poor turgor.

segments.text: History of hypertension diagnosed before today
segments.rationale: Background history. It shapes her risk and is not a finding requiring action this morning.

segments.text: Takes metformin twice daily and lisinopril once daily
segments.rationale: The prescribed regimen. What matters is that she has not been taking it, which is a separate finding.

segments.text: Passing urine four to five times each night for two weeks
segments.rationale: Polyuria from osmotic diuresis, and it explains the dehydration and the weight loss.

segments.text: Accompanied by her daughter
segments.rationale: Useful for collateral history and not itself a clinical finding.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.takeaway: The dividing line between DKA and HHS is ketones, not the glucose number. Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.
questions.strategy: Type 2 diabetes points you toward HHS, and the fruity breath overrides it. Sort by the findings, not by the diagnosis on the chart. Her chart says type 2, which usually points away from this answer. One finding in the note overrides it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 462 mg/dL rules out a low.
Fruity breath means ketones.
HHS would have no significant ketones.

elimination.verdict: Blank 1 is A and blank 2 is A.

questions.scenario: A stat fingerstick glucose results at 462 mg/dL (25.6 mmol/L). The provider is notified and the client is transferred to the emergency department.
questions.sentence: Based on the documented findings and the glucose result, the client is most likely experiencing [[1]], because [[2]].

options.text: diabetic ketoacidosis
options.rationale: Fruity breath indicates ketones, and the picture developed over days in a client who stopped her medication. Although DKA is typically type 1, it occurs in type 2 under enough physiological stress, and she has a fever suggesting infection.

options.text: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS produces extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones. The fruity breath tells you ketones are present.

options.text: a hypoglycemic episode
options.rationale: Her glucose is 462 mg/dL (25.6 mmol/L).

options.text: an acute stroke
options.rationale: Would not explain the polyuria, the weight loss, the fruity breath, or the fever.

options.text: ketones are present alongside marked hyperglycemia and dehydration
options.rationale: The presence of ketones is what separates this from HHS, and it is the finding that names the condition.

options.text: her glucose exceeds 600 mg/dL with no ketones
options.rationale: Neither figure matches. Her glucose is 462 and ketones are indicated by the breath odor.

options.text: her blood pressure has fallen below her usual range
options.rationale: A consequence of dehydration rather than the finding that identifies the condition.

questions.concept: Diabetic ketoacidosis involves hyperglycemia with ketones and acidosis, typically in type 1. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state involves extreme hyperglycemia without significant ketones, typically in type 2. Ketones are the dividing line.

questions.stem: The provider orders intravenous isotonic fluids, an intravenous insulin infusion with hourly glucose checks, potassium replacement per protocol, and continuous cardiac monitoring. Laboratory orders include a complete blood count, a complete metabolic panel, a venous blood gas, serum ketones, urinalysis, hemoglobin A1C, and a urine culture. Which 2 results will the nurse prioritize reviewing?
questions.takeaway: In DKA the two results that guide the next hour are potassium and pH. The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.
questions.strategy: Ask of each result whether it changes what you do in the next hour. Three of these are useful later and none is urgent now. Several of the others are appropriate orders that will not guide care in the next hour.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Insulin is running and cardiac monitoring is in place.
Potassium and pH direct immediate management.
A1C, culture, hemoglobin, and urine glucose are all retrospective or slow.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Serum potassium
options.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells and correcting the acidosis reverses the shift, so the level can fall quickly and cause dysrhythmias. It is why cardiac monitoring was ordered.

options.text: Venous pH and blood gas
options.rationale: Confirms the acidosis and shows whether the ketone production is stopping, which is how the treatment is judged.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C
options.rationale: Reports average control over about three months. Useful for the discharge plan and it changes nothing in the next hour.

options.text: Urine culture
options.rationale: The fever suggests infection and the result takes 24 to 48 hours, so it cannot guide immediate management.

options.text: Complete blood count hemoglobin
options.rationale: No bleeding is described, and the hemoglobin will not direct the acute treatment.

options.text: Urinalysis glucose
options.rationale: Adds nothing beyond the serum glucose already being measured hourly.

questions.caseTitle: Older adult with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
questions.concept: The A1C reports average blood glucose over about three months, with a target under 7%. Diagnosis rests on a fasting blood glucose over 126 mg/dL on two occasions.

questions.stem: For each requested order, determine whether it is INDICATED or UNNECESSARY given this new information.
questions.takeaway: A falling potassium during insulin treatment is expected, anticipated, and replaced. It is not a reason to stop the insulin. CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.
questions.strategy: Two orders here respond to the potassium by stopping or escalating treatment. Neither is correct: the shift is predictable and it is managed by replacing, not by withdrawing. One requested order responds to the potassium by withdrawing treatment. Consider whether the fall was expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Potassium 4.2 to 3.2, glucose trending down, urine output adequate.
The acidosis has not cleared.
No indication of kidney failure.

elimination.verdict: Four orders are indicated and two are unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Several hours into treatment the client's mental status has improved and her glucose is trending down appropriately per protocol. Her potassium has fallen from 4.2 to 3.2 mEq/L (mmol/L) and urine output has been adequate. The nurse contacts the provider to discuss the plan.

rows.text: Add potassium to the intravenous fluids per protocol
rows.rationale: Her potassium has fallen from 4.2 to 3.2 mEq/L (mmol/L) while insulin is running, and urine output is adequate, so replacement is appropriate.

rows.text: Discontinue the insulin infusion immediately
rows.rationale: Glucose is trending down appropriately per protocol. Stopping the insulin would allow ketone production to resume before the acidosis has cleared.

rows.text: Continue hourly fingerstick glucose checks
rows.rationale: Ordered with the infusion and still required while the glucose is being titrated down.

rows.text: Prepare for emergent dialysis
rows.rationale: Nothing described indicates kidney failure. Urine output is adequate and the acidosis is metabolic from ketones, which insulin and fluids treat.

rows.text: Continue cardiac monitoring given the potassium trend
rows.rationale: A falling potassium is precisely why the monitoring was ordered, and dysrhythmias are the risk.

rows.text: Recheck the serum potassium after replacement
rows.rationale: The level is moving, so a single value does not tell you where it will settle.

questions.concept: CUS escalates a concern with graded language: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue. SBAR reports; CUS escalates when reporting has failed.

questions.stem: After transfer to the medical unit the nurse repositions the client and notes a stage 1 pressure injury on the left heel. Which 2 actions should the nurse take at this time?
questions.takeaway: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable redness. Relieve the pressure and get specialist input.
questions.strategy: Four wrong options treat it as an open infected wound. Stage 1 has no break in the skin, and recognizing that eliminates all four at once. Four options describe care for an open or infected wound. Consider what stage 1 actually means.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stage 1 means the skin is intact.
Culture, wet-to-dry, antibiotic, and alcohol all assume an open wound.
Pressure relief and specialist assessment.

elimination.verdict: A and B are selected.

options.text: Obtain a pressure-relieving device or heel protector
options.rationale: Stage 1 means the skin is intact with non-blanchable redness. Removing the pressure is what allows it to resolve and prevents progression.

options.text: Request a wound care consultation
options.rationale: Brings specialist assessment to a client whose diabetes already impairs healing and circulation.

options.text: Clean the area gently with alcohol to disinfect it
options.rationale: Alcohol dries and damages intact skin, and there is no open wound to disinfect.

options.text: Obtain a wound culture of the area
options.rationale: The skin is intact at stage 1, so there is nothing to culture and no sign of infection described.

options.text: Apply a wet-to-dry dressing to the heel
options.rationale: A debriding dressing applied to intact skin, which would damage it.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a 74-year-old being discharged on six medications, including an enteric-coated tablet, a topical ointment, and eye drops. He lives alone and will manage the regimen himself. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If a tablet is hard to swallow I will crush it and mix it with applesauce."
options.rationale: An enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split, because the coating protects the stomach lining from the medication. A different form is requested from the prescriber or pharmacist instead.

options.text: "Temporary blurring after my eye drops is expected rather than a reaction."
options.rationale: Accurate. Temporary burning or blurring may follow ophthalmic medication.

options.text: "I will keep the head of my bed raised for an hour after my tube feed medication."
options.rationale: Accurate. A minimum of 30 degrees for one hour reduces aspiration risk.

options.text: "I will clean the skin before applying the next dose of my ointment."
options.rationale: Accurate. New medication is never applied over a previous application.

questions.takeaway: Never crush or split an enteric-coated tablet. Change the form, not the technique.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is what a client with swallowing difficulty would reasonably do. It destroys the coating that protects the stomach.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the unsafe practice.
Enteric coating cannot be broken.
Topical, tube feed positioning, and eye drops are correct.

questions.stem: A nurse is working with assistive personnel and reviews which parts of medication administration may be assigned and what the AP must be told. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administering oral medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel
options.rationale: The skill itself stays with the nurse.

options.text: Administering medications through an enteral feeding tube cannot be delegated
options.rationale: And the aspiration risk is why.

options.text: Assistive personnel may give oral medications if the nurse observes
options.rationale: Observation does not change scope. Administration remains with the nurse.

options.text: The AP reports coughing, choking, gagging, or drooling of liquid to the nurse immediately
options.rationale: The AP is told what to watch for and what to report, which is what makes the instruction complete.

options.text: Assistive personnel may crush tablets if the nurse has checked they are crushable
options.rationale: Preparing a medication is part of administration and remains with the nurse.

options.text: Ophthalmic and otic medications may be delegated if the AP has been shown the technique
options.rationale: Neither may be delegated. Being shown a technique does not change the scope.

questions.takeaway: The administration itself stays with the nurse. What is delegated is observation, positioning, and reporting. The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.
questions.strategy: Topical is the single exception where agency policy may allow trained AP, and being shown a technique never expands scope on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the skill from the support
steps.detail: Administration stays; positioning and reporting go.
Some topical agents, by agency policy.
Technique training does not change scope.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.

questions.stem: A client with asthma has been prescribed a pressurized metered-dose inhaler but cannot reliably coordinate pressing the canister with inhaling. His technique has been assessed twice with the same result. Which options should the nurse discuss with the provider?

options.text: Increasing the number of puffs to compensate for poor delivery
options.rationale: Delivers more of a dose that is not reaching the airways, and it risks adverse effects.

options.text: Switching to an oral tablet because inhalers are unsuitable
options.rationale: Abandons the inhaled route without trying the adaptations that exist for this problem.

options.text: A spacer device or a breath-actuated inhaler
options.rationale: Both remove the need to coordinate actuation with the breathing cycle, which is the specific problem.

options.text: Having the AP administer the inhaler for him
options.rationale: Administering inhaled medication cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

questions.takeaway: A pMDI requires coordination during the breathing cycle. Poor coordination calls for a spacer or a breath-actuated inhaler. A pressurized metered-dose inhaler uses a propellant and requires coordination during the breathing cycle. A breath-actuated inhaler triggers on inhalation. A dry powder inhaler has no propellant, needs no spacer, and depends on the client's inspiratory effort.
questions.strategy: The three inhaler types differ in what they ask of the client: a pMDI needs coordination, a BAI triggers on inhalation, and a DPI needs inspiratory effort but no propellant and no spacer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Coordination, not effort or understanding.
More puffs of an undelivered dose.
One abandons the route, one exceeds AP scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: remove the coordination requirement.

questions.concept: A pressurized metered-dose inhaler uses a propellant and requires coordination during the breathing cycle. A breath-actuated inhaler triggers on inhalation. A dry powder inhaler has no propellant, needs no spacer, and depends on the client's inspiratory effort.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to administer a newly prescribed oral medication to a client admitted this morning. She wants to be sure she has gathered what safe administration requires before she goes into the room. Which actions are part of safe medication preparation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess the client for drug allergies
options.rationale: Always assessed before administration, and a documented allergy changes whether the drug is given at all.

options.text: Determine the purpose, usual dose and route, common side effects, onset and peak, and contraindications
options.rationale: The information gathered about any ordered drug before it is given.

options.text: Confirm the client has not eaten within the past hour
options.rationale: Food timing matters for specific medications rather than as a universal preparation step.

options.text: Check the expiration date
options.rationale: Checked for all medications.

options.text: Administer the dose if the calculation looks approximately correct
options.rationale: Calculations are double-checked, and a dose that appears incorrect is not given.

options.text: Check that a second nurse is available to witness
options.rationale: A second check applies to high-alert medications rather than to every oral dose.

questions.takeaway: Allergies, drug information, interactions, expiry, and the client's sensory and physical capacity.
questions.strategy: The wrong option lowers the standard on a calculation. If a dose appears incorrect it is not given, and approximately correct is not a standard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five actions occur before the drug reaches the client.
Approximately correct is not a safety standard.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to apply the next scheduled dose of a prescribed ointment to a client's forearm. The previous application from twelve hours ago is still visible on the skin, and the area is intact with no redness. Which action is correct?

options.text: Apply the new dose to an adjacent area of skin instead
options.rationale: Changes the prescribed site rather than preparing it.

options.text: Clean the skin thoroughly to remove the previous application, then apply the new dose
options.rationale: New medication is never applied over a previous application, and the skin or wound is cleaned before each new dose.

options.text: Withhold the dose until the previous application has worn off
options.rationale: Delays a prescribed dose when cleaning the site resolves the problem.

options.text: Apply the new dose over the existing layer to avoid disturbing the skin
options.rationale: Layering doses makes the amount absorbed unpredictable.

questions.takeaway: Never apply new medication over a previous application. Clean the skin or wound thoroughly before each new dose. Topical medications are applied to skin, mucous membranes, or tissues. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin.
questions.strategy: Topical doses look forgiving and are not. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin, so the amount matters.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Previous application still present.
Layering makes absorption unpredictable.
One moves the site, one delays the dose.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to give medications through a newly inserted small-bore nasogastric tube. The medications are in liquid form and the correct connector is attached. The tube was placed 20 minutes ago. Which action must she take before administering?

options.text: Verify correct placement of the tube
options.rationale: Placement is verified before medications are given, because a displaced tube delivers the dose into the airway.

options.text: Flush the tube with 200 mL of water to confirm patency
options.rationale: A large flush before confirming placement risks delivering fluid into the lungs.

options.text: Position the client flat to ease instillation
options.rationale: The head of the bed is elevated, not lowered, and flat positioning increases aspiration risk.

options.text: Crush the medications finely before mixing
options.rationale: They are already in liquid form, and crushing requires pharmacist consultation in any case.

questions.takeaway: Verify tube placement before giving anything through it. A newly inserted tube requires x-ray confirmation. Medications given through a feeding tube should be in liquid form, and a pharmacist is consulted before crushing or dissolving any tablet. The correct enteral access connector is used and tube placement is verified before administration.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option here delivers something into a tube whose position has not been confirmed. Placement comes before patency, positioning, and preparation.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Newly inserted.
Flushing precedes confirmation.
Flat positioning raises aspiration risk.
The medication is already liquid.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: confirm placement first.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the precautions for administering eye and ear medications with a student before a shift on a unit where two clients receive both. The student asks what differs between the two routes. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ear medications are administered at room temperature
options.rationale: Cold solution instilled into the ear canal causes dizziness and discomfort.

options.text: Sterile drops and solutions are used in case the eardrum is ruptured
options.rationale: A ruptured drum means the solution reaches the middle ear.

options.text: Warm ear drops in hot water immediately before instillation
options.rationale: Drops are at room temperature. Hot water risks burning the canal.

options.text: Temporary burning or blurring of vision may follow eye medication
options.rationale: Expected, and the AP is told about it so it is not mistaken for an adverse reaction.

options.text: Eye ointments are instilled directly onto the cornea
options.rationale: Medication is placed in the conjunctival sac. The cornea is sensitive and direct instillation causes pain and injury.

options.text: Occlude the ear canal with the dropper to prevent leakage
options.rationale: Occluding the canal creates pressure during instillation.

questions.takeaway: Ear drops at room temperature, sterile, without occluding the canal. Eye medication into the conjunctival sac, never onto the cornea. Medications applied to membranes such as the cornea or the rectal mucosa are absorbed quickly because of the vascularity of the membrane and can produce systemic effects.
questions.strategy: The wrong option names an anatomical target that sounds plausible and is wrong. The cornea is highly vascular and highly sensitive, which is why medications applied to membranes absorb quickly and why the cornea is not the target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Temperature, sterility, and not occluding.
Temporary burning or blurring.
The conjunctival sac is the target.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Medications applied to membranes such as the cornea or the rectal mucosa are absorbed quickly because of the vascularity of the membrane and can produce systemic effects.

questions.stem: During medication administration through a feeding tube the client begins coughing, his respiratory rate rises from 18 to 30, and his saturation falls from 96% to 89%. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: Necessary, and another staff member makes the call while the nurse stays with the client.

options.rationale: Follows once the instillation has stopped and the head of the bed is elevated.

options.text: Stop all medications and fluids going through the tube
options.rationale: Stopping the instillation halts what is entering the airway, and it is the first step before positioning or assessment.

options.text: Continue the medication slowly to avoid wasting the dose
options.rationale: Continues delivering fluid into a client showing signs of aspiration.

Stop all medications and fluids, elevate the head of the bed, stay with the client, and assess while another staff member notifies the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing scheduled 0800 medications for four clients. Her preceptor asks her to name when each of the three safety checks occurs. At which points does she perform them?

options.text: At the start, midpoint, and end of the shift
options.rationale: Checks are tied to each medication rather than to the clock.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after receiving a newly prescribed oral antibiotic, a client develops a raised itchy rash, reports his nose is running, and has audible wheezing. Which nursing actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Withhold further doses of the medication
options.rationale: Further doses would add to a reaction already in progress.

options.text: Notify the health care provider and pharmacy immediately
options.rationale: Both are notified, and emergency medications may be needed.

options.text: Assess the client's vital signs
options.rationale: Establishes how far the reaction has progressed and whether the airway is threatened.

options.text: Enter the allergy in the client's medical record
options.rationale: Prevents the drug being given again by anyone caring for him later.

options.text: Give the next scheduled dose and observe whether the reaction repeats
options.rationale: Deliberately re-exposes a client to a drug he is reacting to.

options.text: Document the findings and reassess at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Wheezing indicates airway involvement and cannot wait.

questions.takeaway: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing indicate an allergic reaction. Withhold, notify provider and pharmacy, assess vital signs, and record the allergy. Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction and the need for emergency medications. Withhold further doses, notify the provider and pharmacy immediately, assess vital signs, and add the allergy to the medical record.

strategies: Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Rash, rhinitis, and wheezing together.
Re-exposes him deliberately.
Wheezing cannot wait until the end of the shift.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction and the need for emergency medications. Withhold further doses, notify the provider and pharmacy immediately, assess vital signs, and add the allergy to the medical record.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receives 18 units of Humulin N subcutaneously at 0800. He eats breakfast at 0830 and lunch at 1230. The nurse plans when to monitor most closely for hypoglycemia from this dose. Which window is correct?

options.rationale: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

questions.stem: A 58-year-old newly started on insulin is preparing for discharge and demonstrates his technique to the nurse while explaining what he plans to do at home. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
