options.text: Pituitary: the master gland that regulates other endocrine glands
options.rationale: It also controls growth hormone and regulates water balance through ADH.

options.text: Thyroid: controls metabolism, energy, and body temperature
options.rationale: Which is why symptoms cluster around rate and temperature.

options.text: Parathyroids: regulate calcium and phosphate in blood and bone
options.rationale: And calcium is essential for nerve conduction, muscle contraction, and cardiac rhythm.

options.text: Hypothalamus: produces reproductive hormones
options.rationale: The ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.

options.text: Thymus: regulates blood glucose
options.rationale: The pancreas regulates blood glucose. The thymus is lymphatic.

options.text: Adrenal glands: produce insulin and glucagon
options.rationale: The pancreas produces insulin and glucagon. The adrenals manage stress response and fluid balance.

questions.takeaway: Hypothalamus links the systems, pituitary directs, thyroid sets the pace, parathyroids manage calcium, adrenals handle stress and fluid, pancreas handles glucose. Hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and regulates pituitary output. Pituitary is the master gland. Thyroid controls metabolism, energy, and temperature. Parathyroids regulate calcium and phosphate. Adrenals manage stress, fluid balance, and blood pressure. Pancreas regulates glucose. Ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones.
questions.strategy: Disorders affect the whole body, not just the gland. Once you know what a gland regulates, its dysfunction predicts which systems will show symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five correct pairings.
Reproductive hormones come from the ovaries and testes.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and regulates pituitary output. Pituitary is the master gland. Thyroid controls metabolism, energy, and temperature. Parathyroids regulate calcium and phosphate. Adrenals manage stress, fluid balance, and blood pressure. Pancreas regulates glucose. Ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones.

questions.stem: A student asks the nurse how the body keeps blood glucose within such a narrow range after eating. The nurse describes the sequence: glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, cells absorb glucose, blood glucose falls, and insulin secretion decreases. Which mechanism does this describe?

options.text: Negative feedback, where the response counteracts the original change and then stops
options.rationale: The body detects a change, adjusts secretion to counteract it, restores balance, and signaling stops. It is what prevents dangerous extremes.

options.text: Receptor specificity, which determines which tissues are able to respond to the circulating hormone
options.rationale: Explains which tissues respond, not how secretion is regulated.

options.text: Osmotic diuresis, the mechanism by which elevated blood glucose produces increased urine output
options.rationale: The mechanism by which high glucose produces polyuria.

options.text: Positive feedback, where the response amplifies the original change until an endpoint is reached
options.rationale: Amplification would drive glucose further from normal rather than back toward it.

questions.takeaway: Negative feedback detects a change, counteracts it, restores balance, and switches off. Diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop. Negative feedback: the body detects a change in hormone or substance level, glands adjust secretion to counteract it, balance is restored, and signaling stops. It prevents dangerous extremes, and diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop.
questions.strategy: When feedback fails, disorders emerge. Framing diabetes that way makes the complications follow logically rather than needing separate memorization.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rise, response, fall, secretion stops.
The response opposes the change rather than amplifying it.
A targeting principle and a fluid mechanism.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the body detects a change, adjusts secretion to counteract it, restores balance, and signaling stops.

questions.concept: Negative feedback: the body detects a change in hormone or substance level, glands adjust secretion to counteract it, balance is restored, and signaling stops. It prevents dangerous extremes, and diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old is admitted with symptoms her provider suspects are thyroid-related. She reports feeling constantly warm, has lost weight over three months despite eating well, and her hands are visibly tremulous. Which findings are consistent with hyperthyroidism? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weight loss despite normal or increased appetite
options.rationale: Metabolism is running fast.

options.text: Heat intolerance and excessive sweating
options.rationale: The thyroid controls body temperature regulation.

options.text: Restlessness, anxiety, and tremors
options.rationale: Everything speeds up, including the nervous system.

options.text: Increased heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: Correct, and it is the reason cardiovascular monitoring is a nursing priority.

options.text: Cold intolerance and dry skin
options.rationale: Hypothyroidism, where metabolism slows.

options.text: Constipation and slowed reflexes
options.rationale: Hypothyroidism.

questions.takeaway: Hyper speeds everything up: weight loss, heat intolerance, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia. Hypo slows everything down. Hyperthyroidism speeds metabolism: weight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, raised blood pressure. Hypothyroidism slows it: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, slowed reflexes, bradycardia.
questions.strategy: You do not need to memorize two lists. Decide whether metabolism is fast or slow, then predict what each system does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hyperthyroidism means metabolism is fast.
Weight, temperature, mood, and heart rate all speed up.
Cold intolerance and constipation are the slow picture.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Hyperthyroidism speeds metabolism: weight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, raised blood pressure. Hypothyroidism slows it: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, slowed reflexes, bradycardia.

questions.stem: A client with adrenal dysfunction has an unstable blood pressure, a serum sodium of 128 mEq/L, and reports profound fatigue. Which hormone's action best explains the blood pressure and sodium findings?

options.text: Parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium when circulating levels begin to fall
options.rationale: Calcium regulation rather than sodium and pressure.

options.text: Insulin, which moves glucose from the bloodstream into cells and lowers the blood glucose level
options.rationale: A pancreatic hormone affecting glucose, not sodium.

options.text: Aldosterone, which controls sodium and water retention to maintain blood pressure
options.rationale: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium, and disruption produces both the electrolyte abnormality and the unstable pressure.

options.text: Antidiuretic hormone released from the thyroid gland, which governs water retention by the kidney
options.rationale: ADH is pituitary, not thyroid, and the option misattributes it.

questions.takeaway: The adrenal glands manage stress response, blood pressure through aldosterone, fluid and electrolyte balance, and glucose metabolism through cortisol. The adrenal glands release cortisol and epinephrine in the stress response, regulate blood pressure through aldosterone's control of sodium and water retention, manage sodium and potassium balance, and influence glucose metabolism through cortisol.
questions.strategy: Adrenal dysfunction shows up as unstable blood pressure, electrolyte imbalance, fatigue, and an impaired stress response. Those four together are the pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sodium and blood pressure together.
Glucose and calcium.
ADH is pituitary.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: aldosterone.

questions.concept: The adrenal glands release cortisol and epinephrine in the stress response, regulate blood pressure through aldosterone's control of sodium and water retention, manage sodium and potassium balance, and influence glucose metabolism through cortisol.

questions.stem: A client with a pituitary disorder has a urine output of 4,200 mL over eight hours with a specific gravity of 1.002, and reports constant thirst. Which assessment is the priority?

options.text: Thyroid function and temperature tolerance
options.rationale: Fits a thyroid disorder and does not explain dilute polyuria.

options.text: Serum sodium and fluid balance
options.rationale: Pituitary dysfunction disrupts water balance through ADH, and dilute polyuria with thirst fits diabetes insipidus.

options.text: Blood glucose and serum ketones
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus produces glucose-laden urine, not urine this dilute.

options.text: Serum calcium and phosphate
options.rationale: Parathyroid concerns rather than pituitary.

questions.takeaway: The pituitary regulates water balance through ADH. Monitor urine output, fluid balance, and serum sodium.
questions.strategy: Diabetes insipidus and diabetes mellitus both cause polyuria and thirst. The urine tells you which: very dilute points at ADH, glucose-laden points at osmotic diuresis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Large volume and very dilute.
Parathyroid concerns rather than pituitary.
Fits a thyroid disorder and does not explain dilute polyuria.
Osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus produces glucose-laden urine, not urine this dilute.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: pituitary dysfunction disrupts water balance through ADH, and dilute polyuria with thirst fits diabetes insipidus.

questions.concept: The pituitary regulates water balance through ADH. Nursing focus includes monitoring urine output and fluid balance, assessing serum sodium, and recognizing diabetes insipidus, which presents with excess dilute urine and thirst.

questions.stem: A client's serum calcium is 7.4 mg/dL on the first day after a thyroidectomy. She reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips, and the nurse is planning her assessments and safety measures. Which nursing actions and findings are relevant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess for Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs
options.rationale: Neuromuscular indicators of hypocalcemia, and they are the assessments.

options.text: Monitor cardiac rhythm
options.rationale: Calcium is essential for cardiac rhythm, and imbalance produces arrhythmias.

options.text: Watch for muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones
options.rationale: The picture of hypercalcemia, which is the opposite imbalance.

options.text: Encourage a high-phosphate diet
options.rationale: Phosphate and calcium move inversely. Raising phosphate lowers calcium further.

options.text: Restrict dietary calcium
options.rationale: Calcium is already low. Restricting it worsens the problem.

options.text: Implement fall prevention measures
options.rationale: Safety is a priority given the neuromuscular effects.

questions.takeaway: Hypocalcemia produces tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias. Hypercalcemia produces weakness, confusion, and kidney stones. PTH raises blood calcium when levels drop; calcitonin lowers it when levels are high. Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias, assessed through Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Hypercalcemia causes muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones.
questions.strategy: PTH raises calcium when it drops; calcitonin lowers it when it is high. Knowing which hormone is missing predicts which direction the calcium moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium after thyroid surgery.
Neuromuscular irritability: tetany, seizures, arrhythmias.
Weakness and kidney stones describe hypercalcemia.

elimination.verdict: A, B and F are selected.

questions.concept: PTH raises blood calcium when levels drop; calcitonin lowers it when levels are high. Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias, assessed through Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Hypercalcemia causes muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones.

questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews endocrine physiology with a student before a clinical shift, asking her to explain how hormones reach their targets and what happens when regulation fails. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Hyperthyroidism speeds everything up, so I would expect weight loss and heat intolerance."
options.rationale: Accurate. Setting the direction predicts what each system does.

options.text: "Hypocalcemia causes tetany and seizures; hypercalcemia causes weakness and confusion."
options.rationale: Accurate. The direction of the calcium determines the presentation.

options.text: "Negative feedback counteracts a change and then switches off."
options.rationale: Accurate, and diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop.

options.text: "A hormone only reaches the tissues it is meant to affect."
options.rationale: Hormones are released into the bloodstream and reach every tissue. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, which is why the same hormone produces different effects in different places.

questions.takeaway: Hormones reach every tissue. Receptors decide which ones respond.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement sounds like targeting and describes delivery. The targeting happens at the receptor, not in the bloodstream.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
Circulation is universal; response is selective.
Feedback, thyroid direction, and calcium are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: hormones reach everywhere, receptors decide.

questions.stem: A student asks why insulin circulates through the entire body but does not affect every tissue in the same way. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Hormones are broken down before reaching most tissues
options.rationale: Circulation to all tissues is the point; the response depends on receptors.

options.text: Only cells with matching receptors respond
options.rationale: Receptor specificity determines which tissues are affected, which is why the same hormone produces different responses in different places.

options.text: Every cell reached responds equally
options.rationale: Would make targeted hormonal regulation impossible.

options.text: Hormones reach only the organ that produced them
options.rationale: Hormones are released into the bloodstream and travel to distant targets.

questions.takeaway: Hormones reach every tissue. Only cells with matching receptors respond, which is why one hormone produces different effects in different places. Hormones are chemical messengers released directly into the bloodstream and travel to distant target cells. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, so the same hormone produces different responses in different tissues.
questions.strategy: Receptor specificity explains a great deal at once: why insulin resistance affects some tissues more than others, and why a single gland disorder produces symptoms across several systems.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Why circulation is universal and effect is not.
Hormones are released into the bloodstream and travel to distant targets.
Circulation to all tissues is the point; the response depends on receptors.
Would make targeted hormonal regulation impossible.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: receptor specificity determines which tissues are affected, which is why the same hormone produces different responses in different places.

questions.concept: Hormones are chemical messengers released directly into the bloodstream and travel to distant target cells. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, so the same hormone produces different responses in different tissues.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four clients with endocrine disorders at the start of a shift and must decide what to assess first on each. Two have laboratory results pending and one has been increasingly drowsy overnight. Which questions guide her priorities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Are the ABCs affected, with a patent airway, adequate breathing, and stable circulation?
options.rationale: The first priority-setting question in any acute situation.

options.text: Are vital signs within a safe range, including blood pressure and temperature extremes?
options.rationale: Endocrine disorders produce hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia, and temperature extremes.

options.text: Is there altered mental status, confusion, or decreased level of consciousness?
options.rationale: A specified priority, and mental status change is often the first sign of a critical glucose or electrolyte value.

options.text: Determine how long the endocrine diagnosis has been present
options.rationale: Duration of a diagnosis does not determine acute priority. What is happening now does.

options.text: Confirm the client has a follow-up appointment booked
options.rationale: A discharge consideration rather than a question that sets priority at the bedside.

options.text: Has the client's gland disorder been present for more than a year?
options.rationale: Duration of the diagnosis does not determine acute priority. What is happening now does.

questions.takeaway: ABCs, vital signs, mental status, fluid and electrolytes, and glucose. Endocrine emergencies deteriorate rapidly. Endocrine priority questions: are the ABCs affected, are vital signs in a safe range, is there altered mental status, is there a fluid or electrolyte imbalance in sodium, potassium, or calcium, and is blood glucose at a critical level.
questions.strategy: Every question on this list asks what is happening now. The wrong option asks about history, which never sets acute priority.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Airway, vitals, mentation, electrolytes, glucose.
History does not determine acute priority.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Endocrine priority questions: are the ABCs affected, are vital signs in a safe range, is there altered mental status, is there a fluid or electrolyte imbalance in sodium, potassium, or calcium, and is blood glucose at a critical level.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old newly prescribed levothyroxine for hypothyroidism tells the nurse he plans to take it only on the days he feels sluggish, since he does not want to take medication he does not need. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Document that he is non-adherent with his prescribed regimen and notify the provider of his intent
options.rationale: Labels a misunderstanding as non-adherence before teaching has occurred.

options.text: Agree with his plan, since the dose can reasonably be adjusted according to how he feels each day
options.rationale: Self-titrating a hormone replacement by symptom leaves the level unstable.

options.text: Explain that consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications
options.rationale: Adherence is the nursing priority, and intermittent dosing leaves the deficiency untreated.

options.text: Tell him to take a double dose on the days he feels sluggish to compensate for the missed doses
options.rationale: Improvises a dose and risks overtreatment.

questions.takeaway: Levothyroxine requires consistent daily dosing. Symptoms are not a guide to whether the dose is needed. Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, and consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications. Myxedema coma is a rare but life-threatening complication of severe untreated hypothyroidism.
questions.strategy: Untreated severe hypothyroidism can progress to myxedema coma, which is why adherence is a safety issue rather than a compliance one.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: Symptom-guided dosing.
Both let symptoms set the dose.
Labels before teaching.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: adherence is the nursing priority, and intermittent dosing leaves the deficiency untreated.

questions.concept: Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, and consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications. Myxedema coma is a rare but life-threatening complication of severe untreated hypothyroidism.

skills.title: Donning and Doffing PPE
skills.subtitle: Standard, contact, droplet, and airborne precautions and the sequences that keep them working

questions.stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. She is wearing a gown, gloves, a surgical mask, and a face shield. Which item does she remove FIRST?

options.text: The gown
options.rationale: Removed after the gloves, touching only the inside.

options.text: The face shield
options.rationale: Removed after the gown, by the headband or earpieces.

options.text: The gloves
options.rationale: The outside of the gloves is the most contaminated surface, so they come off first using a glove-in-glove or pinch-pull method.

options.text: The mask
options.rationale: Removed last of the PPE items, before the final hand hygiene.

questions.takeaway: Doffing order: gloves, gown, hand hygiene if contaminated, goggles or face shield, mask or respirator, final hand hygiene. Doffing sequence: gloves, gown, hand hygiene if hands become contaminated, goggles or face shield, mask or respirator, then thorough final hand hygiene immediately after all PPE is removed.
questions.strategy: Donning and doffing are not simple reverses of each other. Doffing runs most contaminated first, which puts gloves at the front and the mask near the end.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The outside of the gloves.
The gown follows the gloves.
Eye protection and mask come later.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: gloves first.

questions.concept: Doffing sequence: gloves, gown, hand hygiene if hands become contaminated, goggles or face shield, mask or respirator, then thorough final hand hygiene immediately after all PPE is removed.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old is admitted with a surgical wound colonized with MRSA and is placed on contact precautions. The nurse will be changing the dressing, which has been draining moderately. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wear gloves and a gown at minimum for client care
options.rationale: The specified minimum PPE for contact precautions.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before donning and after doffing PPE
options.rationale: Hand hygiene bookends every PPE sequence regardless of precaution type.

options.text: Recognize that MRSA and VRE spread by direct contact and environmental surfaces
options.rationale: Which is why surfaces and equipment matter as much as the client contact itself.

options.text: Wear an N95 respirator when entering the room
options.rationale: N95 is required for airborne precautions, not contact.

options.text: Add eye protection if splashing of secretions is anticipated
options.rationale: Eye protection is added based on the anticipated exposure rather than the precaution label alone.

questions.takeaway: Contact precautions: gloves and gown at minimum, for organisms spread by direct contact and environmental surfaces. Contact precautions are used for infections spread by direct contact or environmental surfaces such as MRSA and VRE. PPE is gloves and gown at minimum.
questions.strategy: PPE is chosen by the route of transmission and by what you expect to be exposed to. The precaution type sets the minimum; the task can raise it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Direct contact and surfaces.
Gloves and gown.
N95 belongs to airborne precautions.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Contact precautions are used for infections spread by direct contact or environmental surfaces such as MRSA and VRE. PPE is gloves and gown at minimum.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to enter the room of a client requiring gown, mask, eye protection, and gloves. She has just completed hand hygiene. Which item does she put on next?

options.text: The gloves
options.rationale: Gloves go on last, so they can extend over the cuffs of the gown.

options.text: The gown
options.rationale: Gown comes first after hand hygiene, covering the torso from neck to knees and the arms to the wrists, then fastened at neck and waist.

options.text: The mask
options.rationale: The mask goes on after the gown.

options.text: The eye protection
options.rationale: Goggles or face shield follow the mask, not the hand hygiene.

questions.takeaway: Donning order: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, gloves. Donning sequence: hand hygiene, gown covering torso from neck to knees and arms to wrists fastened at neck and waist, mask or respirator secured at the back of the head and neck with the flexible band fitted to the nose bridge, goggles or face shield, then gloves extending over the gown cuff.
questions.strategy: The order is built around the gloves finishing on top of the gown cuffs. Work back from that and the rest of the sequence follows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hand hygiene, gown, mask, eye protection, gloves.
Gloves are last so they cover the gown cuff.
Both follow the gown.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the gown.

questions.concept: Donning sequence: hand hygiene, gown covering torso from neck to knees and arms to wrists fastened at neck and waist, mask or respirator secured at the back of the head and neck with the flexible band fitted to the nose bridge, goggles or face shield, then gloves extending over the gown cuff.

questions.stem: A nurse orients a student to infection prevention on a medical unit where several clients have no confirmed diagnosis yet. The student asks which precautions apply before anyone knows what a client has. Which statements about standard precautions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: They are used for all clients, regardless of diagnosis
options.rationale: Which is the point of them. You do not wait to know what a client has.

options.text: They include hand hygiene as the foundation
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Gloves, gown, or mask are added depending on the anticipated interaction
options.rationale: The PPE is matched to what the task will expose you to.

options.text: They apply only to clients with a confirmed infection
options.rationale: Reverses the principle. Standard precautions exist because infection status is often unknown.

options.text: They are the baseline on which transmission-based precautions are added
options.rationale: Contact, droplet, and airborne precautions are layered on top rather than replacing them.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every client regardless of diagnosis. Everything else is added on top. Standard precautions are used for all clients regardless of diagnosis and include hand hygiene plus gloves, gown, or mask depending on the interaction. Transmission-based precautions are added on top of them.
questions.strategy: The wrong option is the intuitive one: precautions for people known to be infectious. Standard precautions exist precisely because you often do not know.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All clients, all the time.
Confirmed infection is not the trigger.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Standard precautions are used for all clients regardless of diagnosis and include hand hygiene plus gloves, gown, or mask depending on the interaction. Transmission-based precautions are added on top of them.

questions.stem: A nurse has donned her gown, mask, and eye protection and is putting on gloves before entering an isolation room. The gown cuffs sit at her wrists and the gloves are the correct size. Which action is correct?

options.text: Extend the gloves to cover the wrist of the isolation gown
options.rationale: Leaves no skin exposed at the wrist, which is why gloves go on last in the donning sequence.

options.text: Tuck the gown cuffs inside the gloves at the forearm
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship and leaves the gown cuff unprotected.

options.text: Apply the gloves before the gown for a better fit
options.rationale: Would make it impossible for the gloves to cover the gown cuffs.

options.text: Leave the wrist uncovered so the skin can breathe
options.rationale: Creates an exposed gap at a high-contact area.

questions.takeaway: Gloves are the last item donned and extend over the cuff of the gown, leaving no exposed skin at the wrist. Gloves are donned last and extend to cover the wrist of the isolation gown, leaving no exposed skin.
questions.strategy: The wrist is where contamination reaches skin during care, which is why this single detail drives the whole donning order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gloves over gown cuff.
Both leave a gap.
Reverses the donning order.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: leaves no skin exposed at the wrist, which is why gloves go on last in the donning sequence.

questions.concept: Gloves are donned last and extend to cover the wrist of the isolation gown, leaving no exposed skin.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old is admitted with a three-week cough, night sweats, and a 6 kg weight loss. Pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected pending sputum results. Which PPE and placement does the nurse prepare?

options.text: Standard precautions with no additional measures
options.rationale: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis requires airborne precautions from the outset.

options.text: N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
options.rationale: Tuberculosis spreads by small aerosolized particles, which remain suspended and are not filtered by a surgical mask.

options.text: Surgical mask within three feet of the client
options.rationale: Droplet precaution practice, which does not protect against aerosolized particles.

options.text: Gloves and gown for all contact
options.rationale: Contact precautions, which do not address an airborne route.

questions.takeaway: Airborne precautions: N95 or higher respirator and a negative-pressure room. Tuberculosis, measles, and varicella. Airborne precautions are used for infections spread by small aerosolized particles such as tuberculosis, measles, and varicella. An N95 or higher-level respirator is required and the client is placed in a negative-pressure room if available.
questions.strategy: The particle size decides the mask. Large droplets fall within about three feet and a surgical mask handles them. Small aerosolized particles stay suspended and need a respirator.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Small aerosolized particles.
Droplet precaution practice, which does not protect against aerosolized particles.
Contact precautions, which do not address an airborne route.
Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis requires airborne precautions from the outset.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: tuberculosis spreads by small aerosolized particles, which remain suspended and are not filtered by a surgical mask.

questions.concept: Airborne precautions are used for infections spread by small aerosolized particles such as tuberculosis, measles, and varicella. An N95 or higher-level respirator is required and the client is placed in a negative-pressure room if available.

questions.stem: A charge nurse reviews four admissions arriving this afternoon and assigns precautions for each before the rooms are prepared. The list includes a wound infection, a respiratory illness, and two clients with rash illnesses. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: MRSA wound infection: contact precautions
options.rationale: Spread by direct contact and environmental surfaces.

options.text: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci: contact precautions
options.rationale: Occurs alongside MRSA.

options.text: Measles: droplet precautions
options.rationale: Measles spreads by small aerosolized particles and requires airborne precautions.

options.text: Tuberculosis: contact precautions
options.rationale: Tuberculosis is airborne and requires an N95 and a negative-pressure room.

options.text: Clostridioides difficile: airborne precautions
options.rationale: C. difficile spreads by contact and environmental surfaces, requiring contact precautions.

options.text: Varicella: airborne precautions
options.rationale: Occurs alongside tuberculosis and measles.

questions.takeaway: Contact: MRSA, VRE. Droplet: influenza, pertussis. Airborne: tuberculosis, measles, varicella. Contact: MRSA and VRE. Droplet: influenza and pertussis. Airborne: tuberculosis, measles, and varicella.
questions.strategy: Measles is the one most often misfiled. It looks like a childhood rash illness and it travels as an aerosol, which puts it with tuberculosis rather than with influenza.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Surfaces, large droplets, or aerosols.
Measles is airborne, not droplet.

elimination.verdict: A, B and F are selected.

questions.concept: Contact: MRSA and VRE. Droplet: influenza and pertussis. Airborne: tuberculosis, measles, and varicella.

questions.stem: A nurse dons an N95 respirator before entering the room of a client on airborne precautions. Which action must she take before entering?

options.text: Loosen the nose bridge slightly
options.rationale: The flexible band is fitted to the nose bridge precisely to create the seal.

options.text: Add a surgical mask over it
options.rationale: Adds no filtration and may disturb the seal.

options.text: Match the size to a colleague's
options.rationale: Fit is individual, and a colleague's size tells her nothing about her own seal.

options.text: Perform a seal check
options.rationale: A respirator protects only if it seals. One that leaks around the edges offers the protection of no respirator.

questions.takeaway: An N95 requires a seal check every time. Fit the flexible band to the nose bridge and fit the respirator snugly below the chin. An N95 respirator requires a seal check each time it is donned. Fit the flexible band to the nose bridge and fit the respirator snugly to the face and below the chin.
questions.strategy: Comfort and protection pull against each other here. Anything that makes an N95 easier to breathe through is usually breaking the seal that makes it work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A respirator works by sealing.
Fit is individual, and a colleague's size tells her nothing about her own seal.
Adds no filtration and may disturb the seal.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultates the peripheral lung fields of a healthy adult during a routine assessment. She hears soft, breezy, low-pitched sounds with an inspiratory phase about three times longer than expiration. Which breath sound is this?

options.text: Vesicular
options.rationale: Created by air moving through the smaller airways, and heard over most of the peripheral lung fields.

options.text: Bronchial
options.rationale: Loud, high-pitched, and hollow, with expiration longer than inspiration in a 3 to 2 ratio, created by air moving through the trachea.

options.text: Bronchovesicular
options.rationale: Medium-pitched and blowing, with inspiration equal to expiration, created by air moving through the large airways.

options.text: Rhonchi
options.rationale: An adventitious sound rather than a normal one.

questions.takeaway: Vesicular is soft, low-pitched, inspiration three times expiration. Bronchovesicular is equal. Bronchial has expiration longer than inspiration. Bronchovesicular are medium-pitched with inspiration equal to expiration, from large airways. Bronchial are loud, high-pitched, and hollow with expiration longer than inspiration in a 3 to 2 ratio, from the trachea.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a client's neurological status. He states his name and that he is in the hospital, identifies the month and year correctly, and explains that he came in after a fall at home. How does the nurse document his orientation?

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to perform an admission physical examination on a 63-year-old who speaks limited English, appears uneasy, and is sharing a room separated only by a curtain. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

questions.stem: A student asks why the abdominal assessment is performed in a different order from every other body system. Which explanation is accurate?

questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews assessment technique with a student after observing her examine two clients on a medical unit. She asks the student to describe the order she used and why. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

questions.stem: A student sets up a sterile field for a dressing change on a wound with a temperature of 38.4 C, then reaches across the field to retrieve gauze from the far side. Nothing visibly touched the drape. Which action should the nurse take?

questions.stem: A quality committee reviews the unit's health care-associated infection data for the past quarter, which shows a rise in central line and urinary catheter infections. The committee is identifying contributing factors before proposing changes. Which factors contribute to these infections? Select all that apply.

options.text: Invasive procedures
options.rationale: They bypass the body's normal barriers and create a portal of entry.

options.text: Antibiotic administration
options.rationale: Disrupts normal flora and selects for resistant organisms, which is why it appears as a cause rather than only a treatment.

options.text: Multidrug-resistant organisms
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Breaks in infection prevention and control activities
options.rationale: The category that covers missed hand hygiene, broken technique, and inadequate cleaning.

options.text: Community-acquired infections present on admission

questions.stem: A client's wound swab grows MRSA. He is afebrile, the wound is clean and granulating, his white cell count is normal, and he has no systemic symptoms. Which term describes his status?

questions.stem: A client on a surgical unit develops a wound infection. The nurse plans interventions and is asked which links in the chain of infection each one breaks. Which are links in the chain of infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reservoir

options.text: Portal of exit

options.text: Susceptible host
options.rationale: The person in whom the organism can establish itself.

options.text: Incubation period
options.rationale: The interval between exposure and symptoms. It describes the course of an infection rather than a link in the chain.

options.text: Antibody titer

questions.takeaway: Six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.

An interval and a property of the organism.
A laboratory measure of the host response.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.concept: The chain of infection has six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. Nursing interventions work by breaking a link.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old receiving chemotherapy has a white cell count of 0.8. He is afebrile with no identified source of infection. Which type of precaution does the nurse anticipate?

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews infection control with staff after an audit found variation in hand hygiene practice on a unit caring for several clients with C. difficile. Which statement by a staff nurse indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Hand hygiene is the single most effective intervention for reducing health care-associated infections."

questions.stem: A nurse assesses four clients for infection risk: an 84-year-old with poor oral intake, a 30-year-old recovering from an uncomplicated appendectomy, a 45-year-old with well-controlled asthma, and a 22-year-old athlete with a minor laceration. Which client is at greatest risk?

options.rationale: Adds a transfer step and a contamination opportunity.

options.text: Prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule
options.rationale: The vial requires air injection before withdrawal, and doing it first avoids introducing the ampule medication into the vial.

options.text: Draw both medications without a filter needle, since they are being combined in one syringe anyway
options.rationale: The ampule still requires a filter needle regardless of what else is in the syringe.

questions.takeaway: Vial first, then the ampule, using the same syringe and filter needle. When mixing medications from a vial and an ampule, prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule.
questions.strategy: The order follows from the mechanics: vials need air injected in, ampules do not. Whatever needs air pushed into it goes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The vial, because it is sealed.
Air injection with medication already drawn risks contaminating the vial.
The ampule always needs a filter needle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the vial requires air injection before withdrawal, and doing it first avoids introducing the ampule medication into the vial.

questions.concept: When mixing medications from a vial and an ampule, prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews needlestick prevention with a student after a colleague on another unit sustained an injury while disposing of a used syringe. Which statements and actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers
options.rationale: Which is why the prevention measures are federally mandated.

options.text: Injuries occur when workers recap needles, mishandle lines and needles, or leave needles at the bedside
options.rationale: The three specified circumstances.

options.text: Use sharps with engineered sharps injury protection, such as safety syringes and blunt-end cannulas
options.rationale: Required under the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act.

options.text: Dispose of sharps in a puncture-proof, leak-proof container that stands upright and is labeled with the biohazard symbol
options.rationale: And the container is never overfilled.

options.text: Recap the needle carefully with one hand before disposal
options.rationale: Recapping is a cause of needlestick injury. The needle goes straight into the container.

questions.takeaway: Never recap. Use engineered safety devices, and dispose into an upright, puncture-proof container that is not overfilled. Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers and occur through recapping, mishandling lines and needles, and leaving needles at the bedside. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act mandates sharps with engineered sharps injury protection. Sharps containers are puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.
questions.strategy: The wrong option describes a technique taught as safer recapping. It is still recapping, which is one of the three causes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recapping, mishandling, leaving needles at the bedside.
One-handed recapping is still recapping.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers and occur through recapping, mishandling lines and needles, and leaving needles at the bedside. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act mandates sharps with engineered sharps injury protection. Sharps containers are puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the Z-track method to administer an intramuscular medication known to be irritating to subcutaneous tissue. A student asks why she displaces the skin before inserting the needle. What is the purpose of this technique?

options.text: To eliminate the need to rotate injection sites between doses of the same medication
options.rationale: Sites are rotated regardless, to prevent induration and abscess formation.

options.text: To allow a larger volume of medication to be given safely in one injection site
options.rationale: Volume limits are set by the muscle mass, not by the technique.

options.text: To reduce the depth the needle must travel before reaching the muscle tissue beneath
options.rationale: The needle still enters at 90 degrees to reach muscle.

options.text: To keep the medication in the muscle and prevent it tracking back into subcutaneous tissue
options.rationale: Displacing the skin before injection means the tissue layers no longer line up when released, sealing the medication in the muscle.

questions.takeaway: Z-track keeps medication in the muscle and stops it leaking back into the subcutaneous layer above. The Z-track method keeps intramuscular medication in the muscle and prevents it tracking back into the subcutaneous tissue layer above.
questions.strategy: Medication that tracks back into subcutaneous tissue irritates it and absorbs at the wrong rate, so the technique protects both comfort and the intended action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Preventing the medication tracking back.
Depth and volume are unchanged.
Rotation is still required.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: displacing the skin before injection means the tissue layers no longer line up when released, sealing the medication in the muscle.

questions.concept: The Z-track method keeps intramuscular medication in the muscle and prevents it tracking back into the subcutaneous tissue layer above.

questions.stem: A student notices that an intramuscular antibiotic is drawn with a 21 gauge needle while an insulin dose uses a 29 gauge, and asks whether the larger number means a larger needle. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: A smaller gauge number means a larger bore, which thicker medications require
options.rationale: Gauge runs inversely to diameter. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.

options.text: Gauge describes the length of the needle rather than the width of its bore or lumen
options.rationale: Length is stated separately in inches.

options.text: A smaller gauge number means a finer needle, which is gentler on the dense tissue of a muscle
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship.

options.text: Gauge is selected according to the client's body weight rather than the medication being given
options.rationale: Needle length may vary with body size; the gauge follows the medication and the route.

questions.takeaway: Gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. IM 20 to 25, SQ 25 to 30, ID 25 to 27. Needle gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25 gauge, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.
questions.strategy: This one relationship makes the three tables coherent. The route needing the thickest medication has the lowest numbers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smaller number, larger bore.
Reverses it.
Length and body size are separate considerations.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: gauge runs inversely to diameter.

questions.concept: Needle gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25 gauge, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.

skills.title: Medication Administration and Safety
skills.subtitle: Legal responsibility, the ten rights, assessment before the dose, error response, and patient education

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a 66-year-old about a newly prescribed medication before discharge. He nodded throughout the explanation and said it made sense, and she now wants to confirm he actually understood. Which question is most effective?

options.text: "Do you understand everything I have explained to you?"
options.rationale: A yes tells you nothing, and a client who does not know what he does not know will say yes.

options.text: "Do you have any questions about what we covered today?"
options.rationale: Useful and it confirms nothing about what he retained.

options.text: "Can you tell me how you will take this when you get home?"
options.rationale: Teach-back asks the client to describe the plan, and phrasing it as a check on the nurse's explanation removes the sense of.

options.text: "I have gone through everything, so let me know if anything comes up."
options.rationale: Closes the exchange without checking anything.

questions.takeaway: Do not ask whether they understand. Ask them to tell you how they will take it. Teach-back asks the client to explain how they will take the medication rather than whether they understand. Cover what the medication is, why they are taking it, how and when to take it, what to expect, and when to call.
questions.strategy: The phrasing matters as much as the technique. Framing it as checking your own explanation makes it easier for a client to admit he is unsure.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.detail: One returns a description; three return yes or nothing.
Both can be answered without understanding.
Closes the conversation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: teach-back asks the client to describe the plan, and phrasing it as a check on the nurse's explanation removes the sense of.

questions.concept: Teach-back asks the client to explain how they will take the medication rather than whether they understand. Cover what the medication is, why they are taking it, how and when to take it, what to expect, and when to call.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to give a scheduled morning medication to a client admitted two days ago with a changing clinical picture. Before she goes into the room she considers what she needs to know. Which assessments come before administration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allergies
options.rationale: Checked before every medication, every time.

options.text: Vital signs and relevant laboratory values
options.rationale: Both may contain a parameter that decides whether the dose goes ahead.

options.text: Level of consciousness and ability to swallow
options.rationale: Both determine whether the route is safe for this client right now.

options.text: Confirm the client's insurance covers the medication
options.rationale: An access consideration at discharge rather than an assessment before this dose.

options.text: Verify the medication was dispensed by the hospital pharmacy
options.rationale: Dispensing source is not among the assessments made before administration.

options.text: The client's insurance coverage for the medication
options.rationale: A discharge and access consideration rather than a pre-administration assessment.

questions.takeaway: Before you give: allergies, vital signs, relevant labs, pain, level of consciousness, swallowing, current medications, indication, and previous response. Assess before administration: allergies, vital signs, relevant laboratory values, pain level, level of consciousness, swallowing ability, relevant physical assessment, current medications, the indication, and the previous response.
questions.strategy: Each of these can stop the dose. That is what makes it an assessment rather than a formality.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Ask what could stop the dose
steps.detail: Allergies, vitals, labs, swallowing, interactions.
Coverage matters at discharge, not before this dose.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Assess before administration: allergies, vital signs, relevant laboratory values, pain level, level of consciousness, swallowing ability, relevant physical assessment, current medications, the indication, and the previous response.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she has administered a scheduled medication to the wrong client during the morning round. The client is alert, has no symptoms, and the drug is not one he takes. Which action does she take FIRST?

options.text: Assess the client
options.rationale: Assessment comes before notification, documentation, and reporting, because it establishes whether the client needs immediate protection.

options.text: Complete the facility's safety report
options.rationale: Required, and it is not the first action.

options.text: Notify the provider and the charge nurse
options.rationale: Required, and it follows the assessment that tells you what to report.

options.text: Document the error in the client's record
options.rationale: Documentation follows the assessment and the immediate response.

questions.takeaway: Assess the client, protect the client, notify, follow policy, document, complete safety reporting, continue monitoring. After a medication error: assess the client, protect the client, notify the appropriate persons, follow facility policy, document appropriately, complete required safety reporting, and continue monitoring.
questions.strategy: Three of these four options are genuinely required. The key word FIRST separates sequence from content, and the client comes before the paperwork every time.

strategies: Priority key word
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Seven steps, beginning with the client.
All required, all after assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: assess the client.

questions.concept: After a medication error: assess the client, protect the client, notify the appropriate persons, follow facility policy, document appropriately, complete required safety reporting, and continue monitoring.

questions.stem: A nurse orients to a medical unit and reviews the medications that require additional safeguards, including those stored in the controlled substance cabinet. The unit stocks insulin, opioids, and anticoagulants. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes are high-alert medications
options.rationale: Errors with these may cause significant client harm.

options.text: The DEA regulates controlled substances including opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and certain sedatives
options.rationale: Under the Controlled Substances Act.

options.text: Nursing responsibilities for controlled substances include secure storage and accurate counts
options.rationale: Along with accurate documentation and waste procedures.

options.text: Nurses are responsible for recognizing and preventing diversion
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: High-alert medications are those most frequently prescribed on the unit
options.rationale: Frequency is not the criterion. The criterion is the severity of harm when an error occurs.

questions.takeaway: High alert means the harm is severe when an error occurs, not that the drug is dangerous or common. High-alert medications include insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes. The DEA regulates controlled substances including opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and certain sedatives, and nursing responsibilities include secure storage, accurate counts, accurate documentation and waste procedures, and recognizing and preventing diversion.
questions.strategy: Insulin appears on both lists: high-alert here, and the medication with its own safety checks in the glucose material. That is not a coincidence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, concentrated electrolytes.
Opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, certain sedatives.
Severity of harm, not frequency of use.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: High-alert medications include insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes. The DEA regulates controlled substances including opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and certain sedatives, and nursing responsibilities include secure storage, accurate counts, accurate documentation and waste procedures, and recognizing and preventing diversion.

questions.stem: A nurse manager reviews medication safety with a new graduate after her first month on the unit, asking her to describe how she decides whether a dose is safe to give. Which statement by the new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If all ten rights match, the dose is safe to give."
options.rationale: The ten rights check the order. Right medication plus wrong client condition is unsafe administration, and the nurse integrates assessment, labs, vital signs, and clinical condition alongside the rights.

options.text: "Errors can occur at prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring."
options.rationale: Accurate. All six are points in the medication use process.

options.text: "After an error I assess the client before I notify anyone."
options.rationale: Accurate. Assessment establishes whether the client needs immediate protection.

options.text: "I ask a client to tell me how he will take it rather than whether he understands."
options.rationale: Accurate. Teach-back confirms understanding rather than agreement.

questions.takeaway: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. They check the order, not the client.
questions.strategy: This is the central claim of the whole lecture, and the wrong statement is exactly what students conclude from learning the rights.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the mistaken belief.
The rights verify the order against the record.
Error response, error points, and teach-back are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: matching the rights does not make a dose safe.

questions.topic: An order is not a substitute for judgment
questions.stem: A nurse receives an order she believes is inconsistent with the client's current condition. A colleague tells her the provider wrote it, so the responsibility is his. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The provider carries sole responsibility once the order is written
options.rationale: Prescribing and administering are separate acts and each carries its own accountability.

options.text: The nurse determines whether the order is complete, appropriate, safe, and in scope
options.rationale: An order does not transfer responsibility. The nurse who administers answers for the administration.

options.text: The nurse should administer the dose and document her concern afterward
options.rationale: Documents a concern about a dose she has already given.

options.text: The nurse may administer any order that is legible, complete, and signed
options.rationale: Legible and complete are two of six considerations, and appropriateness and safety are among the others.

questions.takeaway: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment. Check that it is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the condition, and within your scope.
questions.strategy: Six tests, and the two that catch most unsafe orders are appropriate and consistent with the client's condition. The other four can all be satisfied by an order that should not be given.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That the order transfers responsibility.
Each act carries its own accountability.
One stops at legibility, one acts before questioning.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: an order does not transfer responsibility.

questions.concept: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment. The nurse determines whether the order is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the client's condition, and within the nurse's scope.

questions.stem: A student tells the nurse she has learned the five traditional rights of medication administration and asks what the remaining rights cover. Which are among the additional rights? Select all that apply.

options.text: Right documentation
options.rationale: Covers what was given, when, and how the client responded.

options.text: Right reason
options.rationale: Why this client is receiving this drug, which is what makes the order make sense.

options.text: Right to refuse
options.rationale: The client's right, and it belongs to the client rather than the nurse.

options.text: Right prescriber
options.rationale: Verifying the prescriber's authority matters and is not one of the ten rights.

options.text: Right cost
options.rationale: Affordability affects adherence and is not one of the ten rights.

options.text: Right pharmacy
options.rationale: Where the drug was dispensed is not among the rights.

questions.takeaway: Ten rights: client, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response, education, and the right to refuse.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are real considerations that are not rights. The additional five describe what happens around the dose, plus one that belongs to the client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Recall the five beyond the traditional
steps.detail: Documentation, reason, response, education, refusal.
Prescriber authority and dispensing location.
Cost affects adherence rather than being a right.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.concept: The ten rights: right patient, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response, education, and the right to refuse.

questions.topic: When the order does not fit the client
questions.stem: An 82-year-old has a scheduled order for metoprolol 50 mg orally daily. At the time the dose is due his blood pressure is 88/52 and his apical rate is 54. The order is complete and all ten rights match. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Administer half of the ordered dose to reduce the effect on his heart rate
options.rationale: Altering a prescribed dose is outside nursing scope and improvises a decision that belongs to the prescriber.

options.text: Administer the dose, since all ten rights have been verified
options.rationale: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. Matching every right does not make a dose safe.

options.text: Document that the client refused the medication and notify the provider
options.rationale: The client has not refused. Recording a refusal that did not occur falsifies the record.

options.text: Hold the dose, notify the provider, and document the assessment
options.rationale: The right medication given to a client in the wrong condition is unsafe administration. Metoprolol lowers both blood pressure and heart rate, and both are already low.

questions.takeaway: Right medication plus wrong client condition equals unsafe administration. The ten rights do not replace assessment. The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. Right medication plus wrong client condition equals unsafe administration. The nurse integrates assessment, medication knowledge, labs, vital signs, clinical condition, provider orders, and nursing judgment.
questions.strategy: This is the scenario the whole lecture is built around. Every right can match and the dose can still be wrong, because the rights check the order rather than the client.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Both already low, and the drug lowers both further.
Rights verified does not equal safe.
One alters the dose, one falsifies the record.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: hold, notify, document.

questions.concept: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. Right medication plus wrong client condition equals unsafe administration. The nurse integrates assessment, medication knowledge, labs, vital signs, clinical condition, provider orders, and nursing judgment.

questions.stem: A quality committee maps every point in the medication use process where an error can occur, from the moment an order is written to the follow-up after a dose is given. Which set is correct?

options.text: Administering only, since that is the final step
options.rationale: The final step is where errors become visible, not where they all originate.

options.text: Prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring
options.rationale: Six points, and the nurse is involved in the last three as well as in verifying the first.

options.text: Dispensing and administering only, since those involve the pharmacy and nurse
options.rationale: Also incomplete.

options.text: Prescribing and administering only, since those are the two clinical decisions
options.rationale: Omits four points where errors regularly originate.

questions.takeaway: Errors occur at six points: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring. Medication errors can occur at six points: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring.
questions.strategy: Monitoring is the one people forget. An error can occur after the dose is given, by failing to watch for the response the drug required.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Six, from order to follow-up.
Each omits points where errors originate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: six points, and the nurse is involved in the last three as well as in verifying the first.

questions.concept: Medication errors can occur at six points: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old declines his scheduled antihypertensive, saying it makes him dizzy and he would rather manage without it today. He is alert and understands he has high blood pressure. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine why he is refusing
options.rationale: The reason is clinically useful and often solvable.

options.text: Assess his understanding of the medication
options.rationale: A refusal frequently reflects a gap in what he has been told.

options.text: Provide education and respect his right to refuse
options.rationale: The right to refuse is one of the ten rights.

options.text: Notify the provider when indicated and document according to policy
options.rationale: The prescriber needs to know, and the record needs the refusal and the reason.

options.text: Conceal the medication in food so the dose is not missed
options.rationale: Covert administration removes his decision entirely.

options.text: Document that the client is non-compliant
options.rationale: Automatically recording non-compliance labels a decision rather than describing it, and it discards the reason he gave.

questions.takeaway: Do not force, hide, shame, or automatically label. Determine why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right, notify, and document. If a client refuses: do not force the medication, hide it in food, shame the client, or automatically document non-compliant. Determine why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right to refuse, notify the provider when indicated, and document according to policy.
questions.strategy: Non-compliant is the entry to avoid. It converts a reason you could have acted on into a judgment about the client.

strategies: Client-centered option

steps.action: Read the four things not to do
steps.detail: Force, hide, shame, label.
One conceals, one labels.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: If a client refuses: do not force the medication, hide it in food, shame the client, or automatically document non-compliant. Determine why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right to refuse, notify the provider when indicated, and document according to policy.

questions.stem: A client taking an antihistamine for allergic rhinitis reports his sneezing and congestion have improved and that he feels drowsy every afternoon. Which terms describe these two outcomes?

options.text: Therapeutic effect and adverse effect
options.rationale: An adverse effect is harmful or unwanted. Expected drowsiness from an antihistamine is a side effect.

options.text: Adverse effect and toxic effect
options.rationale: Neither describes the symptom relief, which is what was intended.

options.text: Therapeutic effect and side effect
options.rationale: The therapeutic effect is the desired response. A side effect is an expected secondary effect.

options.text: Side effect and toxic effect
options.rationale: Symptom relief is the intended response rather than a side effect.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic is the desired response. Side effect is expected and secondary. Adverse is harmful. Toxic is excessive drug effect. Therapeutic effect is the desired response. A side effect is an expected secondary effect. An adverse effect is a harmful or unwanted response. A toxic effect is an excessive drug effect or toxicity.
questions.strategy: Side and adverse are the pair students blur. Expectedness separates them: a known secondary effect is a side effect, and a harmful unwanted response is adverse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Symptom relief is therapeutic.
An adverse effect is harmful or unwanted.
Symptom relief is the intended response rather than a side effect.
Neither describes the symptom relief, which is what was intended.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the therapeutic effect is the desired response.

questions.concept: Therapeutic effect is the desired response. A side effect is an expected secondary effect. An adverse effect is a harmful or unwanted response. A toxic effect is an excessive drug effect or toxicity.

skills.title: Personal Hygiene, Perineal Care, and Bedmaking
skills.subtitle: Bathing and CHG, oral and hair care, catheter care, enemas, and occupied and unoccupied beds

questions.stem: A nurse performs catheter care for a 78-year-old with an indwelling urinary catheter inserted three days ago. The meatus is intact with no discharge and the client reports no discomfort. In which direction does she clean the catheter?

options.text: From the drainage tubing back toward the meatus, in one continuous motion
options.rationale: Moves organisms along the catheter toward the urinary tract.

options.text: Only at the meatus itself, leaving the catheter surface untouched
options.rationale: The first few inches of catheter carry organisms toward the meatus and are cleaned.

options.text: From the meatus outward for about four inches, without pulling or creating friction
options.rationale: Cleaning away from the meatus moves organisms away from the entry point rather than toward it, which is the cleanest-to-dirtiest principle applied to this site.

options.text: In a back-and-forth motion along the length of the catheter
options.rationale: Returns the cloth to the meatus after it has been soiled, and the friction irritates the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Clean from the meatus outward for about four inches. Cleanest to dirtiest, always moving away from the entry point. Catheter care: assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort, perform perineal hygiene with 2% chlorhexidine cloth or mild soap and warm water, and clean the catheter from the meatus outward for about four inches without pulling or friction.
questions.strategy: The whole of hygiene runs on one principle: cleanest to dirtiest. Catheter care is that principle applied to the shortest route into the bladder.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cleanest to dirtiest means away from the meatus.
Both return organisms toward the meatus.
The proximal catheter is cleaned too.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: cleaning away from the meatus moves organisms away from the entry point rather than toward it, which is the cleanest-to-dirtiest principle applied to this site.

questions.concept: Catheter care: assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort, perform perineal hygiene with 2% chlorhexidine cloth or mild soap and warm water, and clean the catheter from the meatus outward for about four inches without pulling or friction.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a bed bath to an 82-year-old who tires quickly and has fragile skin over her shoulders and sacrum. She has been in bed for four days and her daughter is visiting. Which principles apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use lukewarm water and mild cleansers to prevent irritation
options.rationale: Hot water and harsh cleansers dry and damage skin.

options.text: Avoid excessive force and friction
options.rationale: Both damage skin that is already fragile in a dependent client.

options.text: Bathe the client at the same time each day regardless of tolerance
options.rationale: Timing is matched to the client rather than to the routine.

options.text: Encourage normal range of motion during bathing
options.rationale: Movement that would otherwise require a separate intervention.

options.text: Use hot water to improve circulation during the bath
options.rationale: Lukewarm water is used. Hot water damages fragile skin and is unsafe.

options.text: Complete a full bath daily regardless of the client's tolerance
options.rationale: Contradicts the guidance on partial bathing and prioritizes the routine over the client.

questions.takeaway: Lukewarm water, mild cleanser, minimal friction, assess while you bathe, encourage movement, and match the bath to the client's tolerance. Bathing principles: clean skin when soiled and at regular intervals, use lukewarm water and mild cleansers, avoid excessive force and friction, minimize factors that dry the skin, use the bath to interact with and assess the client, encourage range of motion, and consider a partial bath for a client who fatigues easily.
questions.strategy: Three separate things happen during a bath: hygiene, skin assessment, and range of motion. That is why it is worth doing well rather than quickly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Tires quickly.
A full bath regardless of tolerance ignores what the stem tells you.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Bathing principles: clean skin when soiled and at regular intervals, use lukewarm water and mild cleansers, avoid excessive force and friction, minimize factors that dry the skin, use the bath to interact with and assess the client, encourage range of motion, and consider a partial bath for a client who fatigues easily.

questions.stem: A client is being transferred from the emergency department by stretcher after a fall and will arrive on the unit within the hour. The bed is empty and the linen has been changed. How does the nurse prepare the bed?

options.text: As an open bed, with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in
options.rationale: An open bed is prepared for immediate use, and fanfolding the linen allows transfer from a stretcher without fighting tucked bedding.

options.text: As a closed bed, with the top sheets pulled up to the head of the bed
options.rationale: A closed bed is usually made by housekeeping after discharge and is not prepared for an arriving client.

options.text: As an occupied bed, with the client already lying in it
options.rationale: An occupied bed is made with a client already in it.
